papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) enable robots to reason about semantic and spatio-temporal context, verify task-relevant objects, and guide sensing and navigation. Persistent memory can reduce redundant search for field robots, but when should a memory continue to guide behavior? Repeated misses may suggest that a memory is stale. Our experiments show why this evidence can remain ambiguous under VLM-based perception. Using a Boston Dynamics Spot with four fixed cameras and a persistent spatio-temporal visual memory, we measure negative-verification behavior across targets, viewpoints, language queries, and repeated revisits. False-negative rates vary substantially across objects, nearby revisits often reproduce the same detector outcome, and some matched target-present and target-removed experiments yield identical miss histories. This ambiguity persists under changed observation geometry, identity-preserving query reformulation, and conditioning on a previously verified target image. These findings raise two questions: is the object still there, and is this memory still useful for navigation? We introduce a dependence-aware, reversible memory-update mechanism that avoids double-counting correlated misses and stops using unsupported memories as direct navigation goals without claiming that the object is absent. Later positive evidence can restore a memory's use for navigation. One resident onboard VLM is shared across memory verification, semantic frontier reasoning, and in-motion perception. In three matched real-robot decision contexts, an episode-local baseline selected a stale memory as its navigation objective in every case, whereas our method selected semantic frontiers in all three. A complementary trial re-verified the target during motion and promoted fresh memory. These results support revising memory actionability rather than interpreting failed detection as object absence.
authors: Sumukh Shrote, Shenbagaraj Kannapiran, Eric Eaton, Camillo Jose Taylor
bullets: VLM-based negative detections are ambiguous: false-negative rates vary, repeated nearby views can reproduce misses, and target-present and target-removed scenes may look identical.
The proposed dependence-aware, reversible updates avoid double-counting correlated misses and stop unsupported memories from serving as direct navigation goals.
Semantic frontiers become alternatives when memory confidence is insufficient; later positive evidence can restore navigation use.
On a Spot robot in three matched decision contexts, the baseline chose a stale memory every time, while the proposed method chose semantic frontiers in all three.
A motion-time recheck demonstrated that fresh positive evidence can promote memory again.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Persistent semantic-navigation system architecture. The robot combines four fixed cameras, persistent CLIP/FAISS visual memory, semantic frontier exploration, and a shared resident VLM. Historical observations are retrieved and strictly reverified before they can influence navigation. Negative evidence updates memory actionability from VERIFIED ACTIVE to SUSPECT and eventually DORMANT UNTRUSTED, while later strict positive evidence can restore navigation authority. When no trusted memory remains, the system selects a semantic frontier instead. A single resident Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct instance is shared across target verification, memory verification, frontier reasoning, and asynchronous perception during motion.

Fig. 1. Memory is not ground truth. A previously verified object can fail current VLM verification either because the environment has changed or because perception has failed. An episode-local policy forgets earlier failed verification and can repeatedly revisit the same remembered location. Our method instead revises the memory’s navigation authority without asserting that the object is absent, redirects search toward a semantically selected frontier, and preserves the memory for future positive evidence. The inset in (c) shows frontier candidates in the deployed 2-D navigation representation.

Fig. 3. Repeated VLM misses are redundant and can be ambiguous with respect to physical object state. In E2, Spot repeatedly leaves and returns to human-visible target viewpoints; nearby revisits frequently preserve the previous verifier outcome, with 90.0% of adjacent observations producing the same result. In E3, the corresponding objects are physically removed and the same anchor regions are revisited. For the three blue-chair anchors C1-C3, both target-present and target-removed conditions produce the identical six-observation history MMMMMM. Thus, the deployed detector observations alone cannot distinguish the two physical states.

papers.selection_reason: Persistent spatio-temporal memory for semantic navigation with VLM-based verification, fitting embodied memory and vision-language navigation.
papers.title: Memory Is Not Ground Truth: Revising Navigation Authority under Unreliable VLM Evidence for Persistent Semantic Navigation
papers.tldr: Robots should reduce a memory’s navigation authority after correlated detection failures without assuming the remembered object is absent.

papers.abstract: Cross-modal place recognition (CMPR) matches natural language descriptions against databases of geo-tagged reference images, enabling localization without visual queries. Despite its potential for language-guided navigation, existing vision-language models lag far behind visual place recognition (VPR) baselines, even after task adaptation. Unlike general-purpose text-to-image retrieval, place recognition relies on subtle local cues to distinguish visually similar locations. We therefore hypothesize that a primary bottleneck in CMPR is capturing fine-grained correspondences between image regions and text details, which requires higher visual token granularity, strong text representation capacity, and local cross-modal matching. To address this challenge, we propose CrossPlace, a two-stage CMPR framework. Stage 1 performs global retrieval by pairing a jointly aligned DINOv2-B/14 visual backbone with a progressively fine-tuned BGE-Large text encoder, while Stage 2 refines top candidates using a lightweight token-level cross-attention reranker. Through systematic analysis, we isolate the drivers of retrieval accuracy and show that visual token density provides the largest performance improvement, while text encoder capacity and task fine-tuning offer complementary gains. To evaluate robustness under realistic conditions, we also extend CMPR evaluation to city-scale and severe weather and illumination settings. Across all existing and new benchmarks, CrossPlace achieves double-digit Recall@1 improvements over prior cross-modal methods, closes the gap to unimodal text retrieval, and narrows it to unimodal VPR. Code and benchmarks are available at https://github.com/oferidan1/CrossPlace
authors: Ofer Idan, Dan Badur, Yoli Shavit
bullets: CMPR matches natural-language descriptions to geo-tagged reference images, but trails visual place recognition because subtle local details are difficult to align.
A two-stage pipeline first performs global retrieval with DINOv2-B/14 and a fine-tuned BGE-Large text encoder, then reranks candidates with lightweight token-level cross-attention.
Analysis identifies visual token density as the largest accuracy driver, with text capacity and task fine-tuning providing complementary gains.
Evaluation includes existing benchmarks plus city-scale and severe weather/illumination conditions.
CrossPlace reports double-digit Recall@1 gains over prior cross-modal methods and narrows the gap to unimodal VPR.

papers.title: Towards Closing the Performance Gap in Cross-Modal Place Recognition
papers.tldr: CrossPlace improves cross-modal place recognition by combining high-resolution visual tokens, a stronger text encoder, and token-level reranking to better match fine-grained image–text cues.

papers.abstract: Dexterous mobile manipulation is essential for robots to perform useful tasks in complex, unstructured environments. However, existing systems face two challenges. First, navigation remains too coarse for downstream manipulation, which often requires a precise base position and approach orientation rather than merely reaching a meter-scale goal region. Second, navigation and manipulation are commonly trained in isolation, lacking a feedback loop that enables the two capabilities to co-evolve. These limitations prevent current systems from reliably executing long-horizon dexterous mobile-manipulation tasks in real-world environments. To address them, we introduce Nav4Manip, a bidirectionally coupled co-evolution system for long-horizon dexterous mobile manipulation. It comprises two complementary architectures: Nav4Manip-N learns long-horizon navigation and refines its policy through manipulation feedback, while Nav4Manip-M trains a world-action model (WAM) for downstream dexterous manipulation. We train Nav4Manip-N in three stages: multi-task co-tuning learns navigation behavior and manipulation-aware affordance prediction; rejection sampling fine-tuning (RFT) rejects low-quality policy-generated paths and fine-tunes the model on retained trajectories; and reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF) uses counterfactual preferences to further improve navigation decisions. To support this framework, we establish the Nav-N-Manip benchmark and construct Nav4Manip-Pairs from benchmark rollouts, providing large-scale paired navigation--manipulation trajectories and affordance supervision. Extensive experiments on public vision-language navigation (VLN) benchmarks and Nav-N-Manip demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, while real-world evaluations show that Nav4Manip completes diverse dexterous mobile-manipulation tasks. Project website: https://nav4manip.github.io/.
authors: Yusen Feng, Zixi Kang, Zhijun Yin, Changxiao Liu, Tianhong Gao, Jiazhao Zhang, Jiahang Liu, Libin Liu, Zhizheng Zhang, He Wang
bullets: Targets navigation that must achieve manipulation-ready base positions and orientations, not just coarse goal regions.
Uses two coupled components: Nav4Manip-N for manipulation-aware navigation and Nav4Manip-M with a world-action model for dexterous manipulation.
Trains navigation through multi-task co-tuning, rejection-sampling fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning from AI feedback.
Introduces the Nav-N-Manip benchmark and paired navigation–manipulation trajectories with affordance supervision.
Reports state-of-the-art results on public VLN benchmarks and Nav-N-Manip, plus successful real-world task execution.

papers.abstract: Instruction-following robots need navigation policies that reach high accuracy and remain inexpensive to train and to run on a single graphics processing unit (GPU). The most accurate vision-language navigation policies for continuous environments rely on language models with 4 to 8 billion parameters, long observation histories, and large auxiliary corpora. Two properties of the standard training setup limit smaller policies. Imitation labels cover the states that an expert visits, whereas the running policy reaches states that its own errors produce. In addition, an image-plane waypoint exists only while the route lies inside the camera view. We present \textbf{\paper}, a monocular red-green-blue (RGB) policy with 2 billion (2B) parameters that addresses both limitations. \paper adapts Qwen3-VL-2B with low-rank adapters and processes an eight-frame memory and the current view in one forward pass. The policy predicts the route direction as a bearing in the body frame of the agent, which remains defined for every heading, and a deterministic controller converts this bearing into motion. This design allows training to relabel the states that the policy itself visits. On-policy correction improves success, while bearing decoding outperforms image-plane waypoint scanning across all evaluated start headings with identical weights. On the \valunseen split, \paper achieves \rFinSR\% success on Room-to-Room in Continuous Environments (\rtor), averaged over three seeds, and \rRxFinSR\% on its Room-Across-Room counterpart (\rxr). Inference requires \rDecMs\,ms and \rInferGB\,GiB of memory, while training takes \rCostTrainTyp\ GPU-hours on one 12\,GB consumer GPU.
authors: Reshad Ul Karim, Syeda Maliha Tabassum, Md. Khalilur Rhaman, Md Rashad Al Hasan Rony
bullets: Targets accurate, low-cost instruction-following navigation for robots in continuous environments.
Uses Qwen3-VL-2B with low-rank adapters, an eight-frame memory, and the current RGB view in one forward pass.
Predicts route direction as a body-frame bearing, which remains defined even when the route is outside the camera view.
On-policy training relabels states induced by the policy’s own errors and improves success; bearing decoding outperforms image-plane waypoint scanning across start headings.
Evaluated on R2CE and RxR-CE unseen splits, with reported inference and training costs on a single 12 GB GPU.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of AlphaNav. The instruction ℓ, an eight-frame memory M , and the current frame enter a Qwen3-VL-2B backbone with LoRA adapters as 192 visual tokens. papers.abstract: Recent advances in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have improved semantic and visual reasoning, enabling UAVs to search for open-vocabulary queries in unstructured environments at high altitude. However, existing systems mainly follow low-altitude strategies, focusing on close-range iterative exploration, requiring storage-intensive dense 3D metric-semantic reconstructions or relying on large cloud-serviced VLMs assuming constant internet access. We propose SkySearcher, an aerial semantic search navigation method designed for large outdoor scenes. SkySearcher integrates onboard VLM reasoning with a lightweight probabilistic representation that guides an information-driven exploration. The VLM extracts semantic information at high altitude about the target or cues informing about its location. This information is projected to the ground using the camera frustum instead of limited-depth sensors, actively exploiting the expansive field of view offered by elevated sensing. The information regarding the presence or absence of semantic cues is then integrated into a probabilistic map by modeling the spatial belief of the query, maintaining a task-driven memory for the mission and guiding the exploration towards semantically promising regions. Extensive simulations for Aerial Object Goal Navigation on public benchmarks demonstrate that SkySearcher significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in success rate, flight time, and navigation precision, while a deployment of SkySercher running fully onboard a drone demonstrates the applicability of our approach.
authors: Giacomo Vianello, David Morilla-Cabello, Juan Dendarieta Serrano, Ruggero Carli, Eduardo Montijano
bullets: Targets large outdoor scenes without dense 3D reconstructions or continuous cloud connectivity.
Uses high-altitude VLM observations to identify targets or location-relevant semantic cues.
Projects semantic information onto the ground through the camera frustum, leveraging the wide elevated field of view.
Maintains a probabilistic query-belief map and task-driven memory to guide information-driven exploration.
Simulations report improved success rate, flight time, and navigation precision over baselines; onboard drone deployment demonstrates feasibility.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. System Overview. A ground-station LLM parses the user query Q into the target, semantic cues, and their expected co-occurrence distance, and variability. Onboard, the drone maintains a geometric coverage map and a probabilistic semantic map, while a compact VLM detects and verifies the target and cues in the RGB stream. NBV optimization fuses this geometric and semantic evidence to select the next viewpoint, until visual servoing approaches the target detection and confirms (or rejects) it.

Then, it prioritizes exploring the region around the cue (3) until finding the target and performing a final approach (4,5).

papers.abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) with general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offers a flexible alternative to task-specific navigation policies, while reliable long-horizon execution remains challenging. Agents must track navigation progress, detect discrepancies between commanded and actual motion, and recognize when movement has passed relevant landmarks or entrances. We present Navigent, an agentic VLN framework built around a frozen MLLM and a Geometry-Grounded Execution Critic (GEC). GEC performs two complementary checks: action-to-motion consistency, which evaluates measured displacement against commanded movement, and motion-to-landmark consistency, which tracks agent-selected visual anchors and entrance candidates in world coordinates. Detected discrepancies interrupt the remaining action sequence and trigger reobservation, local adjustment, or node-based recovery. Historical visual memory supports progress tracking across extended routes. An offline self-improvement procedure further analyzes successful and failed training trajectories to refine navigation prompts and GEC logic while keeping model weights fixed. On the R2R-CE validation-unseen split (1,839 episodes) and RxR-CE validation-unseen split(3,669 episodes), Navigent achieves 84.0%/86.0% SR and 72.9%/69.1% SPL, respectively, demonstrating the value of geometry-grounded execution verification for reliable agentic navigation. Uses a frozen multimodal large language model with a Geometry-Grounded Execution Critic (GEC).
GEC checks action-to-motion consistency and motion-to-landmark consistency using visual anchors and entrance candidates in world coordinates.
Detected discrepancies trigger reobservation, local adjustment, or node-based recovery; historical visual memory tracks progress.

papers.abstract: Open-world aerial object search methods often rely on persistent spatial maps, learned world models, or task-specific policy training. To examine how far a minimal, training-free design can go, we introduce SimpleUAV, an agent built around a frozen, off-the-shelf vision-language model (VLM). SimpleUAV separates current-view target assessment from history-conditioned action selection, combining fresh candidate evidence with lightweight search context. Local geometry converts visual selections into bounded straight-line movements, depth-based checks halt blocked segments, and measured execution feedback guides subsequent decisions. This closed loop sustains search without persistent spatial maps or task-specific training. SimpleUAV achieves 41.61% Success Rate (SR) on UAV-ON and 11.98% on AerialDojo-200K, compared with 23.80% and 3.20% for the strongest prior baselines, respectively. With limited benchmark-specific adaptation, the same core agent transfers to aerial Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) on TravelUAV, improving Full SR by at least 19.66% across all three splits under L1 assistance. These results establish a strong baseline for evaluating when additional architectural complexity benefits aerial search.
authors: Jitai Hao, Liangxing Yang, Zhenyang Li, Fan Liu, Qiang Huang, Jun Yu
bullets: Addresses whether a minimal, training-free agent can handle open-world aerial search.
Separates current-view target assessment from history-conditioned action selection.
Uses local geometry, depth checks, and execution feedback to produce bounded movements and avoid blocked paths.
Achieves 41.61% SR on UAV-ON and 11.98% on AerialDojo-200K, outperforming reported prior baselines.
Transfers to aerial VLN on TravelUAV, improving Full SR by at least 19.66% across three splits with L1 assistance.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Architecture of SimpleUAV. Given a language goal and four RGB-D views (front, left, right, and downward), SimpleUAV executes three stages without persistent maps or task-specific training. (1) Select (Section 3.2): A frozen VLM detects candidate boxes (ℬ𝑡 ) from current RGB views. Depth and camera calibration provide 3D candidate locations to construct (𝒞𝑡 ), and a second VLM query selects an action (𝑎𝑡 ) using this catalog and lightweight interaction history. (2) Fly Straight (Section 3.3): The selected region or candidate determines a 3D waypoint (𝑤𝑡 ) for exploration (Exploreℎ , Explore𝑣) or Approach, and the UAV moves from 𝒙𝑡 along a bounded straightline segment. (3) Check & Halt (Section 3.4): Throughout motion, local depth checks test upcoming segments using a 3D safety capsule and halt the current segment when an obstacle is detected. Execution feedback guides the next observation and decision cycle.

papers.abstract: When the lead robot cannot continue, what should it send the teammate that must finish the route? We replay a frozen receiver at each contact under alternative messages. Across 3,920 autonomous departures in 106 environments, adding the view before the lead's last action block to its executed actions raised success by 7.51 percentage points (pp) per RxR handoff and 8.54 pp per SAGE handoff. Per departure the gains were 2.23 and 1.44 pp, respectively. The lead continuing in simulation defines the empirical full-history ceiling (Solo). At contact, the lead had accumulated a median of 41 frames. Sending one frame when available recovered 24% of the full-history advantage over actions alone in SAGE and 30% in RxR. Over an estimated progress cue in SAGE, the image rescued 100 routes and reversed 54 successes. Near-goal receivers finished outside less often (63.1% to 51.7%, post hoc). In secondary comparisons the earlier view outperformed the contact view by 6-7 pp per handoff. Exact-route specificity and image gains at controlled starts with mostly unknown progress or outside the goal region remained unresolved. Gains were detectable from about 7 kB per handoff. Random transmission matched within size bins nearly equaled the learned sender's team success. At a required handoff, a view of the approach to the last maneuver helps the receiver finish.

papers.abstract: Embodied Spatial Reasoning (ESR) is central to deploying Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in real-world embodied tasks, yet remains inadequately evaluated. Existing benchmarks primarily assess spatial reasoning in static images or synthetic indoor environments, where semantic shortcuts often suffice, making it difficult to faithfully evaluate spatial reasoning capabilities in the wild. In light of this, we present Lost on Campus, a benchmark for evaluating ESR in large-scale real-world outdoor 3D environments reconstructed by 3D Gaussian Splatting. Our benchmark introduces a unified reasoning-action evaluation framework that seamlessly integrates diagnostic QA for isolated reasoning with closed-loop interactive navigation for active reasoning under multimodal instructions. To enable fine-grained diagnosis, we evaluate six capability aspects of ESR: action grounding, spatial foresight, metric awareness, goal-directed planning, ego-allocentric localization, and spatio-temporal consistency. Extensive experiments reveal that: (i) Compared to indoor settings, real-world outdoor environments impose substantially higher demands on spatial reasoning, where existing models exhibit poor performance; (ii) VLMs still struggle with fine-grained visual alignment, with failures in spatial foresight and ego-allocentric localization emerging as primary bottlenecks; (iii) Improving multimodal interaction capabilities and long-term spatial reasoning is crucial for advancing embodied intelligence. These findings highlight that faithful evaluation of ESR demands benchmarks tightly coupling perception, reasoning and action within realistic and continuous environments.
authors: Zehan Zheng, Yanyuan Chen, Deming Li, Yutao Tang, Jianwen Xie, Alan Yuille, Jieneng Chen, Cheng Peng
bullets: Evaluates VLMs in large-scale real-world outdoor 3D environments reconstructed with 3D Gaussian Splatting.

papers.abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) delivery is an important application of the low-altitude economy, enhancing the flexibility and accessibility of last-mile logistics. Existing UAV delivery methods generally rely on precise terminal coordinates, predefined terminal specifications, or task-specific localization procedures, limiting the scope and flexibility of delivery. As UAV logistics becomes more intelligent, open-ended semantic descriptions offer a new paradigm for specifying terminal destinations. However, conventional aerial navigation methods have limited ability to generalize to delivery scenarios that require open-vocabulary terminal navigation. To enable this broader delivery paradigm, we propose CoFiNav, a VLM-guided coarse-to-fine UAV semantic navigation framework that progressively grounds relation-defined terminal destinations through hierarchical semantic search and active 3D observation. Given a task description, a coarse prior map from OpenStreetMap (OSM), and accumulated observations, CoFiNav uses a vision-language model (VLM) to determine which unresolved entity or spatial relation should be verified next. A geometry-aware module converts the semantic observation request into feasible viewpoints using RGB images and LiDAR, while conventional motion planning handles safe execution. Experiments across multiple urban environments show that CoFiNav outperforms representative adapted baselines in success rate while requiring shorter flight paths and fewer observations.

bullets: Addresses the limitations of delivery systems requiring precise coordinates, fixed terminal specifications, or task-specific localization.

papers.abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires an agent to follow language instructions to reach a target in an unseen 3D environment. However, existing methods still struggle to recover from route deviations at test time. We investigate this limitation through the lens of instruction progress, and trace it to a phenomenon we term progress hallucination: agents misinterpret off-route observations as evidence of task progress, causing their internal instruction progress to advance beyond the actual task stage and hindering recovery based on earlier sub-instructions. To address this failure mode, we propose PHAR (Progress Hallucination-Aware Recovery), a test-time recovery framework following a verify-then-steer paradigm. The verifier examines residual-stream representations of the Vision-Language Model (VLM) to identify mismatch of cross-modal evidence along the trajectories, and uses split conformal calibration to control false alarms. When an alarm is raised, the steering module uses a contextual bandit to adaptively select the rewind extent of instruction progress for online recovery. Through extensive experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, our framework enhances the reliability of multiple state-of-the-art vision-language navigation methods at test time.
authors: Jiewen Hou, Guanxiang Qi, Meina Kan, Shiguang Shan, Xilin Chen
bullets: Problem: VLN agents may mistake off-route observations for progress, advancing their internal instruction stage and making recovery difficult.
Method: A verifier detects cross-modal evidence mismatches in VLM residual representations and uses split conformal calibration to control false alarms.
Recovery: When a mismatch is detected, a contextual bandit selects how far to rewind instruction progress before steering onward.
Evaluation: Experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE show improved reliability across multiple state-of-the-art VLN methods at test time.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) requires an embodied agent to relate past experience, current spatial state, and future motion while following natural-language instructions. Recent approaches improve these capabilities through long-horizon memory, state-aware reasoning, and future prediction, yet these components are often modeled separately, leaving navigation state evolution insufficiently connected across time. We argue that camera pose provides a natural geometric representation for bridging past, present, and future states. Based on this insight, we propose PoseVLN, a pose-aware VLN framework that jointly learns navigation decisions and geometric state evolution. PoseVLN organizes visual memory and the current observation in an episode-relative coordinate frame, and jointly predicts the next K navigation actions together with a local $\Delta$Pose over the same horizon. The predicted $\Delta$Pose is composed with the current trajectory-level pose to obtain the future pose state, which is recursively propagated throughout navigation, forming a continuous geometric state evolution from past memory to future motion. Experiments on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE Val-Unseen splits demonstrate the effectiveness of explicitly modeling geometric state evolution, with PoseVLN outperforming the strongest compared baselines by 2.6 and 2.9 percentage points in success rate, respectively, using only single RGB observations.
authors: Pengyu Hou, Mingfei Han, Haihong Hao, Xiaolong Wu, Bo Dong, Xiaojun Chang, Salman Khan, Bin Shi
bullets: Addresses the weak connection between navigation memory, current state, and future motion in existing VLN systems.
Represents visual memory and observations in an episode-relative coordinate frame.
Jointly predicts the next K actions and local pose changes, recursively propagating future pose states during navigation.
Achieves gains of 2.6 and 2.9 success-rate points over the strongest compared baselines on R2R-CE and RxR-CE Val-Unseen, using single RGB observations.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have become strong policies for vision-and-language navigation (VLN). However, most of them encode a sample of past frames again at every decision and are trained on isolated decisions, so computation is redundant and the usable history is short. They also learn from their own mistakes through outcome rewards that give one scalar to a whole episode. We ask whether a navigator can encode each frame only once, at a constant cost per step, and still remember what matters and learn efficiently from its mistakes. We present GlanceNav, a streaming navigator built on a hybrid MLLM. Its Gated DeltaNet layers carry a recurrent state through the whole episode, while its attention layers keep a short window of recent observations and a small bank of keyframes, selected by how much each frame changes the recurrent state. This constant-size memory keeps the cost per step fixed and allows training on whole episodes with the same memory as at inference. Because the entire memory can also be copied in constant time, we further propose Counterfactual Rewind (CoRe), a reinforcement learning stage that rewinds a drifting rollout to its closest approach to the goal, lets an expert correct a few actions, and credits decisions by the resulting change in outcome. Trained only on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE training splits, with 1,000 instructions for reinforcement learning, a 4B GlanceNav reaches success rates of 71.9% and 73.6% on R2R-CE and RxR-CE val-unseen. On R2R-CE, it outperforms the strongest previous single-RGB method trained without external data by 9.1 points, while running at 104 ms per step.
bullets: Addresses redundant re-encoding, short usable history, and coarse episode-level reward signals in MLLM-based navigation.
Uses recurrent Gated DeltaNet state plus a short recent-frame window and keyframes selected by their impact on the recurrent state.
Maintains constant-size memory, enabling fixed computation per step and whole-episode training with inference-level memory use.
Introduces Counterfactual Rewind, which revisits a rollout near its closest goal approach, applies expert corrections, and credits actions by outcome change.
Reports 71.9% success on R2R-CE and 73.6% on RxR-CE val-unseen; runs at 104 ms per step and improves prior single-RGB performance by 9.1 points on R2R-CE.

papers.abstract: We introduce Audio-Visual Rearrangement (AVR), a novel task in which an agent hears a spoken request, retrieves a suitable object, and delivers it to the requesting user or an instruction-specified destination. AVR requires the agent to understand the spoken request and acoustically localize the speaker for delivery. To support this task, we construct a dataset covering three query types: explicit target specification, speaker-relative spatial references, and implicit user intent, spanning eight subtypes with diverse object selection and delivery requirements. Moreover, we propose a framework that integrates a motion-aware spatial audio module into an audio-visual large language model to encode spatial cues from the spoken request and update them as the agent moves. We further incorporate auxiliary supervision for speech understanding, spatial audio perception, and visual grounding through multitask instruction tuning to improve action prediction. Experiments establish baseline performance in both seen and unseen environments, laying the groundwork for future research on embodied intelligence and human-robot interaction. The code will be publicly available soon.
authors: Ruohao Guo, Jiatong Ye, Chenwei Dong, Jinxing Zhou, Dantong Niu, Guangyao Li, Zhenbo Li
bullets: Defines a task combining speech understanding, object retrieval, speaker localization, and delivery.

papers.abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires timely decisions based on instructions and visual observations. However, autoregressive VLN models generate action descriptions token by token, introducing substantial inference overhead. Decision models offer an efficient alternative but face challenges in maintaining short-horizon action coherence and long-horizon goal alignment. To address these challenges, we propose NavDecision, an efficient multi-step VLN decision model. We introduce parallel multi-step action prediction (PMAP) to predict multiple action distributions from a shared vision-language state, and memory-augmented self-referential policy optimization (M-SRPO) to learn from unsuccessful trajectories using successful trajectories as references. A cross-iteration success memory further accumulates historical successful trajectories to provide informative training feedback. NavDecision achieves success rates of 64.60% on R2R-CE and 64.57% on RxR-CE with a 4B backbone. Compared with existing autoregressive VLN methods, it delivers significant inference speedups of up to $22.28\times$ and $18.96\times$ while maintaining comparable navigation performance.
authors: Kai Wu, Yufan Hu, Quan Fang, Boning Zhang, Junyu Gao
bullets: Targets autoregressive VLN inference overhead and difficulties with short- and long-horizon decision coherence.
Uses parallel multi-step action prediction (PMAP) to generate multiple action distributions from one shared vision-language state.

Reports 64.60% success on R2R-CE and 64.57% on RxR-CE with a 4B backbone.
Achieves up to 22.28× and 18.96× inference speedups over autoregressive VLN methods while maintaining comparable navigation performance.

papers.abstract: Gigapixel whole-slide images (WSIs) exceed single-pass vision-language model (VLM) capacity at cellular resolution, while multiple instance learning relies on query-agnostic offline patching without interactive reasoning. Multi-step VLM navigation agents inspect regions on demand, yet face two bottlenecks: (1) autoregressive action decoding incurs heavy latency, throttling exploration and online multi-trajectory RL; and (2) offline distillation suffers from an existential-versus-universal stopping asymmetry between positive detection and negative exclusion, inducing thumbnail and kinematic shortcuts while leaving policies prone to passing metastases without stopping. Under the Jev (System One) paradigm, a model predicts distributions over predefined decision spaces in one forward pass (0 generated tokens) while deterministic code executes navigation. We build JevNavAgent, a 2B-parameter agent combining factorized stopping, spatial-candidate, and contextual-bilinear answer heads with overview modality dropout. We pair Stage-1 offline counterfactual trajectory alignment (mitigating depth and panning shortcuts) with Stage-2 online trajectory-level GRPO (Traj-GRPO), using decoding-free rollouts to optimize branch-level lesion discovery, in-polygon stopping, and step-wise confidence gain. On Clean Visual WSI-VQA, JevNavAgent achieves 51.57% multi-scale (50.43% terminal-step) overall and 51.39% focal accuracy, outperforming frontier VLM agents and 4B-11B open-source cascades while running nearly 12x faster than frontier APIs (5.63s vs. 66.64-70.04s). On CAMELYON16 Official Test, Traj-GRPO reaches 22.45% localization (converting 11/12, or 91.7%, of visited tumors into grounded stops) with 93.75% specificity and 69.77% slide accuracy, surpassing Stage-1 SFT under matched stopping rules alongside zero-shot budget scaling.

papers.abstract: Mobile embodied agents continuously alter their observations through their own motion, while external dynamics further shape future interactions. Different mobile embodied tasks therefore capture complementary patterns of state evolution, yet jointly learning world dynamics across such interactions remains less explored. We investigate this problem through Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) and Embodied Visual Tracking (EVT), which respectively involve navigation toward a stationary goal and interaction with a moving target. We propose WorldWeave, a cross-task world model that couples shared predictive dynamics with task-specific adaptation. Instead of conditioning state transitions on heterogeneous physical actions, WorldWeave learns latent actions from observed state changes via inverse-forward dynamics, establishing a shared transition representation across tasks. The resulting future-state predictions are adaptively integrated into task-specific representations for downstream decision making. Experiments across multiple VLN and EVT benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over specialized baselines.
authors: Xuan Yao, Jiahao Zhang, Rongjunchen Zhang, Kaixuan Huang, Junyu Gao, Changsheng Xu
bullets: Addresses underexplored cross-task world modeling for embodied agents whose actions and environments continually change future observations.
Uses inverse-forward dynamics to learn latent actions and a shared transition representation instead of relying on heterogeneous physical actions.
Combines shared predictive dynamics with task-specific adaptation for downstream navigation and tracking decisions.
Evaluations across multiple VLN and EVT benchmarks show consistent improvements over specialized baselines.

papers.abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) have enabled vision-and-language navigation (VLN) through direct closed-loop perception and action. However, navigation performance depends strongly on the harness governing LLM-environment interactions, while existing harnesses largely rely on manually designed navigation tools, memory, and agent roles. We introduce NavRSI, a harness-centric recursive self-improvement framework that optimizes the navigation behavior of frozen LLMs through closed-loop experience. In each round, NavRSI iteratively collects navigation trajectories and failure diagnostics, employs a designer agent to rewrite the harness, and retains the revisions that prove effective, while the designer accumulates experience from previous revisions so that the harness and this experience co-evolve. Privileged simulator diagnostics guide only the designer and remain inaccessible to the navigating LLM, enabling deployment with a single RGB camera and primitive actions, without task-specific model training or additional navigation tools. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements across LLMs from four vendors, with 85.64% success rate on the full R2R-CE val-unseen split with GPT-6-Astra, surpassing the previously reported best by 4.13%. Evaluations on RxR-CE, NavRAG-CE, and a real humanoid robot further demonstrate its generalizability.
authors: Guangzhao Dai, Guoxin Lian, Shuo Wang, Shengbin Yue, Qianru Sun, Xiangbo Shu, Bin Zhu

Collects navigation trajectories and failure diagnostics, then uses a designer agent to revise and retain effective harnesses across iterations.

Reports consistent gains across LLMs from four vendors, including an 85.64% success rate on R2R-CE val-unseen with GPT-6-Astra.
Shows generalization to RxR-CE, NavRAG-CE, and a real humanoid robot.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Navigation(VLN) requires an embodied agent to follow language instructions through unseen 3D environments, where the target spaces often lie beyond the current observation. Navigation world models address this challenge by predicting future views either as pixels or latent representations, providing valuable look-ahead information for action decision. Both paradigms define the future primarily through what the agent may observe, raising a fundamental question: is predicting future views the ultimate form to represent the future for VLN? Cognitive studies show that the human hippocampus prospectively represents both future goals and intervening locations along planned routes. Inspired by this predictive-map view, we organize the navigation-relevant future around goal-directed spatial states and route structure. We instantiate this perspective with two complementary abstractions: a short-horizon waypoint that specifies the next local state to reach, and a mid-horizon corridor that captures the spatial support of the upcoming route. Based on this design, we propose FS-Nav, a future-state world modeling framework that predicts waypoint-corridor states from spatial memory and language instructions, and communicates them to a VLM navigator through top-down and first-person interfaces. Experiments on standard VLN benchmarks demonstrate that FS-Nav achieves state-of-the-art performance. This highlights navigation-relevant future-state modeling as a promising direction for representing the future in VLN.

Experiments on standard VLN benchmarks show state-of-the-art performance, though the abstract provides no further experimental details.

papers.abstract: Cloud--edge deployment enables asynchronous dual-system VLN on resource-constrained robots, but inference and communication delays cause latent mismatch and navigation errors. Existing adaptation methods reuse historical guidance but cannot provide updated navigation information when it becomes inadequate. We propose AceVLN, a training-free framework for active latent refresh and edge-side compensation. Our analysis reveals that action-relevant mismatch is concentrated in a compact Critical Subspace and can be tracked through fast-system feature drift. Critical Feature Drift Entropy reflects navigation sensitivity and guides adaptive refresh, while Critical Drift Continuity indicates when recent latent updates can support compensation during latency spikes. AceVLN integrates subspace-decoupled mismatch modeling, entropy-guided refresh scheduling, and continuity-guided compensation. Experiments show that \textit{AceVLN} improves success rates by 1.7--2.4 percentage points over the strongest baselines, while reducing amortized computation time by 2.7--10.0\% and FLOPs by 18.4--22.3\%.

papers.abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) demands that agents accumulate and reason over streaming visual observations throughout long navigation episodes. Existing approaches struggle to maintain long-term history, constrained by the finite context capacity of transformer architectures. To solve the problem, fast-weight test-time training (TTT) provides a mechanism for encoding streaming observations into an evolving parameter state. However, existing TTT does not distinguish informative observations from repetitive visual content, allowing redundant tokens to interfere with the retention of information needed for subsequent decisions. We propose Navigation-Conditioned Test-Time Training (NavTTT), which introduces adaptive memory formation and hierarchical memory integration for vision-and-language navigation. NavTTT leverages global navigation context to prioritize informative visual evidence and integrates language instructions with spatial information to construct spatially grounded memory representations. Episode-local nonlinear fast weights store these representations as Adaptive Parametric Memory (APM), preserving history beyond the visual context for later decisions. To reduce cross-layer coupling in memory formation, NavTTT maintains independent fast-weight memories across multiple decoder depths. This decoupled design prevents errors or biases from spreading across different memory levels. Meanwhile, it enables shared historical information to be independently represented at various levels of abstraction. Experiments demonstrate strong navigation performance on VLN-CE benchmarks and effective instruction following on a real robot.
authors: Xiaoyu Luo, Chengxing Lin, Jiaxin Huang, Jiale Liu, Jingyu Guo, Sirui Chen, Aolin Li, Shaoli Huang, Cheng-zhong Xu, Hui Kong
bullets: Addresses transformer context limits and redundancy in streaming visual observations.
Uses navigation context to prioritize informative evidence and combines language with spatial information.
Stores spatially grounded history in episode-local nonlinear fast weights as Adaptive Parametric Memory.
Maintains independent memories across decoder depths to support multiple abstraction levels and limit cross-layer error propagation.
Reports strong performance on VLN-CE benchmarks and effective instruction following on a real robot.

(B) Navigation-relevant visual tokens are selectively encoded to update hierarchical fast weights online. Figure 1. From explicit to parametric memory in VLN. NavTTT replaces explicit or token-based history with episodespecific parametric memory stored in fast weights.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory enables embodied agents to reuse past observations across tasks. However, existing cross-episode vision-and-language navigation (VLN) benchmarks often leave it unclear whether successful navigation relies on historical memory or current exploration. We introduce Mem-X, a benchmark designed to evaluate memory-dependent cross-episode VLN. Mem-X organizes episodes into sessions in which subsequent instructions refer to objects or routes encountered in earlier episodes. Its three levels evaluate historical-object recall, in-memory localization and episodic indexing, and off-memory relocalization and historical-route reproduction. For the latter two levels, agents receive episode-local poses but no transformations between episode frames, requiring them to establish spatial correspondence with historical memory. Mem-X comprises 2,071 episodes across 710 sessions in 34 scenes, including 1,204 memory-dependent episodes. We also provide MemBridge, a modular baseline that combines semantic scene memory, cross-episode localization, and coarse-to-fine retrieval to support existing VLN agents. Experiments with state-of-the-art VLN methods demonstrate the benefits of MemBridge while revealing substantial room for improvement on memory-dependent navigation. The benchmark and baseline code are available at https://github.com/NJU-R-L-Group-Embodied-Lab/Mem-X.
authors: Zhikang Shi, Yuk Tung Samuel Fang, Hongyu Ding, Zixuan Chen, Yujin Wang, Junhui Guo, You Wu, Jieqi Shi, Jing Huo, Yang Gao
bullets: Organizes 2,071 episodes into 710 sessions across 34 scenes, with later instructions referring to earlier objects or routes.
Evaluates three capabilities: historical-object recall, in-memory localization and episodic indexing, and off-memory relocalization with route reproduction.
The latter two levels require agents to align historical memory with current episode frames without cross-episode frame transformations.
Introduces MemBridge, combining semantic scene memory, cross-episode localization, and coarse-to-fine retrieval.
Experiments show MemBridge benefits existing VLN agents, while memory-dependent navigation remains challenging.

papers.abstract: Active geo-localization (AGL) asks an agent to navigate a small aerial search grid and reach a target specified by an aerial image, a ground-level photograph, or text. Existing methods align the goal modalities well, but they keep the navigation state inside a large sequential Transformer and train with a dense distance reward that uses the hidden goal location. This paper proposes EAGLE, an Explicit spatial-belief Agent for Geo-Localization and Exploration. Offline training jointly optimizes a teacher-conditioned Swin branch and a context-free Swin student from the same randomly masked partial mosaics. The teacher branch attends to frozen full-scene context extracted by Qwen2.5-VL-7B, both branches receive masked-cell aerial-feature reconstruction and uncertainty supervision, while the student additionally distills stop-gradient feature predictions from the teacher. After distillation, Qwen, its cached context, and the teacher-attention branch are discarded. The retained student predicts cell-level aerial-feature embeddings and predictive uncertainty from partial observations alone. These predictions are combined with the modality-aligned goal embedding and a trajectory-derived visitation mask to construct the spatial belief tensor. The student is then frozen while a compact CNN actor-critic is optimized with PPO. EAGLE achieves state-of-the-art average success rates of 78.1%, 76.4%, and 76.8% on MASA, xBD zero-shot transfer, and the MM-GAG zero-shot aerial-goal split, respectively, without using a VLM or cached visual tokens at inference. Code will be made publicly available.
bullets: Addresses AGL state representation by replacing implicit sequential Transformer memory with explicit cell-level spatial beliefs.
Trains a Swin teacher–student system on masked aerial mosaics using reconstruction, uncertainty supervision, and feature distillation from frozen Qwen2.5-VL context.
Combines student predictions, the aligned goal embedding, and visitation history into a spatial belief tensor.
Freezes the student and trains a compact CNN actor–critic with PPO for navigation.
Reports average success rates of 78.1% on MASA, 76.4% on xBD zero-shot transfer, and 76.8% on the MM-GAG zero-shot aerial-goal split; inference uses no VLM or cached visual tokens.

papers.abstract: Representative vision-language navigation (VLN) methods typically couple a vision-language model (VLM) brain with a learnable action head and fine-tune the VLM brain on navigation-domain data to predict geometric goals. However, such adaptation can substantially alter base VLM weights and degrade general visual capabilities. We introduce ZeroVLN, a slow-fast navigation framework that achieves effective navigation with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain. Rather than teaching the brain to predict geometric goals, we equip it with a semantic tool-calling interface for conveying movement decisions to an action expert in natural language. We first adapt the action expert to carry out these movement requests, then jointly improve the brain's movement decisions and the action expert's continuous execution through closed-loop reinforcement learning (RL). Trained on the same navigation episodes, ZeroVLN substantially outperforms representative SFT-based hierarchical VLN methods on standard VLN-CE (continuous environments) benchmarks, while inducing only minor changes to the brain's weights and largely preserving its general capabilities. To our knowledge, ZeroVLN is the first slow-fast VLN framework with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain, and the first to jointly optimize its slow and fast policies through closed-loop agentic RL in VLN-CE.
authors: Zixuan Huang, Yang Zhou, Guli Zhang, Sunzhu Li, Hongyan Xie, Zehao Chen, Fuzhen Zhuang, Kaixuan Wang, Xiaozhi Chen, Yikun Ban, Deqing Wang
bullets: Addresses degradation of general VLM abilities caused by navigation-specific fine-tuning.
Uses a semantic tool-calling interface for the VLM to issue natural-language movement decisions to an action expert.
First adapts the action expert, then jointly optimizes high-level decisions and continuous execution with closed-loop reinforcement learning.
Reports substantially better performance than representative SFT-based hierarchical VLN methods on standard VLN-CE benchmarks.
Induces only minor changes to the VLM’s weights, though the abstract does not specify detailed limitations or numerical results.

papers.abstract: Exploration remains a major challenge for reinforcement learning (RL) agents in Craftax-style environments due to sparse rewards and long horizons. Large language models (LLMs) can guide exploration by generating high-level goals, but methods using models without explicit task adaptation often rely on carefully designed prompts and may produce inconsistent or contextually inappropriate goals. We introduce CCGP-2M, a multimodal goal-preference dataset constructed from interaction trajectories in Craftax-Classic, and propose a vision-language model (VLM)-guided RL framework that learns environment-specific goal guidance from this dataset. The framework consists of two stages: offline VLM fine-tuning and online goal-guided RL. In the offline stage, we align the VLM with goal preferences using Kullback-Leibler Token-level Direct Preference Optimization (KLTDPO), which combines token-level KL regularization with distributionally robust reweighting. Experiments on Craftax-Classic show that our method collects diamonds earlier than state-of-the-art baselines, achieves the highest score and reward, and attains the highest success rates on most achievements.

papers.abstract: Multimodal foundation models are advancing embodied navigation, but frequent inference incurs substantial computational cost. We present Cognitive-Horizon Action Chunking (CHAC), a training-free framework for memory-guided adaptive reasoning with a frozen navigation policy. Retained visual context, completion cues, and controller feedback determine the cognitive horizon, or how many cached waypoints the robot executes before refreshing its prediction. At the policy's stop request, local visitation history guides a bounded correction with at most one extra movement and no additional model calls. CHAC reduces vision-language model calls by 33.4% on HM3D-OVON and 64.7% on R2R-CE, with success-rate decreases of 0.63 and 10.82 percentage points, respectively. Success rate and success weighted by path length improve per model call on both benchmarks. Across four physical navigation tasks with 40 runs per method, CHAC achieves 18 successes versus 14 for native execution, reducing model calls by 54.9% and GPU inference time by 49.7%.
authors: Weile Gong, Zijian Lu, Jiahao Zheng, Bo Xu, Yiping Zuo, Jiajia Guo, Xin He, Weijun Wang, Weibei Fan

papers.abstract: Zero-Shot Object Navigation (ZSON) requires an agent to locate target objects in unfamiliar environments without additional training for the test categories or environments. Recent approaches leverage large language models and vision-language models to construct spatial representations and guide exploration. However, whether the available evidence sufficiently supports a navigation choice, and how new evidence changes the search value of previously visited locations, remain insufficiently addressed. We propose RefBeliefMap, an uncertainty-guided mapping framework that distinguishes target-location belief from spatial and semantic evidence uncertainty. By jointly modeling intra-observation uncertainty and inter-observation disagreement over a sliding memory window, RefBeliefMap assesses the reliability of both evidence channels. When competing frontiers remain insufficiently resolved, these uncertainty estimates guide active observation and semantic reasoning to refine the evidence supporting target-location beliefs before navigation commitment. Building on the refined map, we introduce RefBeliefNav, which jointly evaluates unexplored frontiers and historical waypoints according to their target-finding potential, expected information gain, and navigation cost. This unified objective allows historical locations to be reconsidered as new evidence changes their search value, coordinating exploration and revisitation. Experiments on HM3D and MP3D demonstrate state-of-the-art performance among the evaluated zero-shot baselines, with ablation studies examining the contributions of modules. Real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 quadruped robot further demonstrate the sim-to-real transferability of our method.
bullets: Addresses unreliable evidence and changing search value of previously visited locations in unfamiliar environments.

RefBeliefNav ranks unexplored frontiers and historical waypoints by target-finding potential, information gain, and navigation cost.
Experiments on HM3D, MP3D, and a Unitree Go2 show strong zero-shot performance and sim-to-real transfer; ablations assess module contributions.

papers.abstract: Underwater navigation requires translating visual spatial cues into motion, yet marine vision-language datasets rarely include paired robot trajectories. We present NereidVLA, a vision-language-action model that transfers marine spatial knowledge to language-conditioned 3D navigation. We first train Sea2Know on approximately two million marine examples to learn target grounding, spatial relations, and scene structure without paired robot-motion supervision. We then adapt it using expert trajectories executed under simulated underwater vehicle dynamics. Given RGB histories and a language instruction, NereidVLA predicts discrete motion tokens that decode into local 3D trajectories for closed-loop tracking. Evaluation combines an independent six-dimensional underwater navigation understanding benchmark with offline prediction and closed-loop navigation. Under matched navigation training and execution settings, marine spatial pretraining increases simulation success from 72.4% to 84.4%. Without fine-tuning on the real test environment, NereidVLA achieves 78.75% success in laboratory-pool robot trials, compared with 47.50% for InternVLA-N1. These results show that marine spatial supervision can support downstream motion learning and physical underwater navigation.

papers.abstract: Language-goal aerial navigation requires a UAV to reach a destination specified in natural language using observations collected during flight. A key challenge is linking changing egocentric perception with spatial evidence anchored to stable locations for long-range navigation. We propose CityNav-VLA, a dual-frame vision-language-action model for urban navigation integrating dynamic egocentric context with persistent allocentric spatial memory. The UAV incrementally accumulates visual observations on a fixed north-up map initialized with geographic and landmark priors, preserving evidence across viewpoint changes. A dynamic query conditioned on the instruction, current observations, UAV state, and motion history retrieves relevant memory evidence to predict a map-frame target. A deterministic controller converts this target into body-frame commands using the UAV's current pose, connecting global reasoning with egocentric execution. To reduce target fluctuations over long horizons, early goal commitment (EGC) fixes the execution target to the coordinate-wise median of the first $K$ predictions without extra trainable parameters. On Test Unseen, CityNav-VLA reduces NE by 21.2% and improves SR and SPL by 15.8% and 30.9%, respectively. It also reduces NE by 6.2% and improves SR and SPL by 5.6% and 23.2%, respectively, relative to the former SOTA after dataset refinement. Cumulative ablations show that navigation-map features yield the largest gains, while metric coordinates further improve endpoint accuracy. With a 4B-scale backbone, inference averages 0.68 s per decision with 8.6 GB peak memory on a single A100, presenting remarkable model efficiency.
authors: Haotian Xu, Yue Hu, Zhengqiu Zhu, Tuo Feng, Wenguan Wang, Quanjun Yin
bullets: Addresses the challenge of connecting changing viewpoints with stable spatial evidence during long-range flight.
Builds a north-up navigation map from visual observations, geographic priors, and landmarks.
Uses instruction- and state-conditioned memory retrieval to predict map-frame targets, then converts them into body-frame commands.

On Test Unseen, it improves navigation error, success rate, and success-weighted path length, with efficient 0.68-second inference and 8.6 GB peak memory on one A100.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to follow natural-language instructions, yet still fail frequently in closed-loop flight. Correcting these failures requires repairs, i.e., actions that avoid them at the states the policy itself reaches, which human pilots cannot label at scale and rule-based planners cannot supply reliably. In this paper, we present AeroRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework in which an aerial navigation policy iteratively learns from its own failures. Our key insight is that a failing policy should judge its own repairs by flying on from them. Judged in this way, its sampled actions and even rule-based proposals that hurt it when imitated directly become reliable supervision. Moreover, an episode terminates at its first failure, concealing subsequent failures until the earlier ones are repaired. AeroRSI thus renews its supervision in every round, anchoring the failures of the current policy, verifying repairs by its continuation, and distilling them while keeping its behavior elsewhere. On TravelUAV, three rounds raise the success rate of a supervised 2B-parameter policy from 46.4% to 67.5% and reduce collisions by half, surpassing the previous state of the art by 10.6 points from the same initialization without extra human labels or inference cost. Code and models are available at https://github.com/starsholic/AeroRSI.
authors: Shiwei Wu, Yuwen Pan, Zhi Li, Yaowen Li, Yan Zhou, Xuemiao Xu, Yu Liu
bullets: Addresses the lack of scalable human labels and reliable rule-based repairs for failures encountered during closed-loop UAV navigation.
Uses recursive self-improvement: the current policy anchors failures, proposes or samples repairs, evaluates them by flying onward, and distills verified repairs.
Renews supervision each round to uncover failures hidden behind earlier failures while preserving behavior elsewhere.
On TravelUAV, three rounds improve success from 46.4% to 67.5% and halve collisions, with no extra human labels or inference cost.
Scope: evaluated on a supervised 2B-parameter policy and the TravelUAV benchmark.

papers.abstract: Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are expected to achieve semantic reasoning, intelligent decision-making, and long-horizon navigation under strict onboard constraints. While recent foundation-model-driven approaches have shown promising progress toward this goal, existing methods remain limited by challenges in 3D data availability, trajectory feasibility, long-horizon reasoning, and computational efficiency in complex environments. To bridge these gaps, we propose VLN-AR, a hierarchical vision-language-navigation (VLN) framework for aerial robots. VLN-AR decouples multimodal reasoning and low-level control, enabling structured prediction of 3D pose commands and navigation intentions that are translated into dynamically feasible actions. To mitigate data scarcity and domain gaps, we introduce a fully automated 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)-based pipeline to generate scalable photorealistic UAV navigation data. A progressive three-stage training strategy further enhances grounding, scene reasoning, and complex navigation. In addition, a lightweight cognitive agent improves long-horizon reasoning via memory-aware task decomposition. Finally, we design onboard optimization techniques, including token sparsification and model lightweighting, achieving 7.1x-9.4x speedup while maintaining high navigation performance on resource-limited UAV platforms. Experiments show great improvements over existing methods in both simulation and real-world UAV navigation. Project website: https://wyz000.github.io/VLN-AR/

Employs progressive three-stage training for improved grounding, scene reasoning, and complex navigation.
Adds a memory-aware cognitive agent for long-horizon task decomposition and onboard optimizations such as token sparsification and model lightweighting.
Reports 7.1×–9.4× speedups while maintaining high navigation performance, with improvements demonstrated in simulation and real-world UAV experiments.

papers.abstract: Natural language-guided UAV navigation enables intuitive human-robot interaction and flexible autonomous flight in complex environments. However, reliable navigation requires accurate instruction following, continuous task progress tracking, and safe obstacle avoidance, which remain challenging for existing world-action models that primarily focus on action prediction. To address these limitations, we propose a world-action learning framework that integrates three complementary mechanisms: a language-conditioned action interface with targeted post-training for instruction-responsive motion, recurrent instruction-consumption prediction to track task progress and determine termination, and Gaussian-scene post-training to enhance obstacle avoidance through trajectory imitation and differentiable geometric feedback. Closed-loop evaluations and ablation studies demonstrate improvements in sequential task completion, safe goal reaching, and timely termination. Furthermore, direct one-step denoising reduces inference overhead, and real-world indoor and outdoor flights validate the framework's effectiveness.
authors: Zhexuan Zhou, Yanke Sun, Yuhan Zong, Youmin Gong, Jie Mei
bullets: Targets limitations of action-focused world-action models in reliable, safe language-guided UAV navigation.
Uses a language-conditioned action interface with targeted post-training for instruction-responsive motion.
Predicts recurrent instruction consumption to monitor task progress and decide when to terminate.
Applies Gaussian-scene post-training with trajectory imitation and differentiable geometric feedback for obstacle avoidance.
Closed-loop evaluations, ablations, and indoor/outdoor flights show improved task completion, safe goal reaching, and timely termination; one-step denoising lowers inference overhead.

papers.abstract: Bird's-Eye-View (BEV)-conditioned large language models (LLMs) enable language-interactive driving, but onboard deployment requires efficient perception and continuous planning alongside autoregressive language generation. We present GridDriver, an efficient BEV-conditioned LLM framework combining trajectory prediction, structured driving indicators, natural-language navigation, driving explanations, and scene question answering. Lightweight spatio-temporal BEV perception and spatially structured tokens provide scene context to a shared LLM, while frame-wise scheduling interleaves trajectory prediction with asynchronous language generation. GridDriver achieves competitive performance on public benchmarks, reaching 87.9% PDMS on NAVSIM and 57.6% accuracy on nuScenes-QA with a shared planning and QA checkpoint. Spatial representation analyses demonstrate improved geometric information retention and trajectory prediction compared with Q-Former compression. The system achieves 32.7 ms standalone planning latency and 9.4 plans/s in an onboard ROS 2 pipeline. We further evaluate planning on our own data recordings and demonstrate open-loop onboard operation on a research vehicle. Across public benchmarks and real-world evaluations, we identify strengths and limitations of the BEV-based approach.

Evaluations include public benchmarks, proprietary recordings, and open-loop operation on a research vehicle; the abstract notes both strengths and limitations of the BEV-based approach.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon vision-language navigation (VLN) requires agents to track instruction progress and recover from local errors before they propagate across subtasks. However, executors trained on expert trajectories encounter policy-induced state shifts during deployment, and their stop signals do not reliably indicate subtask completion. We introduce Learning and Verifying Progress for VLN (LeaP-VLN), an agentic VLN system that couples progress-aware execution with independent progress verification through plan--execute--verify--recover cycles. LeaP-VLN leverages progress both explicitly, through a progress verifier that verifies subtask completion before the agent advances and triggers dual-phase recovery upon route deviation, and implicitly, by co-training the executor on progress reasoning and action prediction to enhance the executor's progress awareness and corrective control. To adapt the executor to this closed-loop interface, we propose a two-stage progress-enhanced curriculum: behavior cloning on expert demonstrations, followed by joint training on demonstrations, expert action corrections, and progress-reasoning supervision. Policy-generated trajectories expose the executor to both intra-subtask drift and inter-subtask state shifts, aligning training with the deviations encountered during closed-loop execution. Extensive experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE demonstrate state-of-the-art success rates among monocular methods trained without additional navigation datasets, while real-world experiments further validate the effectiveness of LeaP-VLN in long-horizon navigation.
authors: Kangjie Zhou, Sukai Wang, Yuhan Xiao, Qinghang Liu, Zhejia Wen, ChunXuan Jiao, Wei Shan, Guanghui Ren, Maoqing Yao, Chang Liu
bullets: Addresses executor drift and unreliable stopping decisions that can cause errors to propagate across subtasks.
Uses plan–execute–verify–recover cycles with a progress verifier that confirms subtask completion and triggers dual-phase recovery after route deviations.
Co-trains the executor on action prediction and progress reasoning to improve progress awareness and corrective control.
Adapts training through a two-stage curriculum using expert demonstrations, corrections, progress supervision, and policy-generated trajectories.
Achieves state-of-the-art success rates among monocular methods without additional navigation datasets on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, with further validation in real-world experiments.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the proposed closed-loop agentic framework with test-time verification and recovery. Fig. 1. Comparison of long-horizon VLN execution paradigms. End-toend policies map the complete route instruction and visual observations directly to actions, with route progress implicitly inferred within the action policy. Hierarchical planner–executor pipelines without outcome verification dispatch local subtasks and advance based on executor termination. Our LeaP-VLN couples progress-aware execution with progress verification and dual-phase recovery to ground subtask transitions in observed outcomes and limit error propagation.

papers.abstract: Driving vision-language-action (VLA) models can accept navigation instructions, yet predicting a driver's trajectory does not establish that a model follows the instruction. We study how driving-language supervision is collected and evaluated, distinguishing prospective instructions issued before an action from retrospective labels written after observing it. We develop ADVLAT-Engine to synchronize spoken instructions, road-scene video, and vehicle trajectories, and compare three navigation apps on 48 replayed routes. On 87 maneuvers announced by both Google Maps and a passenger, the passenger uses more scene-dependent language. We evaluate four open driving VLAs before and after fine-tuning on prospective navigation-app drives. Fine-tuning reduces passenger-drive trajectory error by 23-59%, but instruction effects remain inconsistent. At real intersections, counterfactual instructions reveal stronger responsiveness: fine-tuned Alpamayo~2 Super gains 31 and 18 accuracy points at 15 and 5~m, while Qwen-Drive follows alternative maneuvers more reliably with a discrete command than with a sentence. We additionally collected retrospective annotations from four people for the driving recordings and describe controlled comparisons of annotation content, timing, and downstream learning; those analyses are pending. Our findings separate maneuver prediction from instruction-following and establish a framework for comparing prospective and retrospective supervision.
bullets: Distinguishes prospective instructions given before actions from retrospective labels written after observing them.
Introduces ADVLAT-Engine to synchronize spoken instructions, road video, and vehicle trajectories.
Across 48 replayed routes and 87 shared maneuvers, passengers used more scene-dependent language than Google Maps.
Fine-tuning on prospective navigation-app drives reduced passenger-drive trajectory error by 23–59%, but instruction effects remained inconsistent.
Counterfactual intersection tests showed improved responsiveness for some models, while Qwen-Drive followed alternative maneuvers more reliably from discrete commands than sentences.

papers.abstract: Language-guided navigation enables mobile robots to interpret natural language commands and navigate toward user-specified targets in unstructured environments. However, integrating open-vocabulary visual perception with classical robotics pipelines for mapping and navigation remains a challenging problem. In this work, we present a complete ROS2-based system that combines frontier-based exploration, open-vocabulary object detection using Grounding DINO, depth-based 3D localization, and semantic mapping to enable end-to-end vision-language grounded navigation in simulation. The system accepts natural language commands such as ``go to the yellow box,'' detects candidate objects from RGB images using text prompts, estimates their positions in the world frame, and generates navigation goals executed by the Nav2 stack. In a Gazebo-based indoor environment with a TurtleBot3 robot, the system autonomously explored the room, detected three of the five target objects, and successfully executed both natural language navigation commands tested, without task-specific training. The results indicate that open-vocabulary grounding models can be integrated into classical navigation pipelines, though performance is limited by detection uncertainty, depth-based localization error, and incomplete exploration coverage. These findings highlight both the feasibility and current limitations of deploying vision-language grounded navigation systems using lightweight, CPU-only architectures.

papers.abstract: Existing feedback-based methods for online vision-and-language navigation (VLN) primarily learn from current episode outcomes, leaving previously acquired feedback underutilized. Inspired by human episodic memory, we propose R2A, an online VLN adaptation framework that continually reuses successful and failed navigation experiences for policy learning. Specifically, Success-Failure Memory (SFM) retains successful and failed navigation episodes with acquired feedback and retrieves task-relevant experiences based on incoming instructions, enabling historical feedback to guide subsequent navigation. Prior-Anchored Adaptation (PAA) learns from these experiences by reinforcing successful trajectories and suppressing failed ones relative to a frozen pretrained policy, while regularizing behavioral drift. Together, these modules enable continual feedback reuse and stable policy adaptation without source-domain data or expert supervision. Extensive experiments across three benchmarks, REVERIE, R2R, and R2R-CE, and five navigation backbones demonstrate consistent performance gains. On the REVERIE validation unseen split, R2A improves DUET's SR from 46.98% to 69.84% and SPL from 33.73% to 50.98%.

papers.abstract: Although object-goal navigation (ObjectNav) approaches are usually evaluated in simulation, which offers scale and repeatable environments, real-world deployments are rarely examined beyond feasibility demonstrations. This paper presents the deployment of Room-Mediated Co-occurrence, an ObjectNav policy that reasons over Room Probability Vectors (RPVs), on two robotic platforms (Boston Dynamics Spot and Clearpath Robotics TurtleBot 4) through a robot-agnostic ROS 2 bridge. We study how these semantic priors generalise to physical environments and describe the adaptations required to transfer RPV from simulation to hardware, covering sensing, localisation, and the action interface. Across 66 trials on Spot, searching for 11 object categories from two starting positions in a university postgraduate research facility, RPV achieves a raw Success Rate (SR) of 0.455. Our analysis identifies undetected glass walls, entry into off-limits areas, limited usable depth range, target size, and mismatch between the room lexicon and physical layout as plausible contributors to the 8.4 percentage-point gap between the real-world SR and the reported simulated SR of 0.539. Code is available at https://github.com/Matthew-K-Chua/rpv-ros2-bridge.
authors: Matthew Chua, Adam Scicluna, Gavin Paul

Identifies glass walls, restricted areas, limited depth sensing, target size, and room-layout mismatch as likely causes of the real-to-simulation performance gap.
