papers.abstract: When a vision-and-language navigation policy generates an action sequence autoregressively, the robot waits for a chain of dependent predictions. A small discrete action vocabulary makes it possible to score all short-horizon plans in parallel. We introduce VLN-Flash, a training-free decoder that evaluates the complete action-prefix tree in a single forward pass. Branch-specific attention and matched token positions preserve the original policy's conditional action distribution for each prefix in exact arithmetic. We use the score margin between the stepwise-greedy prefix and its strongest alternative at each depth to decide how many actions to execute. The robot then executes the plan with the highest joint score at the chosen depth before observing again. On matched inputs, VLN-Flash achieves a nearly $3\times$ speedup in action decoding over native autoregression on Uni-NaVid and StreamVLN. Compared with the native autoregressive decoders, it improves success rate and success weighted by path length (SPL) on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, with success gains up to 2.7 percentage points. On a Unitree GO2, VLN-Flash improves navigation success and cuts the mean wait between actions by about 160 ms after subtracting network transmission time.
authors: Ruizhe Xie, Honghua Chen, Binglin Wang, Tong Guo, Xu Tang, Puti Yan, Shaoxiong Cai
bullets: Addresses the latency of autoregressive action-by-action decoding in robot navigation.
Training-free decoder evaluates the complete short-horizon action-prefix tree in one forward pass while preserving conditional action distributions.
Uses score margins to adaptively choose how many actions to execute before observing again.
Achieves nearly 3× faster action decoding and improves success/SPL, with success gains up to 2.7 percentage points on reported benchmarks.
On a Unitree GO2, improves navigation success and reduces mean inter-action wait by about 160 ms, excluding network transmission time.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of parallel action decoding. The instruction and observation history are formatted as the model query x, followed by candidate action tokens. An attention mask restricts each candidate action token to attending only to the query, its branch ancestors, and itself. The VLN backbone processes the resulting sequence in a single forward pass. The hidden state of the last query token and those of all candidate tokens are then decoded into action distributions through the shared LM head. The last query token predicts the first action, so K = 3 uses two candidate levels. Scoring K = 4 adds a third level with 27 candidate tokens.

Figure 5. Real-world deployment trajectories on a Unitree GO2. The left and right scenes show a corridor and a classroom, respectively. In each scene, both methods start from the same position and receive the same instruction shown above. Baseline and Ours correspond to the autoregressive and parallel decoding variants of StreamVLN, respectively. Across the decision steps shown in these two scenes, our method reduces the average wait by 172 ms.

Figure 2. Comparison between autoregressive and parallel decoding. Autoregressive decoding (left) requires three sequential forward passes to predict a1, a2, and a3, whereas parallel decoding (right) computes all candidate action distributions in a single forward pass. For each action prediction, the visible tokens (highlighted) are identical along the corresponding branch in both methods, yielding equivalent conditional action distributions in exact arithmetic.

Figure 3. Adaptive execution via joint path scoring. Nodes are labeled with conditional action probabilities, while L(path) denotes cumulative joint log-probabilities. The greedy path can be outscored by the selected path in joint probability. The scan compares the fixed greedy prefix with its strongest alternative at each depth. When their score margin falls below δ, the highestscoring branch at that depth is executed and deeper actions are skipped. Here, m1 = 0.58 > δ continues the scan, whereas m2 = −0.18 < δ at δ = 0.2 selects a left turn followed by a forward step (L → F ).

papers.abstract: Efficient aerial visual-language navigation (VLN) requires reducing model storage and inference costs while maintaining instruction-conditioned action prediction. We present ARC-VLN, a token-type-aware recursive computation framework built on a language backbone with shared parameters. ARC-VLN retains full-depth computation for text and action tokens while adaptively selecting exit depths for visual tokens. Representations of early-exiting visual tokens are retained, and active-token compaction shortens the sequences processed by subsequent recursive blocks. To mitigate routing collapse to a single exit depth, we design a dedicated learning strategy that encourages the model to distribute visual tokens across multiple exit depths.On OpenFly's Test-Seen and Test-Unseen subsets, ARC-VLN achieves the lowest navigation error and the highest success rate and success weighted by path length among all compared methods. Meanwhile, it reduces the average number of decision steps per trajectory, total floating-point operations, mean model inference time per trajectory, and average GPU memory usage during inference, indicating its great potential as a VLN backbone for lightweight applications.
authors: Xiang Zhang, Xiangyu Dong, Yang Lu, Xiaoguang Ma
bullets: Targets lower storage, computation, latency, and memory costs in instruction-conditioned aerial VLN.
Uses shared-parameter recursive computation with token-type-aware routing: text and action tokens run to full depth, while visual tokens exit adaptively.
Retains early-exited visual representations and compacts active tokens to shorten later processing.
Introduces a learning strategy that distributes visual tokens across multiple exit depths and avoids routing collapse.
On OpenFly Test-Seen and Test-Unseen, reports the best navigation error, success rate, and success weighted by path length among compared methods, while also reducing inference costs.

papers.abstract: Accessible mobility is user-conditioned rather than scene-intrinsic, as walkable paths for one embodiment are inaccessible to another. Yet, existing benchmarks evaluate traversability under a fixed and limited embodiment. We present Vision-Language Accessible Navigation (VLAN), containing 1,000 scenes, 20K navigation trajectories, and 160K keyframes across diverse lighting, environmental conditions, scene semantics, and path geometries. For each trajectory, VLAN provides embodiment-specific actions and accessibility features for legged and wheeled agents, including humanoid and quadruped robots and people with visual or mobility impairments, while everyday obstacles and accessibility labels are categorized as Passable, Bypass, HighRisk, and Blocked. Unlike goal-only evaluation, our benchmark measures physical safety and alignment with user-specific constraints via goal-reaching, collision-aware, and accessibility-aligned metrics. We benchmark modern vision-language models and find they often fail to consistently adapt obstacle relevance, path selection, and safety criteria across user profiles, suggesting accessibility-aware navigation requires dedicated datasets, tasks, and metrics beyond conventional embodied navigation evaluation. All data and code open-source at https://github.com/InSAI-Lab/VLAN.
authors: Jie Hu, Yu Zheng, Wenzhi Wu, Weixing Feng, Cunlei Cheng, Jiaming Zhang

papers.abstract: Semantic exploration methods for object-goal navigation use large language models (LLMs) to score how strongly a target object is associated with a room type or with a nearby object. This paper considers obtaining from the LLM a spatial prior instead: a distribution over the position of the target in a room. We evaluate whether two open-weight LLMs, Qwen3.5-27B and Gemma-4-31B-it, can provide such a prior. Using real room layouts from CubiCasa5K and ScanNet, we measure the likelihood the models assign to real and perturbed layouts, and the layouts they generate. The object frequencies and room sizes of the generated rooms follow the room type, but the proximity of the objects to the walls does not follow the differences between room types found in real rooms. The likelihood distinguishes real layouts from perturbed ones partly through their geometry and partly through the agreement between the coordinates and a field that states the wall each object touches; for the movable furniture of ScanNet, it is higher for layouts with all objects piled near the room center than for the real layouts in most rooms. When an object is given in the prompt, the models place a related object relative to it. When the wall of each object is given, they place most objects against that wall, but do not keep all objects inside a given room rectangle. As a prior for object search, the generated placements reduce the searched area relative to a uniform prior, but by less than a third of the reduction obtained with a prior built from real layouts, and by less than two thirds when both priors are spatially smoothed. These results support the use of LLMs for object-room associations and for writing coordinates under constraints determined by another component, followed by a geometric check, but not as a source of placement priors where real layouts are available.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates LLMs as spatial priors for object-goal navigation, relevant to vision-language navigation and spatial reasoning.
papers.title: Evaluating Language Models as Spatial Priors for Object-Goal Navigation
papers.tldr: LLMs can encode object–room associations and constrained spatial relationships, but are weaker than real-layout priors for predicting where objects are placed in rooms.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon navigation from indoors to outdoors remains an open problem for humanoid robots: one instruction covers rooms, doors and roads, and the camera moves with the gait. Worken, AGIBOT's measure of productive robot work, depends on robots that reach their workplaces autonomously. We present X-Nav, to our knowledge the first system to take a bipedal humanoid through a language-instructed long-horizon mission from indoors to outdoors. X-Nav covers a pipeline from data to deployment. Its data engine collects navigation data in open-source scenes, in digital twins of deployment sites and on real robots. Its navigation model, MELIOR, takes only RGB images from the robot's built-in camera and comes in two versions: MELIOR-A predicts actions, and MELIOR-N predicts a navigation goal. Its agentic workflow, X-Navarch, turns a brief human instruction into sub-tasks and deploys MELIOR on the robot with explicit target navigation and obstacle avoidance. On the Lingxi X2, X-Nav completes a mission of about a hundred metres from an office lobby to a store in a neighbouring building; LiDAR and odometry are used for target approach and low-level control. The mission is completed with both versions of MELIOR: the robot follows a change of destination and walks through a door from the lobby to the road, and with X-Navarch it also passes static and dynamic obstacles on the route. During deployment, MELIOR is adapted with data collected in a digital twin of the site; the adaptation raises its closed-loop success rate in the twin, and the adapted model is then deployed on the robot at the real site. In addition, MELIOR achieves competitive results on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks.
authors: Jiaxin Huang, Chengxing Lin, Xiaoyu Luo, Sirui Chen, Jingyu Guo, Aolin Li, Kairui Chen, Rui Zhen, Cheng Wen, Kerui Gu, Shunyao Wang, Zhihui Peng, Shaoli Huang
bullets: Addresses autonomous navigation across rooms, doors, roads, and changing destinations for humanoid robots.
Uses MELIOR, an RGB-only navigation model with action-prediction and goal-prediction variants.
X-Navarch decomposes brief instructions into subtasks and coordinates navigation with explicit target and obstacle avoidance.
Demonstrated on a Lingxi X2 over roughly 100 metres from an office lobby to a neighbouring-building store, including door traversal and static/dynamic obstacle avoidance.
Digital-twin adaptation improved closed-loop success in simulation before deployment; MELIOR also achieved competitive R2R-CE and RxR-CE results.

(3) Replay & annotation. We replay the reference routes to record RGB-D observations and camera poses. A vision–language model generates instructions. papers.tldr: X-Nav enables a humanoid robot to execute language-directed, long-horizon indoor-to-outdoor navigation using camera-based visual navigation, task decomposition, and obstacle avoidance.

papers.abstract: A rescue robot entering a building with thirty seconds on the clock should sprint toward the single most promising room; given ten minutes, it should instead explore a broader tour. Yet vision-language-navigation (VLN) models are typically evaluated under a fixed episode limit that the policy never observes, even though time-critical missions require behavior to adapt to the available budget. We study budget-conditioned object search: given a target category and an explicit action budget, an agent must find as many distinct target instances as possible before the budget expires. We investigate how to supervise VLNs for this task by comparing a privileged TSP expert, which plans near-optimal routes using the full map and true target locations, with a room-level Bellman expert that maximizes expected return under partial observability using high-level cross-scene semantic priors. Despite the TSP expert achieving substantially higher expert performance, its demonstrations are less effective for learning exploration: on held-out HM3D scenes, the Bellman-supervised VLN consistently outperforms the TSP-supervised VLN, with the advantage becoming more pronounced at longer budgets. At 2000 steps (500m), the Bellman-supervised VLN finds 71.4% of reachable target instances, compared with 65.5% for the TSP-supervised VLN and 44.8% for the pretrained VLN. These results highlight a distinction between optimal routing and optimal exploration: effective exploration supervision should optimize decisions under partial observability rather than imitate routes that are optimal only once the environment is fully known.
authors: Maitree Meher, Siming He, S. Shankar Sastry, Jitendra Malik, Claire Tomlin, Jonas Frey
bullets: Studies object search where agents must find as many distinct targets as possible within an explicit action budget.
Compares a full-map, true-location TSP expert with a room-level Bellman expert that plans under partial observability.
Despite lower expert-route performance, Bellman supervision consistently yields better learned exploration on held-out HM3D scenes.
At 2,000 steps, Bellman-supervised VLN finds 71.4% of reachable targets versus 65.5% for TSP supervision and 44.8% for pretrained VLN.
The findings distinguish optimal routing in known environments from effective exploration under uncertainty, especially at longer budgets.

papers.abstract: Industrial inspection robots must reach work areas and specific equipment. These destinations span spatial scales from regions to objects, so robots must relate each target to its surroundings to interpret the task and determine where to go. Existing methods support multi-scale navigation through rich environment representations, but at substantial computational and storage cost. These costs limit deployment where wireless coverage is incomplete and robots must rely on onboard computation to keep navigating. We introduce EMS-Nav, a biologically inspired multi-scale navigation framework for online, on-device operation. Its core innovation is to organize perception, spatial understanding, and navigation around regions, making local spaces the basic units of both environmental understanding and computation. EMS-Nav groups objects and their relationships into functionally meaningful spaces and builds a hierarchy from local areas to the broader environment. This organization supports efficient map construction alongside the interpretation and execution of language goals at different scales. In multi-scale navigation experiments, EMS-Nav achieves the highest success rates across all four target categories: objects, rooms, regions, and specific instances. It outperforms state-of-the-art open-vocabulary mapping and navigation methods, improving overall first-attempt success by 9.39 percentage points over the strongest baseline while reducing mapping overhead and language-model input size. Local deployment in real indoor environments further demonstrates its applicability to on-device embodied navigation. By establishing regions as the organizing basis for perception, spatial understanding, and language-guided action, EMS-Nav provides a system that combines multi-scale understanding with computational efficiency to support diverse language goals on resource-constrained robots.
bullets: Addresses the computational and storage costs of rich environment representations for industrial inspection robots operating with limited connectivity.
Builds a hierarchical representation from local areas to the broader environment, grouping objects and relationships into meaningful regions.
Supports online map construction and language-guided navigation for objects, rooms, regions, and specific instances.
Achieves the highest success rates across all four target categories and improves first-attempt success by 9.39 percentage points over the strongest baseline.
Real indoor deployments demonstrate applicability to resource-constrained, on-device embodied navigation.

papers.abstract: Vision language navigation (VLN) is very challenging for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) since small errors in 3D motion prediction can lead to navigation errors and collisions. Unable to fathom execution outcomes in 3D environments, existing methods often struggle to predict accurate navigation waypoints from language instructions. To solve this, we introduce the Prototypical Visual Imagination framework, shortened as ProtoVis-Nav, which forces the model to imagine an outcome-associated local visual representation for the intended next UAV movement. Specifically, we predict feature prototypes and use their linear combination to estimate the visual feature of the target region. In this manner, the VLN model first imagines the local visual representation of the next intended location, and then uses predicted prototypes as context for generating the final action, promoting alignment between visual context and waypoint outputs. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the ProtoVis-Nav framework and show substantial improvements over existing baselines.
authors: Guangyuan Sui, Yunzhong Hou, Chi Harold Liu
bullets: UAV VLN is difficult because small 3D motion errors can cause navigation failures or collisions.
The framework predicts feature prototypes associated with possible outcomes and linearly combines them to estimate the target region’s visual features.
These imagined local visual representations provide context for generating waypoints and actions.
Experiments show substantial improvements over existing baselines.
The abstract does not specify datasets, numerical gains, or detailed limitations.

papers.abstract: Language-guided UAV navigation has largely focused on long-horizon route planning, leaving short-range, object-relative flight maneuvers underexplored. To address this gap, we formulate Flying-on-a-Word (Flow), a task requiring a UAV to convert concise natural-language instruction, egocentric visual observation, and current state dynamics into continuous flight actions. Flow encompasses both primitive motion commands and complex object-interactive behaviors, assessing motion intent comprehension and spatial context grounding. To enable policy learning and closed-loop evaluation, we introduce UAV-Flow, a comprehensive dataset comprising 30,692 expert-piloted real-world trajectories across eight distinct motion categories, alongside 10,109 simulation trajectories in the UAV-Flow-Sim environment equipped with task-specific completion criteria. Furthermore, we develop FlowVLA, which undergoes imitation pretraining on mixed real-sim demonstrations and online post-training via Tail-Aware GRPO (TGRPO). By leveraging group reward distributions, TGRPO effectively reinforces high-reward action sequences. Evaluated on 273 held-out UAV-Flow-Sim episodes, pretrained FlowVLA achieves a mean success rate of 75.58%, outperforming the strongest baseline by 6.72 percentage points, which TGRPO post-training further elevates to 93.16% with superior sample efficiency. Physical UAV experiments demonstrate robust execution of object-relative commands in both indoor and outdoor real-world scenes. Together, Flow establishes a novel benchmark and learning framework for language-conditioned flight maneuvers.
authors: Donglin Yang, Xiangyu Wang, Yantong Zhong, Wenhao Zheng, Zihan Ding, Yue Liao, Hongsheng Li, Ke Xu, Si Liu
bullets: Targets the underexplored problem of converting concise language, egocentric vision, and UAV dynamics into continuous object-relative flight actions.
UAV-Flow includes 30,692 real-world expert trajectories across eight motion categories and 10,109 simulation trajectories with task-specific completion criteria.
FlowVLA uses mixed real-simulation imitation pretraining followed by Tail-Aware GRPO online post-training.
On 273 held-out simulation episodes, FlowVLA reaches 75.58% mean success after pretraining and 93.16% after TGRPO post-training.

papers.abstract: Open-world navigation requires a robot to locate a user-specified target in an indoor scene under open-vocabulary queries. Realistic indoor environments are semi-static: walls and furniture largely persist while smaller objects move, relocate, or vanish between visits. Prior-map systems answer queries from object poses recorded at reconstruction time, which expire as soon as objects move, whereas online methods re-derive where to look from current observations every few steps, often through expensive calls to a vision--language model. Assuming that walls and large furniture do not move, we keep their map to plan paths, but use a target--furniture co-occurrence prior to decide where to search. We present PreNav, an ObjectNav framework on semi-static environments. Rather than invoking a vision-language model at each step, PreNav generates a single global search reference before the robot moves: an LLM converts target--furniture co-occurrence into a spatial prior, a conditional diffusion model turns that prior and the persistent structure into an ordered centerline with a band around it, and the robot approaches the target once it is detected online. Experiments on a Gibson ObjectNav benchmark show that PreNav outperforms a strong online baseline under matched structural priors, using a generator trained only on room-level ScanNet++ scenes and applied to floor-level Gibson without fine-tuning. Real-world experiments under object relocation and open-vocabulary queries further validate the approach.
authors: Yuxuan Feng, Fujing Xie, S\"oren Schwertfeger, Hermann Blum
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between stale object maps and costly step-by-step vision–language-model planning when objects move.
Keeps persistent walls and large furniture for navigation while using target–furniture co-occurrence to predict where to search.
An LLM creates a spatial prior, and a conditional diffusion model converts it into an ordered centerline with a search band before movement begins.
Experiments on Gibson show improved performance over a matched online baseline, despite training only on room-level ScanNet++ scenes without fine-tuning.
Real-world tests with relocated objects and open-vocabulary queries support the method’s practical validity.

papers.abstract: Embodied Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are backbones for robotic planning and manipulation. However, for coordinate prediction in grounding tasks, existing architectures suffer from two distinct bottlenecks: discrete tokenization disrupts spatial continuity with high decoding latency, while standard point regression fails on multi-contact affordances and irregularly shaped targets. To resolve these challenges, we propose PhysMoE, introducing three core contributions: (1) sharing lower layers for multimodal context while routing upper layers to specialized spatial (pixel) and linguistic (text) experts by physical modality, eliminating gradient interference; (2) encoding each coordinate as a single token by reusing the visual encoder's learned positional embeddings, injecting 2D spatial priors to natively align coordinates with visual features and ease training; and (3) differentiable Signed Distance Field (SDF) supervision on pointing, accommodating affordances and irregular geometries without costly mask decoders. Compared to the base model, PhysMoE achieves a 15.7% average gain and an 8.31x throughput speedup across 9 coordinate-based grounding benchmarks (trajectory, affordance, and localization), while preserving multimodal understanding and reasoning across 11 text-based embodied benchmarks.
authors: Ruimeng Liu, Denan Liang, Ruofei Bai, Fuming Zhang, Kuan Xu, Shenghai Yuan, Lihua Xie
bullets: Targets slow, discontinuous discrete coordinate decoding and inadequate point regression for multi-contact or irregular affordances.
Shares lower multimodal layers while routing upper layers to specialized spatial and linguistic experts to reduce gradient interference.
Represents each coordinate as one token using visual positional embeddings, aligning coordinates with image features.
Uses differentiable Signed Distance Field supervision without requiring costly mask decoders.
Reports a 15.7% average gain and 8.31× throughput speedup across 9 coordinate-grounding benchmarks, while preserving performance across 11 text-based embodied benchmarks.

papers.abstract: We study humanoid navigation across multiple destinations under long-horizon language instructions. This task is challenging because robots must maintain progress across successive goals while continuously producing natural, stable whole-body motion through confined spaces. However, task decomposition in existing methods does not by itself ensure progress throughout execution, while waypoint-based navigation does not guarantee natural, route-faithful whole-body motion. Our key idea is to organize navigation into three complementary roles operating at different time scales: a Brain for task reasoning, a Cerebellum for local motion generation, and a Brainstem for whole-body execution. We realize this idea in LHNav, an asynchronous system that uses progress and arrival feedback to coordinate navigation goals, VLA motion-token prediction, and whole-body control. To train the Cerebellum for natural, route-faithful motion, we develop a physics-grounded data engine that improves physical tracking of motion references along collision-aware routes and pairs the resulting demonstrations with rendered visual observations. Together, these designs allow task planning to proceed alongside continuous movement and extend single-goal navigation to successive destinations with natural, route-faithful whole-body motion. In simulation, our navigation VLA outperforms OmniNav and DualVLN in single-goal success and motion smoothness, with fewer collisions and falls. Using a VLA trained only on single-goal demonstrations, LHNav achieves a 75.56% success rate on long-horizon navigation tasks. Deployment on the Unitree G1 further demonstrates single-goal navigation and zero-shot long-horizon task execution in real-world environments, including layouts with repositioned objects. Project website: https://robbyant-research.github.io/LHNav/.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of maintaining progress across successive goals while producing stable, natural whole-body motion in confined spaces.
Coordinates three asynchronous roles: a Brain for task reasoning, a Cerebellum for local motion generation, and a Brainstem for whole-body control.
Uses progress and arrival feedback to coordinate navigation goals, VLA motion-token prediction, and execution.
Introduces a physics-grounded data engine for collision-aware, route-faithful motion demonstrations paired with visual observations.

In simulation, LHNav improves success and smoothness while reducing collisions and falls; it reaches 75.56% long-horizon success using only single-goal training, and transfers to real-world zero-shot execution on a Unitree G1.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Our asynchronous three-layer navigation system. The Brain uses task management (Tool 1) to maintain an explicit plan and revise pending goals during execution, with goal-completion feedback from arrival verification (Tool 2). A subtask buffer supplies an instruction and target image to the Cerebellum, which uses current RGB and proprioceptive state st to jointly predict motion-token chunks and auxiliary waypoints at approximately 8 Hz. An action buffer supplies the latest motion-token chunk to the Brainstem’s frozen SONIC controller, which combines it with proprioception to produce joint targets at 50 Hz for PD control. The independent arrival-verification VLM updates the results buffer at up to 1 Hz. Geometric supervision encourages waypoint traversability during training.

papers.abstract: Directing a robot to locate a target object in unseen environments remains a central challenge in embodied AI. Vision-Language Model (VLM)-based methods provide rich semantic reasoning but often produce uncalibrated and overconfident action decisions. We introduce CPNav, a navigation framework that combines collision-aware planning with statistically calibrated VLM action scoring for map-free object-goal navigation. From RGB-D input, CPNav constructs a navigability map, generates collision-free motion primitives, and queries two VLMs for goal detection and action scoring. The resulting scores are calibrated offline via conformal prediction (CP) using oracle actions obtained through a tree-structured exploration procedure with backtracking, providing finite-sample guarantees at a user-specified risk level. The CP layer is model-agnostic and can wrap any VLM policy. Online, calibrated VLM scores guide action selection, while a tree-structured exploration history records alternative actions and allows backtracking. We evaluate CPNav in both simulation and real-world hardware settings. In AI Habitat simulation, compared with the uncalibrated baseline method, CPNav achieves relative SR and SPL improvements of 6.2% and 11.4% on HM3D v0.2, and 12.4% and 8.8% on MP3D, respectively. In real-world deployment on a modified Hiwonder MentorPi robot, the corresponding improvements in SR and SPL are 24.9% and 15.2%, respectively. Code is available at https://github.com/practice-lab-ucla/CPnav.
bullets: Targets overconfident, uncalibrated VLM action decisions in map-free object-goal navigation.
Uses RGB-D input to build a navigability map and generate collision-free motion primitives.

papers.abstract: Recommender systems are transitioning from static retrieval engines into interactive assistants grounded in physical environments. However, current studies largely neglect the combined complexities of spatial navigation, visual grounding, and multi-turn social interaction. To bridge this gap, we introduce SituRecBench, an interactive benchmark for evaluating frontier vision-language models (VLMs) as situated recommendation assistants within high-fidelity 3D environments. We reformulate recommendation as a situated assistance process in which an assistant interacts with a user while sharing the user's egocentric view. Our benchmark simulates real-world shopping environments (e.g., supermarkets and home furnishings stores), requiring assistants to elicit preferences, ground recommendations in the environment, and guide the user to relevant locations through dialogue. The benchmark evaluates dialogue quality, recommendation utility, and navigation effectiveness through a unified interactive protocol. Extensive experiments reveal persistent challenges in spatial grounding and preference elicitation, highlighting limitations in their ability to integrate global contextual information with local observations. SituRecBench provides a rigorous foundation for advancing the development of situated assistants in the real world.
bullets: Targets the combined challenges of spatial navigation, visual grounding, and multi-turn social interaction.

papers.abstract: Models for physical AI tasks, such as robotics and autonomous driving, need not reason solely in language. They can use visual plans--points, bounding boxes, and trajectories--to represent spatial goals and anticipate motion. However, autoregressive vision-language models generate these plans one coordinate token at a time, making richer predictions increasingly costly. We introduce VFlash, a method for fast, accurate visual planning through Flash Primitive Decoding. VFlash exploits the known structure of visual primitives to predict their coordinates jointly, using a lightweight drafter that generates an entire primitive in one forward pass. The layout adapts to the primitive's type, dimensionality, and length, supporting compact boxes and long, variable-length trajectories. Crucially, spatial accuracy need not require reproducing an autoregressive model's exact token sequence. VFlash therefore trains on annotated primitives and directly accepts structurally valid predictions without target-token agreement. Across the evaluated 2D and 3D robot trajectory tasks, VFlash consistently reduces prediction errors relative to autoregressive decoding. Preliminary single-rollout measurements indicate approximately 25x faster generation for 3D point motion forecasting. A world action model conditioned on VFlash plans achieves 70.2% average success across four MolmoSpaces task suites, compared with 62.6% for the baseline.
bullets: Targets the high cost of autoregressively generating coordinates for visual plans such as points, boxes, and trajectories.

A world action model using VFlash plans reaches 70.2% average success across four MolmoSpaces suites, versus 62.6% for the baseline.

papers.abstract: Real-world environments are messy, with paths often blocked by everyday objects like chairs and toys, requiring robots to perform interactive navigation by manipulating obstacles to clear a path. Existing methods rely on extensive simulation-based learning or per-scene instructions specifying which objects to avoid or manipulate. They struggle to generalize across novel objects, diverse environments, and varied contexts such as a cart of fragile glassware that should be avoided while an empty one can be pushed. We formalize this problem as open-world interactive navigation and present MessyNav, a zero-shot framework based on vision-language models (VLMs). At its core, MessyNav performs explicit VLM-based affordance reasoning before task planning to decide whether to swipe, pick up, or avoid an object and produce a high-level plan. Evaluated on a mobile manipulator across real-world indoor and outdoor environments, MessyNav improves success rate by 27 percentage points (pp) over the strongest baseline in real-robot trials and achieves statistically significant gains in a larger-scale offline evaluation, without task-specific training.
bullets: Addresses open-world interactive navigation where obstacles may need to be moved rather than avoided.
Uses explicit VLM affordance reasoning before planning to choose actions such as swiping, picking up, or avoiding objects.
Handles context-dependent cases, such as pushing an empty cart but avoiding one carrying fragile glassware.
Evaluated on a mobile manipulator in real indoor and outdoor environments.
Improves real-robot success by 27 percentage points over the strongest baseline, without task-specific training.

figures.caption: Figure 2: MessyNav: A framework for zero-shot open-world interactive navigation. MessyNav consists of an Affordance Reasoner that infers object interactability from an RGB image using a VLM to evaluate both robot-centric physical feasibility and object-centric interaction safety. For example, it will label a cart with a laptop as non-interactive while labeling a wheeled crate with a bin as interactive. Given the object affordance labels, a Task Planner then sequences manipulation and navigation actions from an open-language skill library containing a simple set of motion primitives (pick up, swipe left, swipe right) and a LiDAR-based navigation stack (move to) that we find can tackle a wide range of interactive navigation scenarios. Finally, the generated plan is executed by grounding object references in 3D coordinates using VLM keypoint identification, semantic segmentation, and depth-based deprojection.

Figure 4: Explicit affordance reasoning improves context-dependent task planning. In this scene, a suitcase supporting a stack of books is inherently unstable, while the black cart holding a single book can be safely cleared. [Left] MessyNav reasons about affordances before planning, correctly labeling the suitcase as non-interactive and the cart as interactive, and swiping the cart aside to clear the path. [Middle] vlm-planner-only plans directly from the image without an explicit affordance stage and incorrectly decides to swipe the unstable suitcase. [Right] closed-set-planner assigns fixed category-level affordances that misclassify the suitcase as interactive, leading to an unsafe plan.

Figure 5: Qualitative Results across Environments. We deploy MessyNav in varied settings to test its zero-shot capability. The robot successfully reasons about affordances and executes interactions across different lighting conditions, environments, and object types.

MessyNav succeeds on 10/15 trials versus 6/15 for vlm-planner-only. While most of vlm-planner-only’s failures are planning failures in which vlm-planner-only decides to interact with non-interactive objects (7 of 9), MessyNav reduces these to 2, showcasing the importance of explicit affordance reasoning.

Figure 3: MessyNav reasons about context, not just object category. In this cluttered scene, closed-set-oracle assigns affordances by category alone, misclassifying the rolling cart as interactive (ignoring the glassware it carries) and the suitcase as interactive (ignoring its fragile sticker). In contrast, MessyNav reasons at the instance level. It treats the cart and the glass stemware as a single fragile unit and reads the sticker on the suitcase as a contextual cue, correctly labeling both as non-interactive.

papers.abstract: The diagnostic capability of WSI agents relies on effective slide navigation to identify diagnostically relevant regions and efficiently integrate evidence across the slide. While in clinical practice, pathologists dynamically examine slides across multiple scales, integrating global and cellular evidence in a sequential manner, existing AI navigation approaches mostly operate at a single fixed magnification or rely on predefined magnification traversal. This mismatch prevents existing methods from modeling cross-magnification interactions and adaptive magnification selection inherent to real diagnostic workflows. We propose PathPilot, a clinically consistent multi-magnification WSI navigation agent that explicitly models cross-magnification localization and evidence-adaptive exploration. Specifically, we introduce a CrossMagLoc that learns magnification-specific diagnostic localization from pathologist viewing behavior and integrates information from adjacent magnifications to identify the diagnostically most relevant region within the current ROI, thereby providing a diagnostically informed starting point for subsequent question-conditioned exploration. We further introduce an EviRegionSearch that starts question-conditioned exploration from this region, progressively accumulating question-relevant evidence and adaptively determining the next navigation action according to the remaining evidence requirement. Their iterative interaction enables PathPilot to sequentially explore across ROIs and magnifications until sufficient evidence is acquired. Extensive QA evaluations across five cohorts demonstrate consistent superiority over competing SOTA methods on inter/external cohorts, respectively, validating question-conditioned evidence acquisition across regions and magnifications that mirrors the sequential, knowledge-driven navigation of pathologists.
bullets: Addresses the limitations of fixed-magnification and predefined-traversal WSI navigation agents.
CrossMagLoc uses pathologist viewing behavior and adjacent magnifications to localize diagnostically relevant regions.
EviRegionSearch begins from the localized region and selects subsequent actions based on remaining question-relevant evidence.
The two components iteratively explore regions and magnifications until sufficient evidence is acquired.
Evaluations across five cohorts report consistent superiority over competing methods on inter- and external-cohort QA tasks.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: Overview of the datasets and evaluation cohorts used in this study. Top: Three navigation datasets provide pathologist viewing supervision for CrossMagLoc, including the Skin Eye-Tracking dataset and the TUM Liver and TUM Uterine Viewpoint datasets. The Skin dataset additionally provides pixel-level tumor annotations for region-level localization evaluation. Bottom: Five open-ended QA cohorts are used for end-to-end PathPilot evaluation, comprising the internal TUM Liver and TUM-Uteria cohorts and the external TUM Skin, WSI-Bench TCGA-SKCM, and WSI-Bench TCGA-LIHC cohorts. For the TUM cohorts, the circular plots summarize the predefined H&E-visible findings grouped into tissue-level, architectural, and cellular categories; for the WSI-Bench cohorts, they summarize the distributions of question categories.

Fig. 2: Overview of PathPilot and its two complementary navigation components. Given a WSI and pathology question, PathPilot starts from the thumbnail and iteratively alternates between CrossMagLoc and EviRegionSearch until sufficient evidence has been accumulated for answering the question. CrossMagLoc performs question-agnostic localization of diagnostically relevant candidate ROIs at each magnification by combining magnification-specific representations with spatially aligned information from adjacent scales. EviRegionSearch performs question-conditioned exploration over the ROI identified by CrossMagLoc, integrates morphological observations from the selected ROI with the accumulated evidence, identifies the remaining evidence requirement, and adaptively determines the next navigation action (Move, Zoom In, Zoom Out, or Stop) to select the next region.

Fig. 1: Overview of PathPilot for adaptive WSI exploration. For each navigation step (e.g., Step t), CrossMagLoc identifies the diagnostically most relevant region within the current ROI, while EviRegionSearch accumulates question-relevant evidence and adaptively selects the next navigation action (e.g., Step t+1). Their iterative interaction enables sequential movement across ROIs and magnifications until evidence is sufficient (e.g., Step t + N), where Stop is selected and the final answer is generated.

Fig. 4: QA performance of PathPilot across internal and external validation cohorts. Comparisons include pathology-specialized thumbnail-based VLMs (PathGen-LLaVA and Patho-R1-7B), patch-based WSI VLMs (WSI-LLaVA and ANTONI-Alpha), and pathology agents (PathAgent and PathNavigate). The left radar plot summarizes average performance across all questions on two internal cohorts (TUM-Uteria and TUM Liver) and three external cohorts (TUM Skin, WSI-Bench TCGA-SKCM, and WSI-Bench TCGA-LIHC). The four right-hand plots further assess tissue-level, architectural-level, and cellular-level QA on the three TUM cohorts, and morphology-focused QA on the two WSI-Bench cohorts, distinguishing overall QA performance from performance on specific pathological assessment tasks. Each cohort is evaluated using GACC, PBR, and 1− IAR, with higher values indicating better performance on all axes. Colored outer arcs identify cohorts; solid and dashed arcs denote internal and external validation, respectively. The plots summarize the quantitative results in Tables 2–5.

Fig. 5: Pathologist-in-the-loop interpretation of CrossMagLoc across five magnifications (thumbnail, 1.25×, 2.5×, 5×, and 10×; top to bottom). The columns show the pathology images (column 1), CrossMagLoc predictions (column 2), test-set navigation annotations (column 3), and independent annotations with morphological explanations from pathologists trained in Europe (column 4) and Asia (column 5). Across magnifications, CrossMagLoc consistently prioritizes diagnostically relevant regions identified by the pathologists while deprioritizing non-primary or artifact-limited areas. At 2.5×, it assigns higher attention to well-preserved tumor regions than to the crush-artifact region, while at higher magnifications it continues to emphasize morphologically informative tumor regions. Overall, its localization broadly agrees with pathologist viewing behavior while additionally highlighting clinically relevant regions identified during independent review.

Fig. 7: Visualization of a representative question-conditioned navigation workflow. CrossMagLoc-based ROI localization and EviRegionSearch-based evidence reasoning are iteratively coupled to support adaptive exploration across regions and magnifications, evidence requirement reasoning, and final answer generation once sufficient evidence is acquired.

Fig. 6: Quantitative evaluation of CrossMagLoc navigation performance. The radar plot summarizes pathologist-prioritization alignment (ρN , APN 5 , and 1 − JS N ) and tumor-region precision/recall at the thumbnail, 1.25×, and 2.5× magnifications, with PathFinder Ghezloo et al. (2025) and PathAttFormer Chakraborty et al. (2022) as navigation baselines and pathologist navigation as a clinical reference for tumor-region alignment. CrossMagLoc achieves the strongest agreement with pathologist prioritization while maintaining high tumor recall across magnifications, indicating a similar balance between diagnostic focus and broad tumor coverage.

papers.abstract: Large language models understand passengers' driving commands, but as driving agents they reason in generated text for seconds and must infer each action's consequences implicitly from the scene. We present Jev-AD, which pairs Jev, a typed decision model that answers predefined questions with probabilities, not generated text, with a language world model that predicts for every candidate action how nearby vehicles move over the next two seconds. Code turns these predictions into foreseen consequences, which Jev compares instead of inferring them from coordinates. In simulated highway merging (500 car-episodes), this foresight lowers the same decision model's collision rate from 26.0% to 2.4% at 0.25 seconds per decision, and Jev-AD achieves the passenger's intent in 93% of free-form command trials. In 500 replayed real-world NGSIM episodes, foresight lowers the collision rate from 48.2% to 2.8%, and the world model, learned from this traffic, foresees 93% of dangerous actions. Project page: https://ys-qu.github.io/jev-ad-website.
authors: Yansong Qu, Jiancong Chen, Samuel Labi
bullets: Addresses the risk that language-based driving agents reason too slowly and infer action consequences implicitly.
Combines Jev, a typed probabilistic decision model, with a language world model forecasting two seconds of surrounding-vehicle motion.
Uses code to convert forecasts into explicit consequences that Jev compares across candidate actions.
In simulated highway merging, foresight reduced collision rate from 26.0% to 2.4% while maintaining 0.25-second decision latency.
Across free-form commands and replayed NGSIM episodes, the system achieved 93% intent fulfillment and reduced replay collision rate from 48.2% to 2.8%.

papers.abstract: Web services provide walking directions for nearly every city, but following them reliably over long routes remains challenging for autonomous robots. Point-goal navigation policies rely heavily on accurate GNSS, while most vision-language navigation models struggle to execute even short instructions outdoors. We present WayTrace, a hierarchical system that connects web-map directions to robot motion through language. An off-the-shelf orchestrator vision-language model reads the turn-by-turn directions, a satellite map and recent camera images, and issues one atomic language command at a time, such as "cross the road to the left". An onboard trace predictor, trained on over one million automatically labelled samples from street-level images, draws the path for this command in the image, and a reinforcement learning policy tracks it. In long-range simulated missions, WayTrace remains robust to GNSS noise and rarely leaves crosswalks or sidewalks, while point-goal baselines degrade sharply with about ten times more violations. Deployed on a wheeled-legged robot, WayTrace completes real-world missions of up to 1.37 km at about 1.1 m/s through a busy city centre, rural trails and a university campus, handling crosswalks, staircases and construction sites. Project page: https://way-trace.github.io
authors: Manthan Patel, Jonas Frey, Pascal Roth, Marco Hutter, Cesar Cadena
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of reliable outdoor, long-range navigation despite GNSS noise and weak vision-language instruction execution.
Uses a vision-language orchestrator to interpret turn-by-turn maps, satellite imagery, and camera views into atomic commands.
A trace predictor converts each command into an image-space path, which a reinforcement-learning policy follows.
In simulation, it remains robust to GNSS noise and produces about ten times fewer crosswalk and sidewalk violations than point-goal baselines.
A wheeled-legged robot completed missions up to 1.37 km across urban, rural, and campus environments, including stairs and construction sites.

papers.abstract: By harnessing the inherent commonsense capabilities of pretrained Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs), current Vision-Language Action(VLA) models for legged robots excel at interpreting language-based navigation commands but lack the physical grounding and explicit safety assurance required for real-world operation. Therefore, this paper aims to cage Legged-Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) through a safety architecture that provides physical grounding and ensures navigation safety. The key idea is not to abandon the powerful capabilities of end-to-end VLA planning, but rather to augment and cage them. In particular, we integrate a high-level VLA planner with a low-level physical-grounding layer that leverages efficient state estimation, in-situ 3D spatial perception, and an Signed Distance Field (SDF) representation to generate executable trajectories. We provide a navigation planner with provable collision-avoidance guarantees under the stated assumptions by combining a low-dimensional Bezier-parameterized MPPI planner with Discrete Exponential Barrier Function (dEBF) constraints. The proposed Legged-VLN system is modular, making it compatible with various VLM/VLA models and agnostic to the robot platform. The proposed system is validated with extensive real-world experiments on humanoid and quadrupedal robots, demonstrating versatile, efficient, and safe vision-language driven navigation capabilities.
authors: Abhijeet M. Kulkarni, Saimouli Katragadda, Yuze Du, Zijun Sha, Guoquan Huang
bullets: Addresses the gap between language-level VLA planning and the physical safety requirements of real-world legged-robot navigation.
Combines a high-level VLA planner with state estimation, in-situ 3D perception, and signed distance fields to produce executable trajectories.
Uses a low-dimensional Bezier-parameterized MPPI planner with discrete exponential barrier-function constraints for collision avoidance under stated assumptions.
The platform-agnostic system is compatible with different VLM/VLA models and is evaluated on both humanoid and quadrupedal robots.
Real-world experiments demonstrate versatile, efficient, and safe vision-language navigation.

papers.abstract: As embodied agents perform object-goal navigation across residential environments, they accumulate successful experiences whose semantic structure recurs across scenes even when geometric trajectories do not. Reusing such experience is challenging because differences in region naming and observation granularity produce distinct graph representations of similar approaches, while meaningful differences in anchors, branches, and endpoints must stay distinguishable. We introduce HTCE, a homeomorphism-inspired topological framework that canonicalizes and reuses navigation experience. Feature and topology subdivisions characterize representational variations, and their semantically constrained reductions produce comparable semantic sequences and structural signatures while preserving semantic anchors, branching relations, and navigation endpoints. HTCE then retrieves historical successful approaches through subdivision-aware matching as guidance for a frozen vision-language policy. Canonicalization compresses the experience index losslessly, merging 17.7--23.6\% of distinct stored route descriptions while retaining full task performance. Under a single frozen vision-language backbone shared by all compared systems, HTCE attains the best SR and SPL in every setting---59.9\%/31.8\% on HM3D v0.1, 71.0\%/31.5\% on HM3D v0.2, and 46.6\%/16.6\% on MP3D---with SR gains of up to 4.9 points and structured retrieval contributing up to 2.8 SPL points. The code is available in https://github.com/startracker0/htce.git
authors: Xiaoran Xu, Yupeng Wu, Tianyu Xue, Xuanran Dong, Yifan Xu, Xiaoshan Yang, Changsheng Xu
bullets: Addresses mismatched region naming and observation granularity while preserving meaningful anchors, branches, and endpoints.
Uses feature and topology subdivisions with semantically constrained reductions to create comparable route sequences and structural signatures.
Retrieves prior successful approaches through subdivision-aware matching to guide a frozen vision-language policy.
Losslessly merges 17.7–23.6% of distinct route descriptions while retaining full task performance.
Achieves the best reported SR and SPL across HM3D and MP3D settings, with gains of up to 4.9 SR points and 2.8 SPL points from structured retrieval.

papers.abstract: Natural human-robot interaction requires robots to interpret language and gestures within a 3D environment to support tasks such as pick-and-place and object retrieval. 3D Embodied Reference Understanding (3D-ERU) supports this by identifying the 3D location of a target object from a scene (point-cloud) containing a human pointing gesture and an accompanying language description. However, current 3D-ERU models lack alignment of cross-modal representations and incur high processing costs that increase with the point-cloud's size. To address this, we propose GVT3D, which employs an Embodied Fusion module that jointly models language, gesture, and vision inputs within a shared embedding space, promoting cross-modal alignment. We additionally introduce a foveation approach that selectively processes the point cloud within a coarse region around the estimated pointing direction to reduce computations. GVT3D achieves ~8% higher accuracy and foveation enables 2.95x faster execution while maintaining comparable accuracy, relative to prior 3D-ERU models.

bullets: Targets robot understanding of object references from a 3D scene, pointing gesture, and language description.

Applies foveation to focus point-cloud processing on a coarse region near the estimated pointing direction.
Reports approximately 8% higher accuracy and 2.95× faster execution with comparable accuracy when foveation is used, relative to prior models.

papers.abstract: Video games provide a practical setting for collecting vision-language-action (VLA) data, whose acquisition in physical environments is costly. Existing datasets, however, remain limited by restricted game coverage, sparse language supervision, or temporal hierarchies that do not necessarily reflect changes in task objectives. We introduce AceAction, a dataset of human gameplay across multiple 3D games for learning skill composition and subgoal transitions. AceAction organizes demonstrations around complete tasks, linking overall instructions, ordered subgoals, and local skill instructions to temporally aligned visual observations and keyboard-and-mouse actions. To construct these annotations, we develop a vision-language model pipeline that identifies subgoals from changes in objectives or interaction targets, anchors navigation goals to visually recognizable waypoints, and composes adjacent subgoals into task instructions. The resulting demonstrations cover navigation, reconnaissance, combat, interaction, and recovery, with explicit stage boundaries that connect task progression to fine-grained control. We assess annotation quality through model-based verification and human inspection. An audit of 500 trajectories yields a 95.8% pass rate across independent reviewer assessments. AceAction provides a data foundation for studying how agents execute, combine, and switch skills to follow complex instructions in dynamic game environments.
authors: Kailing Li, Ruoxuan Zhang, Zheyuan Zhou, Boyang Chu, Yingshan Lei, Hongxia Xie, Liang Du, Zixun Sun
bullets: Covers diverse 3D-game tasks including navigation, reconnaissance, combat, interaction, and recovery.
Organizes demonstrations into complete tasks with overall instructions, ordered subgoals, local skill instructions, visual observations, and keyboard-mouse actions.
Uses a vision-language pipeline to detect objective or interaction-target changes, ground navigation goals in visual waypoints, and compose task instructions.
Explicit stage boundaries connect task progression with low-level control and skill transitions.
Annotation quality was evaluated through model verification and human inspection; an audit of 500 trajectories achieved a 95.8% pass rate.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal agents have shown promising progress in embodied planning and web interaction. However, existing evaluations often rely on simplified tasks with limited combinatorial structure, leaving it unclear whether current agents can robustly integrate perception and reasoning for multi-goal planning under temporal, physical, and multimodal constraints. We introduce DualWorldBench, a unified benchmark for evaluating agent planning under controlled symbolic--temporal and grounded--topological complexity. Built around a shared pickup--delivery interface, DualWorldBench consists of three complementary components: TextWorld, which isolates symbolic planning under varying task compositions and release dynamics; SimWorld, which evaluates grounded path planning under controlled topological variation with text, image, or multimodal inputs; and DualWorld-VQA, a diagnostic suite spanning perception, scene understanding, and planning. Experiments reveal a common gap between local understanding and globally consistent planning. In TextWorld, agents struggle to derive optimal task sequences under interacting temporal constraints; in SimWorld, grounded observations are not reliably converted into feasible action sequences. DualWorld-VQA further confirms that perception and topology understanding do not necessarily translate into constrained planning. Together, these results identify the central challenge as composing symbolic or grounded evidence into globally feasible and efficient multi-goal plans. These findings establish DualWorldBench as a challenging testbed for agents with tighter perception--reasoning--planning integration. All datasets and code are publicly available at our project website https://dualworld.netlify.app/.
authors: Yang Chen, Bin Wen, Danyang Peng, Hong-Jie You, Zi-Qiao Shang, Lan-Zhe Guo
bullets: Targets embodied and web agents’ difficulty with multi-goal planning under temporal, physical, and multimodal constraints.
Provides TextWorld for symbolic temporal planning, SimWorld for grounded topological path planning, and DualWorld-VQA for perception, scene understanding, and planning diagnostics.
Finds a gap between local understanding and globally consistent planning: agents miss optimal task sequences and produce infeasible grounded actions.
Shows that perception and topology understanding alone do not reliably support constrained planning.
Datasets and code are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Embodied agents are increasingly deployed in open-world environments, yet current robustness evaluations remain biased toward hazardous instructions and jailbreak vulnerabilities. A more fundamental issue is largely overlooked: agents are rarely tested under semantically sufficient but contextually minimal instructions (i.e., common in real-world human communication), where auxiliary contextual cues are absent. For the first, we identify a novel phenomenon termed Ambient Context Illusion, where agents fail to execute tasks correctly when non-essential contextual details are omitted, despite unchanged task semantics. To systematically study this, we establish VagueBench, a benchmark built upon the AI2-THOR interactive simulation environment for the evaluation of context dependency in embodied agents. We systematically consider key semantic components of instructions (entities, procedures, constraints, and prior knowledge) and derive a unified taxonomy with four categories and nine subtypes to reduce auxiliary information. VagueBench contains 1,303 instruction pairs across diverse indoor environments, constructed via a human-agent co-generation framework that integrates semantic redundancy estimation, taxonomy-guided transformation, and rigorous semantic-invariance verification. Through extensive evaluation on 6 state-of-the-art embodied agents, we observe significant degradation on VagueBench in both task performance and executability (relatively -19.65% in task success rate and relatively +54.10% in empty plan rate) revealing a strong reliance on auxiliary linguistic signals rather than core task semantics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this phenomenon persists in real-world robotic systems, where it can lead to incorrect decisions and potential safety risks.
authors: Yang Qu, Qiang Fu, Zonghao Ying, Jiayi Zhao, Yaoyuan Zhang, Jinyang Guo, Jian Yang, Aishan Liu, Yingxun Wang, Xianglong Liu
bullets: Introduces Ambient Context Illusion: removing non-essential details can impair task execution without changing instruction semantics.
Builds VagueBench in AI2-THOR with 1,303 instruction pairs spanning four categories and nine subtypes of omitted context.
Uses semantic redundancy estimation, taxonomy-guided transformations, and semantic-invariance verification to create the benchmark.
Evaluation across six embodied agents shows relative task-success drops of 19.65% and empty-plan rates rising by 54.10%.
The issue also appears in real-world robotic systems, potentially causing incorrect decisions and safety risks.

papers.abstract: Vision-language model (VLM) agents that act in the open world need two abilities: world knowledge to interpret what they see, and exploration to find what they cannot yet see. We study how agents combine the two through interactive visual geolocation. GeoGuesser Bench contains 282 tasks in an offline Street View environment where agents rotate, zoom, and move between real panoramas. Its three task types shift the balance from knowledge to exploration: agents (1) report the coordinates of their starting location, (2) name the enclosing street, city, state, or country, or (3) find, read, and count nearby objects. The coordinate tasks in (1) also include 42 real GeoGuessr World Championship rounds, whose expert guesses provide a human reference. We evaluate 23 VLMs: the best accuracy is 62.5% on place naming and 35.0% on object finding, and the best agent averages 4352.4 GeoGuessr points on the championship rounds, against 4770.3 for the better expert in each round. Beyond these headline numbers, world knowledge and exploration are only weakly correlated across models: agents that localize well do not necessarily explore well. To understand where agents fail, we categorize their errors into vision, navigation, and tool-use failures. Further ablations show that the strongest agents, such as Claude Opus 4.8, still perform well with limited views, while weaker agents degrade; customizing the environment thus adjusts task difficulty. The environment's verifiable rewards and restorable state also support training, and our Planner-Worker-Compressor harness cuts planner tokens by 57-61% by compacting the interaction history. We hope GeoGuesser Bench and its environment serve as a high-quality foundation for simulating real-world exploration at scale.
bullets: Introduces 282 offline Street View tasks involving panorama rotation, zooming, and movement, plus 42 expert-referenced GeoGuessr championship rounds.
Tests three task types: coordinate localization, place naming, and finding, reading, or counting nearby objects.
Evaluates 23 VLMs; best reported accuracy is 62.5% for place naming and 35.0% for object finding, while the strongest agent approaches expert GeoGuessr performance.
Finds only weak correlation between localization and exploration ability, with errors categorized as vision, navigation, or tool-use failures.
Shows that environment difficulty can be adjusted through view limits and that a Planner-Worker-Compressor harness reduces planner tokens by 57–61%.

papers.abstract: Embodied agents that answer questions about their route need a memory of what they saw, and scene graphs are a natural form for it. A vision-language model (VLM) can receive such a graph as text or through a graph encoder, but accuracy alone cannot show whether the graph holds the episode's facts, reaches the model, or is actually relied on. In this diagnostic study, we introduce a graph-swap test for the last of these: each episode is given another episode's graph, and we count how many answers change. On an embodied question-answering benchmark with routes through two to seven rooms, we use it to compare ways of delivering scene-graph memory to a fine-tuned VLM. As text, the memory is used strongly, adding 30 points on route questions. As a graph, it is not, and we trace why: the encoder preserves the information, but standard pooled and late fusion discard it. Giving each node its own input token recovers part of it, a gain of 8.3 points on route questions that the swap test confirms comes from the graph. The test also exposes a shortcut that accuracy hides: when the same facts appear in the text, the model ignores its graph. The test thus offers a cheap check of whether a VLM uses its scene-graph memory, and our analysis points to how that memory should be delivered.
bullets: The study tests whether scene-graph memory is represented, reaches the VLM, and actually influences answers.
It swaps each episode’s graph with another episode’s graph and counts answer changes to measure graph reliance.
Text-based graph memory is strongly used, improving route-question performance by 30 points.
Graph encoders preserve information, but standard pooled and late fusion discard its usefulness.

Giving each graph node its own input token recovers part of the benefit, with an 8.3-point route-question gain confirmed by the swap test; duplicated text facts can cause the model to ignore the graph.

papers.abstract: Embodied question answering asks an agent to navigate, observe, and then answer questions about what it saw, yet answer accuracy alone cannot tell whether any of this happened. A plausible answer can come from the question, the room label, or the answer choices, and a correct answer does not show that the supporting observation was ever made. We present a multi-room benchmark whose 200 test episodes and 800 questions are stratified by route extent, with an evaluation ladder that holds the questions fixed while varying only the evidence supplied to the answerer, from text-only probes through closed-loop agents to replay of the reference trajectory. Questions are generated from symbolic records of rooms, visible objects, and frames, so every answer can be traced to the observations that support it. A closed-loop vision-language agent reaches no target in 200 episodes yet answers 45.5% of questions, within 0.1 points of the same model given no images; replaying the reference trajectory raises the same model to 57.4%, so the evidence exists along the route but is not gathered. A family-level audit then shows that access to evidence is not the same as use of it. Four of eight families are largely answerable from text, one cites frames that cannot establish its own answer, and the oracle conditions reach 59.5% on Rooms-visited by counting the supplied images. Evidence acquisition, answer coverage, and shortcut sensitivity must therefore be established before an accuracy gain can be credited to memory.
bullets: Evaluates 200 multi-room episodes and 800 questions across route extents.
Uses fixed questions with progressively richer evidence: text-only, closed-loop agents, and reference-trajectory replay.
The tested agent reaches no targets but answers 45.5% of questions, nearly matching its no-image performance.
Replay of the reference trajectory raises accuracy to 57.4%, indicating evidence is available but often not acquired or used.
The audit finds substantial text shortcuts and shows that answer accuracy alone cannot establish grounded observation.

papers.abstract: Most agentic robotic systems use vision-language models (VLMs) either to orchestrate predefined skills or to directly generate actions, constraints, and control programs. The former is limited by the available skill library, while the latter requires VLMs to reason about precise geometry and contact. In this paper, we propose WorldSketch, a new paradigm for agentic robotics in which a VLM constructs a world model rather than generating robot actions. The VLM acts as an agent that actively queries perception tools to build and visually validate a minimal kinematic world model, capturing only task-relevant objects, their interaction geometry, and possible motions. A geometric planner then jointly optimizes contact and whole-body motion on the resulting model. Moreover, the world model is self-improving: execution feedback verifies outcomes, updates uncertain hypotheses, and enables the agent to revise the model when its predictions are contradicted. We demonstrate the generality of this paradigm across RoboCasa, LIBERO-PRO, and R2R-CE navigation, achieving zero-shot success rates of 91%, 97%, and 76%, respectively. On RoboCasa, WorldSketch outperforms the next-best zero-shot agent baseline by 58 percentage points while using 10 times fewer VLM input tokens; on LIBERO-PRO, it exceeds CaP-X by 82 percentage points. In navigation, it matches the success rate of step-by-step VLM agents while using 6 times fewer input tokens.
bullets: Addresses the limits of skill-library orchestration and the difficulty of precise geometric reasoning by VLMs.
The VLM actively queries perception tools to construct and visually validate minimal kinematic models of relevant objects, interactions, and motions.
A geometric planner jointly optimizes contact and whole-body motion using the constructed model.
Execution feedback verifies results, updates uncertain hypotheses, and supports model revision when predictions fail.
Demonstrated across RoboCasa, LIBERO-PRO, and R2R-CE navigation, with success rates of 91%, 97%, and 76%, respectively, while using substantially fewer VLM input tokens than comparable approaches.

papers.abstract: Giving embodied agents the freedom to act autonomously, initiate interactions, and understand their surroundings through experience is a step toward bringing them to life in the physical world. Realizing this vision requires action, interaction, and memory to work together, so that each encounter can inform current decisions and contribute experience for future tasks. We present EvoLife, a unified navigation harness that enables a multimodal embodied agent to choose how to move, when to ask, and what experience to carry forward. Its hybrid action space supports waypoint navigation, local discrete adjustments, pixel-based navigation, and object-directed navigation. Active interaction allows the agent to seek clarification or assistance when it encounters ambiguity or difficulty, while persistent spatial memory binds observations and dialogue to places, retaining useful experience to guide subsequent visits. We evaluate eight benchmarks across four task families: vision-language navigation, object navigation, interactive instance navigation, and continuous multi-task navigation. With an average of only 1.87 active interactions per episode, our method achieves a first-visit success rate (SR) of 100% across four 100-episode sets spanning vision-language navigation and object navigation. Complete-sequence SR reaches 98% on 50 LHPR-VLN sequences and 94% on 50 GOAT-Bench sequences. In the R2R revisit setting, success weighted by path length (SPL) increases from 82.23% to 93.31% with retained experience. Multi-day physical navigation further demonstrates exploration, proactive help-seeking, and revisiting remembered places. Together, these results advance the vision of bringing embodied agents to life through autonomous action, proactive interaction, and the accumulation and reuse of experience.
bullets: Supports waypoint, discrete local, pixel-based, and object-directed navigation actions.
Lets agents ask for clarification or assistance when facing ambiguity or difficulty.
Stores observations and dialogue by location to improve future visits.
Evaluated across eight benchmarks spanning four navigation task families and multi-day physical navigation.
Reports strong performance, including 100% first-visit SR across four 100-episode sets and improved R2R revisit SPL from 82.23% to 93.31%.

Only the generated natural-language response is returned to the navigation agent, which independently makes subsequent decisions. papers.abstract: Human cognition flexibly draws on a shared perceptual foundation to understand environments, attend to referenced entities, reason about spatial relationships, and act. Endowing aerial robots with an analogous functional organization remains challenging, as existing systems are often specialized for individual capabilities, dependent on offboard computation, or unable to sustain closed-loop operation on resource-constrained platforms. We present OpenFlyV2, a unified onboard vision-language-action architecture that uses a shared vision-language representation to support semantic understanding, language-grounded perception, spatial reasoning, and continuous aerial control within a single model. A compact action expert converts the shared multimodal context into short-horizon flight waypoints, while motion-aware temporal memory and action priors reduce the computational cost of closed-loop execution. We construct \dataset{}, a simulation-based dataset comprising approximately 70,000 navigation trajectories and 60,000 vision-language instruction--response pairs. OpenFlyV2 generates action chunks, each comprising 12 waypoints, entirely onboard at 10 Hz using an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX. It transfers zero-shot from simulation to physical quadrotor flight, achieving a 48\% navigation success rate across four real-world environments without real-world aerial training data. Extensive results demonstrate that broad vision-language competence and continuous closed-loop flight can coexist within a single model on a resource-constrained aerial platform. Code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/Ideal-ljl/AeroBrain.

papers.abstract: Visual grounding is crucial for robots to understand language instructions with visual observations. This paper addresses the problem of visual grounding uncertainties, where a robot uses a black-box vision-language model (VLM) to ground free-form natural-language instructions to target objects. Prevailing methods derive uncertainty from the VLM itself. Yet, outputs of the VLM, e.g., generated uncertainties, are from the same parameters and structures producing the predictions, and inherit the bias. We give a formal Bayesian definition of the problem that treats the VLM prediction as an observation. An external surrogate Bayesian model then quantifies per-query uncertainty over a local neighborhood of a held-out calibration set, decomposed into aleatoric and epistemic components. A hierarchical retrieval across input modalities realizes a compact joint-space neighborhood, mitigating the curse of dimensionality. The estimator further integrates with conformal prediction or model-based planning for active visual grounding, where robots are allowed to take verbal or physical actions to ground targets. Across grounding benchmarks and state-of-the-art VLMs, it consistently improves both calibration and task performance. On a real Fetch robot under open-world instructions, it enables principled trade-offs between confident action and information gathering, substantially improving robustness.
authors: Hanbo Zhang, Tianrun Hu, Cedar Site Bai, Anxing Xiao, David Hsu

papers.abstract: Embodied instruction following in interactive environments requires agents to interpret natural language commands and complete long-horizon tasks. Existing planners either rely on large labeled trajectories, or use few-shot and zero-shot LLM prompting that produces a whole plan in a single serial reasoning process. These approaches depend on linguistic common sense, commit to a plan from the initial instruction, and only update after failures, which weakens robustness and state awareness. We present AtomTree, a hierarchical framework for state-aware task planning with LLMs. AtomTree incrementally builds a tree of subgoals and actions, where the LLM decides at each step, from the current symbolic state, whether to further decompose or to output a grounded low-level action. A lightweight memory module summarizes past outcomes for reuse in later decisions. When a low-level action stalls, AtomTree triggers hierarchical backtracking replanning to return to the parent node and regenerate the subtree plan from the latest state, preventing continued drift along an incorrect trajectory. In zero-shot evaluation on the ALFRED benchmark, AtomTree outperforms prior LLM-based planners. Project page: https://zhaihaotian.github.io/atomtree-website/.
authors: Haotian Zhai, Tianming Sha, Junnan Li
bullets: Addresses the brittleness of one-shot, serial LLM plans for long-horizon interactive tasks.
