Outperforms prior LLM-based planners in zero-shot evaluation on ALFRED.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of our hierarchical planning framework for embodied instruction following. Given a task instruction and the current visual state, our method recursively decides whether to decompose the current goal into finer-grained subgoals or execute it directly. This process incrementally builds an explicit hierarchical goal tree, shown in the upper-right panel, where higher-level goals are progressively refined into executable actions. In contrast, we compare against two representative paradigms: (1) a fully supervised end-to-end EIF model trained on the full dataset, and (2) an LLM-based method using retrieved few-shot examples. While these baselines may produce incorrect action sequences, our method maintains a structured tree-based plan and performs step-by-step decomposition conditioned on the current state and memory, enabling more accurate long-horizon reasoning and execution.

Fig. 3: Overview of our state-aware decision prompt. The prompt summarizes the role and mission, decision options, input information, available atomic actions, global rules, output format, and a small set of decision-guiding examples. Given the current subgoal together with the current state and memory, the LLM predicts whether to decompose the goal into subtasks or execute it directly.

papers.abstract: Zero-shot vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires an agent to use past observations without navigation-specific training. We study what information an 8B-scale navigation system should retain and how it should be organized for subsequent decisions. Our agent combines instruction progress, hierarchically compressed observation history anchored to poses, and accumulated geometry in complementary task, temporal, and spatial memories. An 8B observer summarizes observations, and an 8B reasoner uses the memories to select waypoint intents or request additional views, a geometric controller executes the selected targets. A semantic information perspective motivates the distinction between retaining evidence, making it accessible to the reasoner, and acquiring further observations. On R2R-CE val-unseen, the complete system achieves the highest among the evaluated Qwen3-based zero-shot baselines. Removing temporal memory reduces SR and sharply increases average path length from 16.9 to 39.1m, removing the spatial-map and planning component reduces SR as well. Real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 show that our zero-shot method achieves higher success rates than the post-trained baseline in both corridor and office environments, suggesting better transfer to the evaluated real-world settings. As a complementary evaluation, LAW2 uses paired instruction interventions to examine behavioral responses, instruction following ability beyond endpoint success. These results support preserving task progress, observation history, and geometry in structured memory for zero-shot navigation with smaller open models.

papers.title: What Should a Navigator Remember? Spatiotemporal Memory for Zero-Shot Vision-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: A structured spatiotemporal memory helps an 8B vision-language navigator perform zero-shot navigation by retaining task progress, observation history, and spatial geometry.

papers.abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE) requires instruction-consistent planning and reliable execution under collision constraints. Yet many hierarchical approaches optimize the planner while keeping execution fixed. We introduce MATCH, a framework that jointly learns a language-conditioned planner and a goal-conditioned primitive-action executor. An execution-aware topological graph represents start-dependent execution options and integrates executor value estimates with realized outcome memory, enabling the planner to select execution requests and refine their targets through bounded continuous offsets. A transition-aware dense macro reward balances ordered progress along the reference route against execution residual, encouraging executable requests without substituting local success for instruction following. A staged curriculum culminates in synchronized on-policy updates, with the executor learning on planner-generated requests and the planner adapting its requests to the executor's current behavior. With 0.5B parameters, MATCH achieves state-of-the-art performance on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks. Preliminary real-robot deployments further demonstrate its practical potential.
authors: Shuhao Ye, Yufei Wei, Demao Wang, Shichao Zhai, Rong Xiong, Yue Wang
bullets: Targets VLN-CE challenges involving collision-aware execution and instruction-consistent planning.
Uses an execution-aware topological graph combining executor value estimates with realized outcome memory.
Allows the planner to issue execution requests and refine targets through bounded continuous offsets.
Introduces a dense macro reward balancing ordered route progress with execution residual.
Staged curriculum and synchronized on-policy learning couple planner and executor adaptation; reports state-of-the-art results on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, with preliminary real-robot demonstrations.

Fig. 5: Real robot deployment. We deployed MATCH on a robot modified from TurtleBot 4 and tested it across four episodes.

papers.selection_reason: Jointly learns language-conditioned planner and goal-conditioned executor for VLN in continuous environments.
papers.title: MATCH: Execution-Aware Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning for Vision-and-Language Navigation in Continuous Environment
papers.tldr: MATCH jointly trains a language-conditioned planner and an adaptive action executor to improve instruction-following navigation in continuous environments.

papers.abstract: General-purpose embodied intelligence requires robots to coordinate diverse skills over long horizons, track task progress, and recover from failures. Specialist policies alone do not ensure task-level reliability, while powerful multimodal agents rely on costly reasoning and external experience that compact models struggle to reproduce. We introduce OmniBrain-0, a lightweight unified embodied agent that coordinates manipulation and navigation through a shared high-level decision model, integrating task understanding, planning, progress tracking, and feedback-driven recovery. Our progressive training framework combines embodied pretraining, domain-specialized agent distillation, and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). It distills powerful teachers' interaction experience into manipulation and navigation experts, then consolidates their decision capabilities into OmniBrain-0. Unification therefore occurs within the learned decision model rather than only at the tool interface. We further introduce Rubric-Guided Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI), a data flywheel in which a Meta-Agent turns execution evidence into refined rubrics, step-level reminders, and verified trajectories for domain-expert updates before their reconsolidation into OmniBrain-0 through MOPD. We evaluate OmniBrain-0 on LIBERO-Pro, LIBERO-Plus, RoboCasa365, RoboTwin 2.0, and R2R-CE Val-Unseen, as well as multiple real-world manipulation tasks. OmniBrain-0 combines strong cross-domain task performance with substantially lower inference and execution overhead than its closed-source teacher, demonstrating efficient transfer and consolidation of embodied capabilities into a compact unified agent.
bullets: Targets reliable long-horizon robot behavior, where specialist policies and costly multimodal agents have limitations.
Uses a shared high-level decision model for task understanding, planning, progress tracking, and feedback-driven recovery.
Trains progressively through embodied pretraining, agent distillation, and multi-teacher on-policy distillation to consolidate domain expertise.
Introduces Rubric-Guided Recursive Self-Improvement, which converts execution evidence into rubrics, reminders, and verified trajectories for iterative updates.
Evaluated across simulated manipulation, navigation, and real-world manipulation tasks, showing strong cross-domain performance with lower inference and execution overhead than its teacher.
papers.selection_reason: Unified embodied agent coordinating manipulation and navigation with language-guided tasks and distillation.
papers.title: OmniBrain-0: A Unified Agentic Model for Embodied Intelligence
papers.tldr: OmniBrain-0 is a compact unified embodied agent that combines manipulation and navigation with planning, progress tracking, and failure recovery at lower overhead than a larger closed-source teacher.

papers.abstract: We present and tackle two problems associated with deploying Foundation Models (FMs) on Embodied Agents performing navigation: 1) Training bias in FMs leading to poor personalization in unseen environments, and 2) Limited FM context length hindering success, especially on long horizon tasks. Our solution for the former involves priming the FM with human-habit data mined from the scene and our solution for the latter involves active memory management via a novel `memory head' augmentation. We first present a taxonomy of existing literature on FM-based Embodied Navigation, and highlight these limitations. We then present our approaches, Transit-Aware Planning (TAP) and MemCtrl to address the limitations. With TAP, we present real-world results in a lab environment with a Turtlebot for personalized target finding that shows an average improvement of 18% over a non-TAP baseline. On MemCtrl, we report a 6% average improvement across various embodied tasks, with 20% on long instruction subsets, all while using nearly half the context used in the baseline model. Motivated by these result, we present our stance the deployability of FM-based embodied agents in real-world environments, and highlight open research directions.
bullets: Targets poor personalization in unseen environments and context-length limits on long-horizon navigation.
Transit-Aware Planning (TAP) primes models with human-habit data mined from the scene.
MemCtrl adds a memory head for active context management.
In a Turtlebot lab setting, TAP improves personalized target finding by 18% over its baseline.
MemCtrl improves embodied-task performance by 6% overall and 20% on long-instruction subsets while using nearly half the baseline context.
papers.selection_reason: Fits embodied navigation with foundation models and active memory management for long-horizon tasks.
papers.title: Deploying Foundation Models for Embodied Navigation
papers.tldr: The paper improves foundation-model-based embodied navigation by addressing personalization bias and limited context through habit-aware planning and active memory control.

papers.abstract: To generate landmark-based route instructions, models must understand both map geometry and human landmark preferences. Although large language models (LLMs) show great abilities in language tasks, the best way to structure map data for these models is not yet established. This paper proposes a structured text representation for landmark selection tasks in route navigation, utilizing SVG format to encode spatial features. The structured text maintains a geometric connection with rendered map images, allowing language models to directly access spatial and semantic data. Using a new dataset created from human-written route descriptions and OpenStreetMap data, we evaluate models on two tasks: landmark selection at turns and around destinations. Experiments with five LLMs show that the proposed structured text input performs as well as or better than image-based PNG inputs. In addition, task-specific fine-tuning enables smaller local LLMs to effectively leverage map layouts to achieve high selection accuracy. These results demonstrate that structured text is an efficient and lightweight interface for spatial reasoning in human-oriented navigation.
authors: Mifu Matsumoto, Yuki Nakanishi, Tomoya Hashiguchi, Hiroaki Ohshima
bullets: Addresses the challenge of representing map geometry and semantic information for landmark-based route instruction generation.
Encodes spatial features in structured SVG text while preserving alignment with rendered map images.
Evaluates landmark selection at turns and near destinations using a dataset combining human-written routes with OpenStreetMap data.
Across five LLMs, structured text performs as well as or better than PNG map inputs.
Task-specific fine-tuning allows smaller local LLMs to use map layouts effectively.
papers.selection_reason: Encodes map geometry as structured text for LLM-based landmark selection, directly relevant to spatial reasoning and navigation instruction generation.
papers.title: Structured Maps for Landmark-Based Route Instructions with LLMs
papers.tldr: An SVG-based structured text representation helps LLMs select human-preferred landmarks for navigation as effectively as, or better than, map images.

papers.abstract: Navigation vision-language-action (VLA) policies repeatedly invoke costly semantic reasoning even when the next command remains unchanged. Command reuse can reduce computation but risks missing instruction-dependent turns or stops. We introduce ASPEN, an event-triggered scheduler based on command persistence prediction: estimating whether the frozen base policy would reissue its previous command. A lightweight multimodal predictor combines temporal observations, language instructions, execution history, and cached VLA confidence. At eligible command boundaries, sufficient predicted persistence permits command reuse. Otherwise, ASPEN triggers fresh semantic reasoning from the VLA. Evaluated with frozen NaVILA on cross-dataset RxR-CE val-unseen, ASPEN reduces VLA calls by 9.5% and estimated inference time by 8.1%, including scheduling overhead. It maintains comparable navigation performance and preserves identical baseline action sequences on 92.1% of episodes.
bullets: Targets redundant semantic reasoning in navigation VLAs when the next command is likely unchanged.
Uses a lightweight multimodal predictor over observations, instructions, execution history, and cached VLA confidence.
Reuses commands when predicted persistence is sufficient; otherwise triggers fresh VLA reasoning.
With frozen NaVILA on RxR-CE val-unseen, reduces VLA calls by 9.5% and estimated inference time by 8.1%.
Maintains comparable navigation performance, with identical baseline action sequences in 92.1% of episodes.
papers.selection_reason: Improves efficiency of navigation VLAs via command persistence prediction, relevant to Embodied AI navigation and Efficient AI.
papers.title: ASPEN: Adaptive Semantic Reasoning via Command Persistence Prediction for Efficient Navigation VLAs
papers.tldr: ASPEN reduces costly VLA reasoning by predicting when the previous navigation command can safely be reused, cutting VLA calls and inference time while preserving navigation behavior.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon embodied navigation may be interrupted by a higher-priority instruction before the current task sequence is complete. The agent must finish its current atomic task, execute the inserted task, and resume the remaining sequence from the updated environment state, where its viewpoint and available navigation candidates may have changed. To evaluate this capability, we introduce PIFR benchmark, a novel task for runtime task preemption and resumption in embodied navigation. PIFR includes single, repeated, and nested interruption settings,with stage-specific metrics for inserted-task completion, resumption of the original task, and completion of the full sequence. Evaluations show that recovery performance varies across interruption conditions, while aggregate success can obscure differences in interruption handling and resumption. We further propose a lightweight candidate-ranking baseline to improve target re-grounding after interruption. Together, PIFR and the baseline provide a systematic framework for studying interruption handling and task recovery in long-horizon embodied navigation.
authors: Zerun Liu, Lechao Cheng, Yimin Liu, Shengeng Tang, Yaxiong Wang, Zhun Zhong
bullets: Targets runtime preemption and resumption when higher-priority instructions interrupt an unfinished navigation sequence.
Introduces single, repeated, and nested interruption scenarios with stage-specific evaluation metrics.
Measures inserted-task completion, original-task resumption, and full-sequence completion separately.
Finds that recovery varies by interruption condition and that aggregate success can hide these differences.
Provides a lightweight candidate-ranking baseline for re-grounding navigation targets after interruption.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and baseline for preemptive instruction following and resumption in embodied navigation; fits vision-language navigation.
papers.title: Preemptive Instruction Following with Resumption
papers.tldr: PIFR evaluates whether embodied-navigation agents can handle interruptions, complete inserted tasks, and resume long-horizon plans from changed states.

papers.abstract: Vision-language navigation (VLN) requires an embodied agent to follow language instructions through 3D environments. Maintaining persistent episodic memory remains a challenge for VLM-based streaming agents in long-horizon navigation. We present MEMVLN, a streaming episodic memory framework that maintains a bounded bank of compressed perceptual features annotated with timesteps and action-derived relative poses, and produces compact memory tokens via cross-attention. We pair the proposed memory with a frozen pretrained geometry encoder. To learn the memory module, we design a masking-based trajectory summarization task with multi-granularity sub-trajectory decomposition, encouraging route reconstruction exclusively from episodic memory. Under navigation training restricted to the official R2R/RxR trajectories, MEMVLN achieves state-of-the-art performance on most reported metrics on standard VLN-CE benchmarks. Long-horizon analyses further characterize when episodic memory is useful. For physical evaluation, we collect 30 instruction-conditioned episodes in one physical scene, use 24 as demonstrations for post-training, and hold out six for testing. On the held-out episodes, MEMVLN improves success over the VLM baseline from 17% to 40%, and post-training further raises it to 47%.
authors: Yan Wang, Jiangyong Huang, Baoxiong Jia, Siyuan Huang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of retaining useful past observations during long-horizon VLN.
Stores compressed perceptual features annotated with timesteps and action-derived relative poses, then converts them into memory tokens via cross-attention.
Uses a frozen geometry encoder and a masking-based, multi-granularity trajectory summarization task to train the memory module.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance on most reported metrics across standard VLN-CE benchmarks under R2R/RxR trajectory restrictions.
In a physical-scene evaluation, success improved from 17% for the VLM baseline to 40%, and to 47% after post-training.
papers.selection_reason: Streaming episodic memory for vision-language navigation; directly relevant to embodied navigation and embodied memory.
papers.title: MemVLN: Streaming Episodic Memory for Vision-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: MEMVLN equips streaming vision-language navigation agents with bounded, pose-aware episodic memory to improve long-horizon navigation in simulated and physical environments.

papers.abstract: Robot tasks require grounding spatial language in physical scenes, but task success alone cannot establish whether spatial instructions are followed. We present BEHAVIOR-Spatial, a benchmark built on BEHAVIOR-1K that measures spatial question answering, point-based target grounding, and robot action to examine how VLM spatial understanding relates to VLA behavior. It comprises 3,256 spatial questions across 49 activities, 1,240 grounding queries across 14 manipulation tasks, and action evaluations covering those 14 tasks and 10 navigation tasks. Our manipulation protocol evaluates held-out configurations and instruction following when the requested target changes within a fixed training layout. The baseline achieves 41.6% on held-out configurations but only 16.1% under changed instructions. VLM adaptation and robot-data pretraining provide limited improvements, whereas oracle visual target cues raise these rates to 60.3% and 38.0%, respectively. Perception evaluations reveal policy-dependent correlations between VLM question-answering and grounding accuracy and VLA manipulation performance. Together, these findings motivate evaluating spatial instruction following alongside task completion and examining when spatial perception performance translates into robot behavior. Project website: https://arielchen07.github.io/behavior-spatial/.
authors: Sirui Chen, Huang Huang, Qineng Wang, Wenlong Huang, Manling Li, Ruohan Zhang, Li Fei-Fei, Jiajun Wu
bullets: Benchmarks spatial question answering, point-based target grounding, and robot actions on BEHAVIOR-1K.
Includes 3,256 spatial questions, 1,240 grounding queries, 14 manipulation tasks, and 10 navigation tasks.
Tests held-out scene configurations and target changes under fixed training layouts.
Baseline action success drops from 41.6% on held-out configurations to 16.1% with changed instructions; oracle visual cues improve both settings.
Shows that perception accuracy does not consistently translate into robot behavior, motivating joint evaluation of spatial understanding and task completion.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark linking VLM spatial understanding to VLA behavior in manipulation and navigation; fits spatial intelligence and embodied robotics.
papers.title: Behavior Spatial Benchmark: Evaluating Spatial Understanding for Robotics
papers.tldr: BEHAVIOR-Spatial evaluates whether vision-language models and robot policies truly understand and follow spatial instructions in physical scenes.

papers.abstract: As Vision-Language Models (VLMs) increasingly enable robots to follow language instructions, understanding their navigation decisions becomes important for reliable deployment. Existing explainability methods overlook a key challenge in Vision-Language Navigation (VLN): evidence for the current action may be distributed across historical and current observations and associated with different instruction stages. We identify instruction-stage insensitivity, where existing methods produce similar explanations despite changes across different navigation stages. To address this issue, we propose a stage-aware attribution framework for VLN. We first construct action-conditioned temporal instruction--visual attributions across observations. These attributions are projected into instruction space to estimate stage associations, which guide the aggregation of relevant historical evidence for refining the current explanation. An instruction-guided spatial filter further suppresses isolated responses while preserving compact, instruction-relevant regions. Experiments across multiple VLN policies and benchmarks show improved attribution quality over existing methods. We further demonstrate that our method acts as a diagnostic tool for analyzing failure cases, and validate its applicability to real-world navigation on a Unitree G1 robot.
authors: Yiyuan Yao, Xinpeng Ding, Minglei Chen, Fei Gao, Lihuo He, Jie Yuan, Aijun Li, Nannan Wang, Xinbo Gao
bullets: Addresses instruction-stage insensitivity in existing VLN explanations.
Builds action-conditioned temporal instruction–visual attributions across observations.
Projects attributions into instruction space to identify stages and aggregate relevant historical evidence.
Uses an instruction-guided spatial filter to remove isolated responses while preserving compact relevant regions.
Improves attribution quality across multiple policies and benchmarks, supports failure analysis, and transfers to a Unitree G1 robot.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses explainability for Vision-Language Navigation, a core configured subtopic.
papers.title: Explaining Navigation Decisions: Stage-Aware Visual Attribution for Vision-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: A stage-aware attribution framework explains VLN actions by linking instruction stages to relevant visual evidence across current and historical observations.

papers.abstract: Deploying a language-guided navigation policy in a new building usually means watching it fail. Public-benchmark VLAs degrade scene by scene as layout, appearance, and language drift, and the standard fix of teleoperating fresh trajectories on site does not scale. We replace human demonstration with a single brief iPhone scan. Scan2Instruction compiles that scan into a complete training environment, automatically synthesizing executable navigation episodes with grounded instructions. PRPT-KS then adapts the policy through a closed-form Pareto utility read directly off the reconstructed scene, with no learned critic and no human labels. Across five real environments, the two designs together drive our RealNav to an 85% real-robot success rate, compared with 49% for a RealNav baseline post-trained on human demonstrations, and still achieve 82% in unscanned regions of the same buildings, compared with 41% for the same baseline. Our work turns demonstration-free scene adaptation for language-guided navigation from an aspiration into a working reality.
authors: Zhuoyuan Yu, Yuxing Long, Du Wang, Junyang Wang, Hongwei Fan, Hao Dong
bullets: Addresses policy degradation under changes in building layout, appearance, and language.
Scan2Instruction converts one scan into a complete training environment with executable, grounded navigation episodes.
PRPT-KS adapts the policy using a closed-form Pareto utility derived from the reconstructed scene, without a learned critic.
Across five real environments, the approach reaches 85% success in scanned areas and 82% in unscanned regions.
The abstract reports higher success than human-demonstration post-training baselines: 49% and 41%, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: Demonstration-free adaptation of language-guided navigation using a single scene scan; directly in vision-language navigation.
papers.title: One Scan is Enough: Demonstration-Free Adaptation for Language-Guided Navigation
papers.tldr: A single brief iPhone scan can adapt a language-guided navigation policy to a new building without human demonstrations or labels, achieving 85% real-robot success across five environments.

papers.abstract: Recent vision-and-language navigation (VLN) policies act on their visual history, and an incorrect action can take them off the instructed route. Paired interventions on four VLN policies show that clearing the history doubles pooled success at the onset of a deviation but lowers it on route, while later in a deviation, removing only the off-route frames helps much less. After a deviation, the retained history keeps the policy from turning where a turn is needed, which we call behavioral inertia. We propose MOON, a framework that equips a frozen VLN policy with two lightweight modules, adding less than 1% of its parameters. A deviation judge decides when to forget, raising an alarm that clears the history when it predicts that the agent is off route. A recovery policy, trained with GRPO from alarm states, learns how to move on, turning more of the successes found only by sampling into a single greedy rollout. Experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE show that MOON reaches the highest R2R-CE success rate among the compared methods and raises the success rate of its frozen base by 5.2 and 6.0 points, and an ablation with a random trigger indicates that this gain depends on when the history is cleared. Without retraining, MOON also improves zero-shot object-goal navigation on HM3D-OVON. Together, these results suggest that deviation recovery depends on knowing when to forget, not only how to act. Code is available at https://github.com/AutoLab-SAI-SJTU/MOON.
authors: Jingmeng Zhou, Seson Sun, Binyao Xu, Lingming Zhang, Hanshi Wang, Fudong Ge, Weiming Hu, Jin Gao, Zhipeng Zhang
bullets: Incorrect actions can create behavioral inertia: retained off-route history prevents the agent from turning when needed.
MOON adds two lightweight modules to a frozen VLN policy: a deviation judge that triggers history clearing and a recovery policy trained from alarm states.
On R2R-CE and RxR-CE, MOON improves its frozen base success by 5.2 and 6.0 percentage points, respectively, and achieves the highest R2R-CE success among compared methods.
A random-trigger ablation shows that recovery depends on clearing history at the right time, not merely clearing it.
MOON also improves zero-shot object-goal navigation on HM3D-OVON without retraining.
papers.selection_reason: Vision-and-language navigation with history clearing and recovery, directly addressing embodied navigation memory.
papers.title: MOON: Learning When to Forget and How to Move On in Vision-and-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: MOON helps vision-and-language navigation agents recover from route deviations by learning when to clear misleading visual history and how to continue afterward.

papers.abstract: Aerial vision-language navigation (AVLN) requires a UAV to reach a language-described target from partial egocentric observations while reasoning over large outdoor scenes. Existing approaches typically fuse view-centered RGB observations and globally anchored history maps as generic visual embeddings, leaving cross-modal spatial alignment to be learned from sparse navigation supervision. We present SP-Guide, a transformer- based goal-prediction framework that addresses this weakness of alignment through a Spatial Prior Cross-Modal Encoder, an Instruction Enhanced Decoder, and a Goal Convergence Filter for terminal target refinement. Experiments implemented on the CityNav benchmark show that SP-Guide improves success rate over the representative baselines, with the largest gains on unseen environments. These results indicate that physically grounded spatial priors provide an effective inductive bias for robust AVLN.
authors: Haoxiang Tang, Dong Zhou, Shen Tan, Minxuan Jiang, Xitong Li
bullets: AVLN must guide UAVs to language-described targets from partial egocentric views in large outdoor scenes.
Existing methods often use generic visual embeddings, leaving spatial cross-modal alignment to sparse navigation supervision.
SP-Guide combines a Spatial Prior Cross-Modal Encoder, Instruction Enhanced Decoder, and Goal Convergence Filter.
On the CityNav benchmark, it improves success rate over representative baselines, with the largest gains in unseen environments.
The approach suggests spatial priors can provide a robust inductive bias for AVLN.
papers.selection_reason: Spatial priors for aerial vision-language navigation directly match the vision-language navigation subtopic.
papers.title: SP-Guide: Enhancing Aerial Vision-Language Navigation with Spatial Priors
papers.tldr: SP-Guide improves aerial vision-language navigation by using physically grounded spatial priors to better align visual observations with language instructions and refine terminal goals.

papers.abstract: Autonomous mobile robots support material transport in warehouses and industrial facilities, where navigation must adapt to changing operating conditions. Sensor observations reveal physical obstacles, but do not by themselves specify temporary access rules, route preferences, or exceptions known to operators. This paper presents a natural-language policy interface that brings this knowledge into ROS 2 Nav2. A local large language model converts instructions into JSON policies specifying destinations, spatial constraints, and temporal or event conditions. Deterministic checks govern mission acceptance, and three costmap adapters project accepted policies into the existing navigation stack without changing its planner or controller. On 150 researcher-authored English commands, four local models produce 107-142 correct accepted policies, compared with 44 for a rule-based parser, with 3-20 incorrect acceptances per model. Fault injection records rejection of eight endpoint/JSON faults and 29 validator-stage faults. Navigation experiments use correct task policies to evaluate keepouts, zone costs, person-dependent regions, and event-conditioned passage in simulation and on a TurtleBot3. For Tasks 1-3, mean travel times are 18.4-24.5% lower in simulation and 23.1-35.0% lower on the physical testbed than with the baseline lacking those policies. A native KeepoutFilter comparison and two-robot demonstrations examine basic keepout behavior and shared policy projection. The interface connects operator instructions to explicit navigation policies while retaining Nav2's planning and control components.
authors: Jiyeong Chae, Hyunkyo Seo, Heonjae Lee, Kyung-Joon Park
bullets: Addresses the gap between sensor-detected obstacles and operator-defined access rules, route preferences, and exceptions.
A local language model generates JSON policies for destinations, spatial constraints, and temporal or event conditions; deterministic validators accept or reject them.
Three costmap adapters project accepted policies into ROS 2 Nav2 while preserving its existing navigation stack.
Across 150 researcher-authored commands, models produced 107–142 correct accepted policies versus 44 for a rule-based parser, with some incorrect acceptances.
Simulation and TurtleBot3 tests showed lower mean travel times for policy-enabled tasks, while fault injection demonstrated rejection of multiple malformed or invalid inputs.
papers.selection_reason: Natural-language instructions converted into navigation policies for a real robot navigation stack fits embodied instruction-driven navigation.
papers.title: Natural-Language to Nav2: Operational Policies for Costmap-Based Navigation
papers.tldr: A natural-language interface converts operator instructions into validated Nav2 costmap policies, enabling adaptive navigation without modifying the existing planner or controller.

papers.abstract: Semantics can provide a proxy for physical traversability. Terrain that looks like loose sand or a rock field is likely to have similar physical properties. Open-vocabulary vision-language models (VLMs) enable this physical reasoning over terrain outside any fixed label set. We present Open-world Language-conditioned Speed Fields (OWLS), which plans directly over the dense feature map of a VLM. Prompted with a description of traversable terrain, the VLM scores every pixel of a single camera image; OWLS projects these scores onto the ground, adapts them to the platform with two morphological operations, and uses the result as the speed field of a minimum-time planner, so terrain appearance and obstacle clearance shape one trajectory. OWLS needs no task-specific training, no terrain annotation, no persistent map, and no exteroceptive sensor beyond the camera. We evaluate it on a physical rover indoors and off-road, on simulated Mars and Moon rovers over 200 procedurally generated terrains, and on real planetary imagery.
authors: Chahyon Ku, Erica Tevere, Georgios Georgakis, Rudra Mukherjee, Bernadette Bucher
bullets: Addresses navigation in unfamiliar terrain by using semantic appearance as a proxy for physical traversability.
Scores each image pixel with a language-conditioned VLM prompt describing traversable terrain.
Projects scores onto the ground, adapts them with morphological operations, and plans a minimum-time trajectory incorporating obstacle clearance.
Requires only a camera, with no terrain annotations, task-specific training, or persistent map.
Evaluated on physical indoor and off-road rovers, simulated Mars and Moon rovers across 200 procedural terrains, and real planetary imagery.
papers.selection_reason: Open-vocabulary language-conditioned speed fields for rover navigation represent a transferable VLM-based embodied navigation method.
papers.title: OWLS: Open-world Language-conditioned Speed Fields for Zero-Shot Rover Navigation
papers.tldr: OWLS uses open-vocabulary vision-language models to convert camera-based terrain semantics into speed fields for zero-shot rover navigation without task-specific training or mapping.

papers.abstract: Supervising a multi-UAV reconnaissance mission usually means plotting waypoints and watching every drone. We present UAV SwarmAgent, a hierarchical multi-agent system in which an operator states the mission in one natural-language sentence and a ground-station agent writes and executes code that turns it into per-UAV routes. The agent grounds inspection targets in an aerial map with a vision-language model, splits them among N UAVs by balancing route length, and dispatches worker agents that verify incidents with a compact onboard decision model. In simulation over 4 incident types and 3 foundation models, the swarm located the incident in 244 of 255 missions (95.7%). A paired scaling study with one to 5 UAVs shows that flight time follows an Amdahl-type law. The second UAV delivers half of the attainable saving and the speedup is bounded at 1.52x. We discuss what this predictability, and the false alarms we observed, imply for an operator who supervises the swarm, and outline the user study needed to test it.
authors: Oleg Sautenkov, Yasheerah Yaqoot, Muhammad Ahsan Mustafa, Grigorii Kalinin, Chih-Yung Wen, Dzmitry Tsetserukou
bullets: A ground-station agent converts a one-sentence mission description into per-UAV routes and executable code.
The system grounds targets on aerial maps, balances route lengths across UAVs, and assigns onboard agents to verify incidents.
In simulation, it detected incidents in 244 of 255 missions (95.7%) across four incident types and three foundation models.
Scaling from one to five UAVs followed an Amdahl-type pattern, with speedup capped at 1.52× and the second UAV providing half of the attainable saving.
False alarms remain a concern, and a user study is still needed to evaluate operator supervision.
papers.selection_reason: Language-driven mission specification, VLM grounding, and per-UAV route generation fit embodied vision-language navigation and planning.
papers.title: UAV-SwarmAgent: Scalable Multi-UAV Reconnaissance and Task Allocation via Code Generation and Vision-Language Reasoning
papers.tldr: UAV-SwarmAgent uses natural-language mission commands, vision-language reasoning, and code-generated routes to coordinate scalable multi-UAV reconnaissance.

papers.abstract: Zero-shot object navigation requires an embodied agent to choose where to search while retaining evidence from previous observations. HGWM couples an LLM-generated room-anchor prior with persistent spatial-semantic memory. A coarse stage assigns visual-semantic scores to candidate headings on a 0-10 scale; a fine stage measures symbolic compatibility between observed objects, room context, and the goal prior. Phase-dependent fusion combines these scores with an LLM direction recommendation before local action selection. On HM3D v0.1, the reported HGWM configuration achieves 62.6% success rate (SR) and 31.5% success weighted by path length (SPL), compared with 58.1% and 31.2% for WMNav. On MP3D, the corresponding values are 46.8% and 17.9%, compared with 45.4% and 17.2%. The results indicate higher success point estimates and modest path-efficiency gains. On HM3D v0.2, the full model obtains 74.4% SR and 31.9% SPL. Additional component ablations reduce SR by 0.9-2.3 percentage points and SPL by 0.6-1.5 points. These are author-reported aggregate measurements. The accompanying implementation repairs pass offline tests; episode-level rerun records are not available. Evaluation is confined to simulation.
bullets: Uses a coarse-to-fine process: heading scoring followed by symbolic matching of observed objects, room context, and the goal prior.
Fuses phase-dependent graph scores with an LLM direction recommendation for local action selection.
Reports higher success and modestly better path efficiency than WMNav on HM3D v0.1 and MP3D.
On HM3D v0.2, the full model achieves 74.4% SR and 31.9% SPL; component ablations lower both metrics.
Evaluation is limited to simulation, and episode-level rerun records are unavailable.
papers.selection_reason: The paper presents HGWM, a hierarchical system for zero-shot object navigation that integrates LLM-generated priors with persistent spatial-semantic memory. It uses a graph-matching approach to combine visual observations with language instructions, directly fitting the Vision-Language Navigation and Robot Navigation subtopics, and utilizes persistent memory for the Embodied Memory subtopic.
papers.title: HGWM: Hierarchical Graph-Guided World Model for Zero-Shot Object Navigation via Graph Matching
papers.tldr: HGWM improves zero-shot object navigation by combining an LLM-derived room prior with persistent graph-based spatial-semantic memory and hierarchical graph matching.

papers.abstract: What visual representation should a navigation policy act on? Navigation policies built on vision foundation models largely leave representation design to the encoders' pretraining objectives. We present RepresentNav, a navigation foundation model built on a self-constructed representation space: a visual representation constructed by the policy's own objectives from vision foundation models. RepresentNav builds this space with Representation Residuals, a compact three-layer transformer that attends over features spanning the full depth of multiple complementary vision foundation models, so that the policy learns to see what it needs for navigation. In the same space it dreams what it wants: before every action a latent chain-of-thought predicts the representation of the scene a moment ahead. The dream is trained end-to-end with the policy as a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), with a next-representation prediction loss and a regularizer on its targets. RepresentNav sets a new state of the art on VLNVerse, VLN-CE R2R, EVT-Bench, and two point-goal benchmarks, and its gains carry over to a physical robot amid clutter and moving people. On VLNVerse fine-grained, RepresentNav achieves 83.80% success, outperforming the previous state of the art by 20.05 percentage points, and on EVT-Bench distracted tracking it reaches 85.5% with a single camera (+10.1). With the same encoders, the self-constructed space clearly outperforms concatenating their outputs and learns to weight their layers unevenly, and a dream in it cuts collisions by a quarter. A single dreamed latent decodes into the depth, semantics, and 3D occupancy of the scene a moment ahead, more accurately than pretrained encoders applied to the real future frame, although occupancy is never supervised, and the rollout tracks the robot's own motion over the next second: the dream emerges as a compact latent world model.
authors: Jiawei Chen, Yinxi Wang, Zihan Yang, Meijun Gao, Yaowei Liu, Shuming Zhang, Zecheng Li, Xiangju Mi, Yuxuan Liu, Runzhong Huang, Tianlin Li, Xun Zhang, Zhengyang Wang, Xu Miao, Tong Yang
bullets: Addresses the limitation of relying directly on representations shaped by generic vision pretraining.
Uses Representation Residuals, a compact transformer over multilevel features from multiple vision foundation models.
Jointly trains navigation with a JEPA-style latent “dream” that predicts the next scene representation before each action.
Reports new state-of-the-art results across VLNVerse, VLN-CE R2R, EVT-Bench, and point-goal benchmarks, with gains transferring to a physical robot.
The learned latent predicts future depth, semantics, and 3D occupancy without direct occupancy supervision; its scope is navigation-focused and evaluated on the stated benchmarks and robot setting.
papers.selection_reason: Navigation foundation model with self-constructed visual representations and latent next-state prediction; state-of-the-art on VLN and robot navigation benchmarks.
papers.title: See What I Need, Dream What I Want: A Navigation Foundation Model on a Self-Constructed Representation Space
papers.tldr: RepresentNav learns a task-specific visual representation and predicts future scene states in latent space, substantially improving navigation and reducing collisions across simulated and real-world settings.

papers.abstract: Human-readable maps provide an intuitive interface for specifying robot destinations, but connecting their schematic geometry to egocentric observations remains challenging. We present NaViRRator, a framework that translates user-specified start and goal locations on such maps into navigation instructions for a pretrained vision-and-language navigation (VLN) policy. Its core method, RouteScribe, separates route inference from verbalization by first generating an explicit route scaffold in map-image coordinates, which a pretrained vision-language model (VLM) converts into a navigation instruction. We construct the scaffold with start--goal line conditional flow matching (SGL-CFM), which deforms a straight start--goal waypoint sequence into a map-conditioned route. During execution, the VLN policy receives only the instruction and egocentric observations, while the map and scaffold remain upstream, allowing executor replacement without retraining the map-to-language modules. Real-world experiments show higher success rates and success weighted by path length (SPL) than direct map-to-instruction generation, A*-based scaffolding, and Gaussian-source conditional flow matching. Qualitative results further show clearer salient turns and better preservation of the intended maneuver sequence, supporting route-grounded language as a modular interface between human-readable maps and pretrained navigation policies.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of connecting schematic map geometry with a robot’s first-person visual navigation.
RouteScribe separates route inference from verbalization by generating an explicit map-coordinate route scaffold before producing instructions.
Uses start–goal line conditional flow matching to deform a straight waypoint sequence into a map-conditioned route.
Real-world experiments report higher success rate and SPL than direct generation, A*-based scaffolding, and Gaussian-source flow matching.
The modular design keeps maps and scaffolds upstream, enabling executor replacement without retraining map-to-language modules.
papers.selection_reason: Map-based route scaffolding converted into instructions for a pretrained VLN policy; directly addresses vision-language navigation.
papers.title: NaViRrator: Robot Navigation from Human-Readable Maps through a Learned Visual Route
papers.tldr: NaViRRator converts human-readable map destinations into route-grounded language instructions that pretrained vision-language navigation policies can execute from egocentric observations.

papers.abstract: Flexible endoscopes exploit structural compliance to traverse narrow lumens, pipes, and cavities, where navigation involves distributed environmental contact. This compliance makes tip motion depend on the evolving support configuration. We present external bird's-eye-view contact-aided navigation (EBV-CAN), a vision-language policy that combines one initial global static bird's-eye image with evolving endoscopic observations and motor state. Three supervised semantic queries locate the tip, next waypoint, and instructed target on the cached global image; their residual representations predict bending and insertion commands. We introduce the Vision-Language Contact-Aided (VLCA) dataset, linking 517 demonstrations and 75k action samples to 958k spatial entries and 93k remaining-route records. On 50 held-out episodes, tip-coordinate and waypoint localization reach 97.5% and 94.8%. Swapping the target instruction under identical observations changes target attention and motor output across 17 dual-target episodes. Across 1,920 physical trials of eight policies trained under a shared protocol, EBV-CAN achieves 183/240 successes (76.25%) under automatic blue-area scoring. Gated recurrent unit behavior cloning (GRU-BC) achieves the lowest matched-task offline mean absolute error (MAE), 0.056, and 1/240 physical successes, establishing distinct rankings for action imitation and task completion. Successful multi-guide executions and representative failures connect spatial progress, steering transitions, and visibility to physical navigation.
authors: Chi Kit Ng, Shuchang Liu, Jinsong Lin, Yidong Zhang, Xizi Wang, Ho Yin Chim, Hongliang Ren
bullets: Addresses navigation in compliant, contact-rich environments where support changes tip motion.
Queries the global image for the tip, next waypoint, and instructed target, then predicts bending and insertion commands from their representations.
Introduces the VLCA dataset with demonstrations, action samples, spatial entries, and remaining-route records.
Achieves 97.5% tip localization, 94.8% waypoint localization, and 76.25% success across 1,920 physical trials.
Offline action imitation and physical task completion produce different rankings: GRU-BC has lower MAE but only 1/240 physical successes.
papers.selection_reason: Vision-language policy for contact-aided endoscope navigation with semantic grounding in global images fits embodied navigation and VLA.
papers.title: EBV-CAN: Vision--Language Grounding for Contact-Aided Endoscope Navigation
papers.tldr: EBV-CAN uses a cached bird’s-eye image, live endoscopic views, and motor state to ground language instructions for contact-aware endoscope navigation.

papers.abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires agents to follow instructions and navigate to target locations. However, current VLN agents often suffer severe performance degradation in unseen environments due to distribution shifts. Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) offers a promising paradigm to bridge this gap, yet existing methods that rely on unsupervised entropy minimization can propagate errors through the trajectory, causing cascading failures in navigation. Recent methods mitigate this by incorporating human feedback, but they apply trajectory-level supervision uniformly across all steps without localizing the actions is truly informative, leading to inefficient feedback utilization and mismatched optimization granularity. To address these limitations, we propose FETA, a Feedback-Efficient Test-Time Adaptation method that improves both feedback efficiency and optimization reliability. To reduce unnecessary human interventions, we introduce a hierarchical sample selection strategy to localize informative samples. Specifically, we first filter trajectories whose normalized policy entropy exhibits large fluctuations. Within each selected trajectory, we further select the critical action via an entropy-gradient saliency criterion and query a single binary feedback on its correctness. A discrepancy-aware entropy optimization objective then updates the policy only at the queried step, with adaptive scaling that assigns larger relative weights to samples with greater prediction-feedback discrepancy. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that FETA achieves state-of-the-art performance with fewer human interventions, while remaining robust under noisy feedback and continual adaptation settings.
authors: Zixu Wang, Huaquan Zhang, Shoukai Xu, Jinwu Hu, Zhiquan Wen, Mingkui Tan
bullets: Unseen environments can cause severe VLN degradation, while entropy minimization may amplify navigation errors.
FETA hierarchically selects high-value feedback: unstable trajectories first, then critical actions using entropy-gradient saliency.
It queries one binary correctness signal per selected action and updates the policy only at that step.
Discrepancy-aware entropy optimization adaptively emphasizes actions where predictions and feedback disagree.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance with fewer interventions, including robustness to noisy feedback and continual adaptation.
papers.selection_reason: Feedback-efficient test-time adaptation for Vision-and-Language Navigation combines embodied instruction following with deployment-time policy update, fitting both configured areas.
papers.title: Asking Less, Adapting Better: Feedback-Efficient Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-and-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: FETA improves vision-and-language navigation under distribution shifts by selecting only informative actions for targeted, feedback-efficient test-time adaptation.

papers.abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) have recently emerged as important remote sensing platforms, and UAV navigation has shown great potential in remote sensing applications. However, existing methods do not explicitly incorporate kinodynamic modeling or safety distances into trajectory generation, resulting in high absolute yaw rates, frequent collisions, and low navigation success rates, which limit safety and motion stability. To address this challenge, we introduce KinoUAV, a kinodynamic benchmark comprising a dataset and KinoUAV-Agent. First, we develop a hierarchical kinodynamic trajectory generation pipeline that drives UAV through acceleration actions. It uses waypoint chains from global planning and generates trajectories segment by segment under velocity, acceleration, and jerk constraints, reducing oscillations and improving trajectory stability. Furthermore, we introduce directional free-space distance (DFD) labels into the constructed dataset to describe the available clearance for safe motion decisions. The proposed KinoUAV-Agent predicts DFDs and uses them to generate safe actions, decoupling perception from action decision-making. This design enables autonomous obstacle avoidance and improves navigation safety. The benchmark incorporates the proposed Cruise-Seek task, in which the UAV first enters the target region and then searches for the target, reducing the difficulty of target search and improving navigation success. Experiments on KinoUAV show that KinoUAV-Agent outperforms existing methods, achieving the highest success rate while maintaining lower absolute yaw rates and collision rates. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of kinodynamic modeling for safe and stable UAV navigation.
authors: Chenyao Yang, Peijin Wang, Yingchao Feng, Wenhui Diao
bullets: Targets unstable and unsafe UAV navigation caused by missing kinodynamic constraints and safety-distance modeling.
Generates trajectories segment by segment from waypoint chains under velocity, acceleration, and jerk constraints.
Adds directional free-space distance (DFD) labels, which the agent predicts to guide safe action selection and obstacle avoidance.
Introduces the Cruise-Seek task, where UAVs first enter a target region before searching for the target.
Experiments report the highest success rate among compared methods, with lower absolute yaw rates and collision rates.
papers.selection_reason: Kinodynamic-aware UAV vision-language navigation with safety distances and obstacle-free space prediction; directly fits embodied navigation topics.
papers.title: KinoUAV: A Benchmark for Safe and Stable UAV Vision-Language Navigation with Kinodynamic Modeling
papers.tldr: KinoUAV is a benchmark and agent for safer, more stable UAV vision-language navigation through kinodynamic trajectory modeling and directional clearance prediction.

papers.abstract: Reliable robotic mapping in dynamic real-world environments is essential for embodied intelligence and long-term autonomy. However, existing methods often involve a trade-off: lightweight online mapping is efficient but captures limited semantic context, while dense mapping provides richer semantics at higher computational cost and is more vulnerable to distractors. They also struggle to relocalize objects after scene changes. To address these challenges, we propose the Online Anchor-centric Scene Inference System (OASIS), a unified system for online mapping, complex open-vocabulary retrieval, and navigation in dynamic environments. Motivated by the observation that indoor scenes are organized around stable semantic anchors, OASIS represents the environment using a sparse set of anchor nodes, each maintaining a unified multimodal representation that integrates semantic descriptions, visual features, and geometric states for reasoning, verification, and navigation. Its compact anchor-centric memory supports on-demand evidence extraction and hierarchical retrieval, reducing redundant storage while improving retrieval reliability. To handle scene dynamics, OASIS further reuses transient observations collected during navigation to relocalize moved objects. Experiments in both simulation and real-world environments, including standard retrieval benchmarks and navigation tasks under both static and dynamic settings, demonstrate that our system can perform complex open-vocabulary retrieval and navigation, while also enabling relocation of displaced objects after scene changes.
authors: Kaiyao Liao, Qingfeng Li, Chen Chen, Xiaoze Wu, Qing Sun, Jianwei Niu
bullets: Addresses the efficiency–semantic richness trade-off in online mapping and the difficulty of relocalizing objects after scene changes.
Represents scenes with sparse anchor nodes that combine semantic, visual, and geometric information for reasoning, verification, and navigation.
Uses on-demand evidence extraction and hierarchical retrieval to reduce redundant storage while supporting complex queries.
Reuses transient navigation observations to relocalize objects that have moved.
Validated in simulation and real-world settings across retrieval benchmarks and static/dynamic navigation tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Anchor-centric multimodal memory for open-vocabulary retrieval and navigation in dynamic scenes; combines spatial understanding with embodied memory.
papers.title: OASIS: Online Anchor-centric Scene Inference System for Open-Vocabulary Retrieval and Navigation in Dynamic Environments
papers.tldr: OASIS enables efficient open-vocabulary object retrieval and navigation in dynamic environments using a sparse, multimodal memory built around stable semantic scene anchors.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) navigation models translate visual observations and instructions into actions. Navigation success assesses whether an agent reaches the goal. However, reaching the goal successfully does not establish whether the model genuinely follows the instructions or relies on visual cues or navigation history. We introduce NavBind to diagnose instruction-action binding: whether changing the instruction influences the probabilistic distribution of the actions, with the navigation context fixed. We construct 3,252 route-fork contexts by recombining route-aligned instruction segments from R2R-CE and RxR-CE. Each context pairs full instructions that share the description of the route already traveled but specify different branches. Both are evaluated under the same agent state and navigation history. We compare generated local action sequences, the likelihoods of fixed reference action sequences under both instructions, and changes in visual attention and attribution. Across the evaluated models, higher reported navigation success does not imply that the model more faithfully follows the instructions.
authors: Josh Qixuan Sun, Xiaoying Xing, Yurun Chen, Huaiyuan Weng, Wentao Zhu, Mark Crowley
bullets: Introduces a diagnostic for instruction-action binding at route forks.
Builds 3,252 matched contexts by pairing instructions that share the traveled route but specify different branches.
Keeps the agent state and navigation history fixed while comparing actions, action likelihoods, and visual attribution.
Finds that higher navigation success does not necessarily indicate more faithful instruction following.
papers.selection_reason: Diagnostic method for instruction-action binding in navigation VLAs, directly relevant to vision-language navigation.
papers.title: NavBind: Diagnosing Instruction-Action Binding at Route Forks in Navigation VLAs
papers.tldr: NavBind tests whether navigation VLAs’ actions truly respond to instructions rather than relying on visual cues or history.

papers.abstract: Object Navigation in unseen environments remains a fundamental challenge in embodied AI, as it requires agents to generalize visual and spatial reasoning to novel layouts. While recent advances in large language model (LLM) and vision-language model (VLM) have enhanced semantic mapping, spatial memory, and waypoint selecting for navigation, successful navigation requires more than selecting the next promising waypoint. A robot must also recognize stalled progress, escape unproductive behaviors, and revisit overlooked target cues. Addressing these challenges requires both specialized navigation strategies and a high-level policy that coordinates their execution. Motivated by the analysis of failed navigation episodes, we propose LERR-Nav, an object navigation framework that coordinates exploration, recovery, and reminiscing through a learned high-level policy. The framework comprises four complementary navigation strategies: value-function-guided exploration, LLM-guided exploration, recovery from stalled or repetitive behavior, and memory-guided reminiscing. To support history-aware coordination, we maintain the execution memory that preserves textual summaries of all strategy executions alongside a sliding window of map sequences. To learn the coordination policy, we initialize a high-level vision-language agent from Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and train it through a two-stage curriculum. The first stage uses map-centric supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to establish spatial grounding. The second stage performs SFT on variable-length navigation segments to learn which navigation strategy to invoke next based on current maps and the hybrid execution memory. Experiments on HM3D and MP3D demonstrate state-of-the-art navigation performance, while ablation studies validate the contributions of individual components.
bullets: Addresses stalled progress, repetitive behavior, and overlooked target cues beyond simple waypoint selection.
Combines value-function-guided and LLM-guided exploration with recovery and memory-guided reminiscing strategies.
Uses execution summaries and a sliding window of map sequences for history-aware coordination.
Trains a high-level vision-language policy with map-centric and variable-length navigation-segment supervision.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance on HM3D and MP3D; ablations support the value of its components.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes LERR-Nav, a framework for object navigation that coordinates exploration, recovery, and reminiscing using a high-level VLM policy.
papers.title: LERR-Nav: Learning to Coordinate Exploration, Recovery, and Reminiscing for Object Navigation
papers.tldr: LERR-Nav learns to coordinate exploration, recovery, and memory-based revisiting so robots can navigate to objects more reliably in unseen environments.

papers.abstract: 3D scene graphs support language-guided navigation by organizing physical entities and their containment and spatial relations into hierarchical maps. Building such structured maps requires a scene representation that consistently distinguishes semantic regions and object instances across viewpoints. To this end, we present PanoGraphGS, a unified framework that integrates panoptic 3D Gaussian representation learning with hierarchical 3D scene graph construction. The framework learns semantic and instance features on shared Gaussian geometry. Prototype-based semantic learning and association-based instance learning produce consistent panoptic predictions across viewpoints. The learned representation supports novel-view panoptic segmentation and direct Gaussian-level panoptic decoding. A semantic-aware scene graph module further recovers a floor-room-stuff-object hierarchy with containment and spatial relations. We further release NaviGS, a real-world dataset for panoramic scene understanding. The dataset provides 3DGS, mesh, RGB, semantic, and depth data. For 3D scene graph identification, PanoGraphGS outperforms the strongest evaluated baseline in object-node accuracy by more than 50\% points on average across Replica and NaviGS. PanoGraphGS also achieves state-of-the-art performance among the evaluated methods in 2D panoptic segmentation. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of PanoGraphGS in both hierarchical 3D scene understanding and 2D panoptic segmentation. The project website is available at: https://github.com/gaojh0333/PanoGraphGS.
authors: Jinghan Gao, Siyu Wang, Dongyu Feng, Yiyuan Pan, Rong Xiong
bullets: Uses shared Gaussian geometry with prototype-based semantic learning and association-based instance learning to maintain consistent panoptic predictions across viewpoints.
Supports novel-view panoptic segmentation and direct Gaussian-level panoptic decoding.
Builds floor–room–stuff–object hierarchies with containment and spatial relations through a semantic-aware scene graph module.
Introduces NaviGS, a real-world panoramic scene-understanding dataset containing 3DGS, mesh, RGB, semantic, and depth data.

Outperforms the strongest evaluated baseline by over 50 percentage points in average object-node accuracy across Replica and NaviGS, while achieving state-of-the-art 2D panoptic segmentation among evaluated methods.
papers.selection_reason: Integrates 3D Gaussian Splatting with hierarchical 3D scene graphs for language-guided navigation, directly supporting embodied AI navigation and 3D scene understanding.
papers.title: PanoGraphGS: Unifying Panoptic Segmentation and Hierarchical 3D Scene Graphs with Gaussian Splatting
papers.tldr: PanoGraphGS jointly learns panoptic 3D Gaussian representations and hierarchical scene graphs for consistent, language-guided 3D scene understanding.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) requires long-horizon instruction-consistent planning and short-horizon local planning in current geometry. Video-action models (VAMs) offer a promising way to learn predictive representations for navigation. However, existing VAMs jointly predict visual futures and local trajectories in a single process, even though they operate at different paces: future prediction remains stable across multiple updates while local trajectories must react to fresh observations. To bridge this gap, we introduce HAVANA, a dual-system VAM that decouples predictive reasoning from reactive local planning. A slow system produces a compact language-conditioned latent plan from observation history, while a fast system combines the latest plan with the current observation to generate local trajectories. Their asynchronous execution enables rapid adaptation without repeated future prediction, and no future video is generated during inference. Experiments on OmniNavBench demonstrate state-of-the-art navigation performance over prior baselines, while real-world deployments further show robust generalization to unseen environments across different robot embodiments. Our code and checkpoints will be available at https://github.com/Anastasiawd/HAVANA.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between stable long-horizon prediction and rapidly changing local navigation needs.
Uses a slow system to create a compact, language-conditioned latent plan from observation history.
Uses a fast system to combine the plan with the latest observation and generate local trajectories asynchronously.
Avoids generating future video during inference while enabling rapid adaptation to new observations.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance on OmniNavBench and generalizes to unseen real-world environments across robot embodiments.
papers.selection_reason: Presents HAVANA, a dual-system Video-Action Model for Vision-Language Navigation that decouples predictive reasoning from reactive local planning, improving navigation performance.
papers.title: HAVANA: A Hierarchical Video-Action Model for Vision-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: HAVANA improves vision-language navigation by separating slow predictive planning from fast reactive trajectory generation.

papers.abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) relies on retaining and using relevant observations. Yet growing histories introduce redundancy, and retained information may remain underused. We introduce ReInsBench, a diagnostic benchmark that examines history utilization through controlled continuation trials. Its results show that history-review reinstruction can recover navigation failures using the existing task context. Motivated by this finding, we propose ReInsVLN, a training-free framework supporting memory construction and utilization in frozen navigators. Coverage- and Instruction-Aware Compression constructs compact visual context through temporal redundancy reduction, coverage-aware protection, and instruction-guided token selection. Forgetting-Inspired History Reminders guide navigators to revisit retained observations according to a predefined schedule, without additional model calls. On R2R Val-Unseen, ReInsVLN improves success rates by 8.48 and 3.37 percentage points over the native StreamVLN and InternVLA-N1, reaching 64.27% and 64.44%, respectively. Visual compression largely preserves navigation performance while reducing prefill latency and KV cache memory by up to 21.77% and 32.25%, respectively, on matched observation workloads. Real-world trials on humanoid and quadruped robots further support the applicability of ReInsVLN to sequential instruction following and ordinal navigation.
authors: Siwei Cheng, Hao Wu, Zitong Qi, Xinming Zhang, Haoyu Xi, Peiran Yin, Haozhe Hu, Xudong Wang, Xiaoyu Shen, Wei Zhang
bullets: ReInsBench diagnoses how effectively vision-and-language navigators use historical observations through controlled continuation trials.
Coverage- and Instruction-Aware Compression removes temporal redundancy while preserving instruction-relevant visual context.
Forgetting-Inspired History Reminders prompt frozen navigators to revisit retained observations on a predefined schedule without extra model calls.
On R2R Val-Unseen, ReInsVLN reaches 64.27% and 64.44% success, improving over StreamVLN and InternVLA-N1 by 8.48 and 3.37 percentage points.
Visual compression reduces prefill latency and KV-cache memory by up to 21.77% and 32.25%; robot trials support broader sequential instruction-following use.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free VLN with history compression and reminders, improving navigation while reducing KV cache; fits VLN, embodied memory, and token/cache efficiency.
papers.title: ReInsVLN: Revisiting Historical Evidence for Training-Free Vision-and-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: ReInsVLN is a training-free memory framework that compresses and periodically reactivates navigation history, improving VLN performance while reducing inference overhead.

papers.abstract: Every driving scene is logged once, but driving is one-to-many: the scene determines which behaviors are feasible, while an instruction selects among them. A log records only the action taken, leaving no direct supervision for alternative feasible actions or instructions the scene cannot support. Consequently, a policy that ignores language and one that follows it without regard to scene constraints can fit the same data. We present Cartender, which learns from the drives not taken. Counterfactual Branching constructs matched and mismatched instruction-action pairs from real recordings without a simulator: a vision-language model proposes alternative futures and their selecting instructions, while unsupported instructions provide negative labels. A learned scene-language compatibility score regulates language conditioning in trajectory generation, and a reward-trained language residual re-ranks generated candidates over a scene-based score. The branches are used for training; instruction following is evaluated by swapping instructions under identical recorded inputs and measuring behavior rather than agreement with generated targets. On WOD-E2E, the best of four proposals achieves an RFS of 8.642 across 3,603 feasible instruction conditions. Across 8,974 admitted proposals, mean RFS is 8.203 versus 7.906 for matched logged trajectories, and 67% score higher than their logged counterpart. Compared with matched-only imitation using the same backbone, Cartender improves same-scene paired instruction success from 23.67% to 57.00% and RFS from 6.32 to 7.10; its gate reduces infeasible-instruction execution from 53.36% to 14.18%.
authors: Zhiwen Chen, Benjin Zhu, Yan Xie, Jun Ma
bullets: Driving logs show only the action taken, providing no direct supervision for feasible alternatives or infeasible instructions.
Counterfactual Branching uses a vision-language model to generate alternative futures and instructions, with mismatches serving as negative labels without a simulator.
A scene-language compatibility gate regulates language conditioning, while a reward-trained language residual re-ranks trajectory candidates.
On WOD-E2E, Cartender improves paired instruction success from 23.67% to 57.00% and reduces infeasible-instruction execution from 53.36% to 14.18%.
Evaluation swaps instructions on identical recorded inputs and measures behavior, rather than agreement with generated targets.
papers.selection_reason: Language-conditioned driving with counterfactual learning and scene-language compatibility.
papers.title: Cartender: Verifiable Language-Conditioned Driving by Learning the Drives Not Taken
papers.tldr: Cartender enables verifiable language-conditioned driving by learning which alternative instructions and trajectories are feasible—or unsupported—from logged scenes.

papers.abstract: Building embodied agents that can perceive, reason, and act across diverse 3D worlds is a central research direction toward artificial general intelligence. Yet most existing work remains confined to specific tasks in a single scene and transfers poorly to new environments, leaving general embodied agents for open-world settings under-explored. We refer to such agents as Embodied World Agents (EWAs), whose defining property is the ability to understand diverse visual environments and execute general actions in open-world conditions. To advance EWA research, we study open-world embodied navigation-planning and release EmbodiedWorld-200K, a large-scale dataset of over 200K samples spanning diverse scenes. Each example is equipped with multi-level annotations, ranging from low-level camera-motion trajectories to high-level semantic instructions. The dataset also provides unified evaluation splits and task-specific metrics, supporting offline pretraining and fair evaluation of EWAs. Beyond offline supervision, a defining characteristic of an EWA is its interaction with the environment; training solely on offline data is therefore insufficient, especially for generalizing to scenes not covered in the training distribution. Building dedicated real interactive environments, however, is often prohibitively expensive. To address this, we propose a novel training scheme that employs a video world model as a low-cost environment proxy and performs interactive reinforcement-learning (RL) post-training of the EWA within it. Empirically, pretraining on EmbodiedWorld-200K substantially improves the open-world embodied planning ability of the EWA, and further RL post-training inside a world model yields clear gains on out-of-distribution scenes. The dataset, baseline checkpoints, and training and evaluation code are available at https://xiaokunfeng.github.io/EmbodiedWorld-200K/.
authors: X. Feng, J. Tang, Z. Lin, L. Chen, S. Shao, Q. Lu, K. Huang
bullets: Targets embodied agents that can understand diverse 3D environments and perform general actions beyond single-scene tasks.
Provides over 200K navigation-planning samples across diverse scenes with low-level motion and high-level semantic annotations.
Introduces unified evaluation splits and task-specific metrics for offline pretraining and fair assessment.
Uses a video world model as a low-cost proxy environment for interactive RL post-training.
Pretraining improves open-world planning, while world-model RL further improves performance on out-of-distribution scenes.
papers.selection_reason: Embodied navigation-planning dataset with interactive video world models for RL post-training directly fits embodied AI and world models.
papers.title: EmbodiedWorld-200K: Toward Embodied World Agents via Embodied-Planning Dataset and Interactive World Models
papers.tldr: EmbodiedWorld-200K advances open-world embodied agents with a 200K-sample planning dataset and video-world-model-based interactive RL.

papers.abstract: We study language-conditioned local navigation, where a robot must navigate to a text-specified target visible in its initial observation and stop at the described location. End-to-end navigation policies require diverse training data to generalize across scenes, yet real-robot data is costly to collect and simulated data leaves a sim-to-real gap. Internet egocentric videos offer a scalable source of real-world navigation experience. Our key insight is to learn goal-directed visual dynamics from Internet egocentric videos, and use these dynamics to support robot action generation. To this end, we propose ScaleNav, a unified world-action framework with three-stage training. We first perform instruction-conditioned video pretraining on these videos to learn how observations evolve as the camera approaches instructed targets across diverse real-world scenes. Action alignment then uses action-labeled simulated data to train the model to predict executable action chunks. Joint fine-tuning subsequently optimizes all trainable components together for navigation. ScaleNav achieves success rates of 86.5% on a single-view adaptation of Short-Horizon OVON and 94.9% on our HabitatGS-LN benchmark, outperforming the evaluated baselines on both benchmarks. We further deploy and evaluate ScaleNav on a real quadruped robot, with results supporting the model's ability to generalize to real-world navigation. Code and videos are available at https://zju3dv.github.io/ScaleNav/
authors: Yihui Yang, Yuanhong Yu, Jiawei Wang, Zhongrui Yu, Jia Shi, Kun Zhan, Ruizhen Hu, Xiaowei Zhou, Yu Liu, Sida Peng
bullets: Addresses the high cost of real-robot data and the sim-to-real gap in local navigation.
Pretrains on instruction-conditioned Internet videos to learn goal-directed visual dynamics.
Aligns learned dynamics with executable action chunks using action-labeled simulation data, then jointly fine-tunes the navigation system.
Reports 86.5% success on a single-view Short-Horizon OVON adaptation and 94.9% on HabitatGS-LN, outperforming evaluated baselines.
Real-quadruped deployment results support generalization to physical-world navigation.
papers.selection_reason: Pretrains on internet egocentric videos to learn visual dynamics for language-conditioned local navigation, spanning VLN, human-video learning, and video world models.
papers.title: ScaleNav: Scalable Internet Video Pretraining for Language-Conditioned Local Navigation
papers.tldr: ScaleNav uses large-scale Internet egocentric videos plus simulated action data to train language-conditioned navigation policies that transfer from simulation to real robots.

papers.abstract: Continuous vision-and-language navigation (VLN) is typically evaluated by goal-reaching success, assuming it reflects an agent's ability to execute language-grounded behavior.
