We show that this assumption can fail: permissive contact models in current simulators may mask physically infeasible actions, creating a physical executability gap between semantic competence and embodied realization. To bridge this gap, we introduce Visual-Semantic Traversability Alignment (VeSTA), a framework that aligns VLN policies with physically executable futures. We define visual-semantic traversability as the ability to predict instruction-conditioned trajectories that are semantically valid, geometrically feasible, and physically robust. VeSTA addresses this misalignment through two complementary mechanisms: improving executable support in trajectory generation and risk-aware selection among multimodal futures. Specifically, Trajectory Relative Group Policy Optimization uses strict-contact feedback to reshape the candidate distribution toward executable regions, while the Traversability Risk Critic learns a risk-adjusted scalar utility for candidate-wise future selection. Experiments on R2R and RxR reveal substantial dependence of existing VLN agents on simulator contact semantics. Under strict-contact evaluation, VeSTA substantially reduces collision-induced failures while preserving or improving goal-reaching performance, and controlled real-world robot experiments provide evidence that the learned preference transfers beyond simulation.
authors: Gang He, Zhile Cheng, Kepeng Xu, Zhenyang Liu, Yu-Wing Tai
bullets: Current VLN success metrics can hide physically infeasible actions because simulators may use permissive contact models.
VeSTA aligns instruction-conditioned trajectories with semantic validity, geometric feasibility, and physical robustness.
Trajectory Relative Group Policy Optimization steers candidate generation toward executable regions using strict-contact feedback.
A Traversability Risk Critic selects among multimodal futures using risk-aware utility.
Experiments on R2R, RxR, and real-robot trials show fewer collision failures under strict-contact evaluation while maintaining or improving navigation performance.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses physical executability in continuous vision-language navigation with trajectory optimization and risk-aware selection.
papers.title: Revealing and Bridging the Physical Executability Gap in Vision-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: VeSTA closes the gap between semantically correct navigation and physically executable behavior by training VLN agents to generate and select safer trajectories.

papers.abstract: Vision-language navigation is moving into photorealistic, physically simulated scenes, where the leading zero-shot agents put a vision-language model in the control loop to choose every move and stop. Robots favour small models, whose abilities are uneven: Qwen3-VL-4B can judge whether a single view looks like the goal, but its route reasoning is at chance, its distance estimates nearly constant, its stop votes unreliable. Our agent therefore asks it two perceptual questions per step, which direction looks like the goal and whether the view justifies stopping, plus one gated frontier query on route-bearing instructions, and treats the answers as evidence, not actions: a route-blind semantic field over a bird's-eye map accumulates the directional scores through a tempered update, a skeleton graph supplies frontiers and geodesic distances, and a two-stage terminator turns stop votes into termini through a trail-consistency gate and a budget-forced return. With every baseline re-run in one installation at one budget, the agent exceeds all four zero-shot baselines of the VLNVerse subset in mean success on both granularities, though the paired interval against the strongest coarse-grained baseline includes zero. Termination is the dominant lever in ablation, thirteen attempts to give the model more of the navigation establish no reliable gain, and the agent runs on a Unitree Go2 quadruped with off-board inference. Code, per-episode logs and a robot video will be released at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/structure-over-reasoning-PAGE.
authors: Zeqi Li, Xunyi Zhao, Zerui Li, Sihao Lin, Qi Wu, ShiJie Li
bullets: Small models show useful visual goal judgment but unreliable route reasoning, distance estimation, and stopping decisions.
The agent asks directional and stopping questions, plus a gated route query, and treats responses as evidence rather than actions.
A bird’s-eye semantic field, skeleton graph, geodesic frontiers, and a two-stage terminator convert these signals into navigation behavior.
It outperforms four zero-shot baselines on both VLNVerse evaluation granularities, although the interval against the strongest coarse-grained baseline includes zero.
Termination is the main ablation lever; additional navigation queries provide no reliable gain, and the system runs on a Unitree Go2 with off-board inference.
papers.selection_reason: Zero-shot vision-language navigation with a small VLM and semantic map; direct fit to VLN.
papers.title: Structure over Reasoning: Unified Zero-Shot Navigation with a Small Vision-Language Model
papers.tldr: A small vision-language model can support zero-shot navigation when structured mapping, frontier planning, and reliable termination—not direct action selection—handle route reasoning.

papers.abstract: In this study, we propose an adaptive question generation mechanism that addresses uncertainty arising from ambiguous instructions. Natural-language instructions for service robots often contain ambiguities. In scenes with multiple similar objects, the robot must identify the target object by asking questions. However, existing question generation methods focus on probabilistic discrimination efficiency and do not sufficiently account for user ease of response. Asking questions without considering the user's ease of response may cause incorrect or uncertain answers. Such incorrect or uncertain answers lead to additional clarification turns and degraded dialogue efficiency. The proposed mechanism integrates probabilistic discrimination efficiency and human cognitive characteristics to generate questions that users can intuitively and easily answer. First, the proposed mechanism extracts visual attributes of candidate objects using a vision-language model (VLM). Next, the proposed mechanism computes the information gain (IG) of each attribute and selects the visual attribute (e.g., color, shape) that most reduces uncertainty in the candidate set. When multiple attributes have the same IG, the proposed mechanism applies a visual attribute filter based on cognitive characteristics to select the visual attribute that users can most intuitively perceive. The proposed mechanism then prompts the VLM with the selected attribute and the corresponding attribute values of each candidate object to generate a concise natural-language question. This process is repeated until the target object is uniquely identified. The proposed mechanism achieved a target identification success rate of 88.5% in the evaluation using a dataset of 120 scenes. Furthermore, the proposed mechanism received high ratings in subjective evaluations of response ease.
authors: Ryo Terashima, Yuga Yano, Hakaru Tamukoh
bullets: Targets ambiguity in service-robot instructions involving multiple similar objects.
Uses a vision-language model to extract candidate-object attributes and selects the attribute with the highest information gain.
Uses a cognitive-based visual-attribute filter to break information-gain ties in favor of attributes users can answer intuitively.
Prompts the VLM to generate concise questions and repeats clarification until one target remains.
Achieved an 88.5% target-identification success rate across 120 scenes and received high ease-of-response ratings.
papers.selection_reason: Embodied instruction following for service robots, resolving ambiguous natural-language instructions through visual attribute questioning.
papers.title: Adaptive Question Generation for Ambiguous Robot Instructions Based on Information Gain and Human Cognitive Characteristics
papers.tldr: An adaptive robot question-generation method combines information gain with human cognitive factors to ask clearer questions when instructions ambiguously identify among similar objects.

papers.abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires embodied agents to ground language in visual observations and make long-horizon decisions. Existing methods often address these demands through task-specific architectures. As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become increasingly capable, an important question remains: Have we truly unlocked the potential of native MLLMs for VLN before introducing task-specific architecture? We present SimpleVLN, an architecture-preserving framework developed through studies of navigation formulation, data construction, and optimization. At the formulation level, SimpleVLN combines single-turn decision inputs with fixed-budget global-local memory to efficiently use navigation history without unbounded context growth, while action chunks enable efficient output of multiple primitive actions per model invocation. For data construction, we combine expert demonstrations with policy-dependent DAgger experience and develop a scalable synthesis pipeline that generates large-scale tasks for reinforcement learning. At the optimization level, a progressive IL-DAgger-RL pipeline advances from action imitation to task-level outcome optimization. Comprehensive experiments validate the effectiveness of these three aspects. We instantiate SimpleVLN across multiple MLLM backbones and model sizes, demonstrating its generality. SimpleVLN achieves 76.7% and 80.1% success rates on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE splits, respectively, substantially outperforming existing methods. These results show that the navigation capabilities of native MLLMs can be effectively unlocked without task-specific architectural designs.
authors: Lingyi Hong, Weiren Cai, Jiayu Chen, Xinyu Zhou, Bailin He, Yunfei Guo, Qiao Sun, Boyu Ma, Jianfei Yang, Wenqiang Zhang
bullets: Uses single-turn decisions with fixed-budget global-local memory to retain navigation history efficiently.
Predicts action chunks, reducing the number of model invocations needed for long-horizon navigation.
Combines expert demonstrations, policy-dependent DAgger data, and scalable task synthesis for reinforcement learning.
Trains progressively from imitation learning to DAgger and task-level reinforcement learning.
Achieves 76.7% success on R2R-CE and 80.1% on RxR-CE across multiple MLLM backbones and sizes.
papers.selection_reason: Vision-and-language navigation framework using native MLLMs; directly matches the VLN subtopic.
papers.title: SimpleVLN: Towards Simple and Frontier Vision-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: SimpleVLN unlocks native MLLMs for vision-language navigation through improved formulation, data, and training—without task-specific architectural changes.

papers.abstract: Reliable vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires not only understanding instructions but also determining whether and how a robot can physically execute them. However, existing VLN benchmarks typically assume executable instructions and focus on long-horizon tasks. This leaves body-dependent local execution, including passability and collision-free execution, largely unexamined. Evaluating these factors within long-horizon tasks would entangle local physical execution with task planning and long-term spatial memory, making navigation failures difficult to attribute. We therefore focus on grounding local navigation commands in executable motion under environmental and robot body constraints. We present PASS-VLN, a passability-aware local-command VLN benchmark and model. The benchmark holds the scene, instruction, start pose, and reference route fixed while varying robot body width, requiring target completion when the instructed passage is feasible and stopping before blockage otherwise. Our model encodes body width through obstacle inflation in a depth-derived local bird's-eye view, fuses geometry with visual and linguistic context, and predicts discrete latent action codes for continuous closed-loop execution. Experiments show that PASS-VLN improves collision-free success by approximately 12 percentage points over a strong VLN model fine-tuned on our benchmark, while adapting reach-versus-stop behavior to body constraints and generalizing to unseen body widths. When integrated with a high-level planner, PASS-VLN achieves higher success with fewer local commands, while real-world deployment further demonstrates its effectiveness as a low-level executor. The benchmark and model will be released.
authors: Cong Zou, Xiangsheng Shi, Xuanhui Wang, Fubin Wang, Guangjun Ge, Chao Wang, Yu Wang
bullets: Targets the underexplored problem of body-dependent, collision-free local execution in VLN, separate from long-horizon planning.
Keeps the scene, instruction, start pose, and route fixed while varying robot width to test passability-aware behavior.
Encodes body width via obstacle inflation in a depth-based local bird’s-eye view, fusing geometry, vision, and language to predict closed-loop actions.
Improves collision-free success by approximately 12 percentage points over a fine-tuned strong VLN baseline and generalizes to unseen widths.
Integration with a high-level planner yields higher success with fewer local commands; real-world deployment demonstrates low-level execution effectiveness.
papers.selection_reason: Passability-aware local-command benchmark and model for vision-and-language navigation.
papers.title: PASS-VLN: Passability-Aware Local-Command Vision-and-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: PASS-VLN benchmarks and enables vision-language navigation that adapts local motion to robot body width, choosing to pass through feasible gaps or stop safely before blockages.

papers.abstract: We study how vision-language models (VLMs) can learn to think and actively explore in 3D space. Instead of providing multi-view images, videos, or 3D representations to the model, we preserve the native visual encoding of VLMs, i.e., a single image, one at a time, just like humans, and treat the 3D representation only as an environment with which the model can interact through actions (e.g., move left) and observations (rendered images). Each rollout begins from an initial first-person view and a visual question. The model can then iteratively reason, navigate, and reorient its viewpoint before committing to a final answer. Following an initial trajectory-supervised finetuning, we apply reinforcement learning (RL) with rewards driven primarily by final-answer correctness. Crucially, RL provides no direct supervision over which viewpoints the model should visit or which exploration actions it should take. Instead, the model must learn an effective exploration policy solely from the extent to which its interactions improve performance. Across six 3D benchmarks, our model ACT3D achieves an average accuracy of 53.2% that improves its base Qwen model by 22.0% and surpasses proprietary Gemini 3.6 Flash. ACT3D also outperforms existing open-source 3D methods while using 50-70% fewer input frames, and generalizes to unseen domains with an average improvement of 5.9% over its supervised initialization. Further analysis reveals adaptive, question-conditioned exploration. Performance gains over the base model increase from 0.6% on questions answerable from the initial view to 16.3% on those requiring extensive exploration. ACT3D searches for occluded targets, avoids unnecessary exploration, and acquires complementary viewpoints for spatial comparisons. These findings demonstrate that outcome-based RL enables VLMs not only to reason over visual evidence, but also to learn when and how to acquire it.
authors: Yijiang Li, Bingyang Wang, Nuno Vasconcelos
bullets: Uses one rendered image at a time, with actions such as moving and reorienting, rather than preloaded multi-view or 3D inputs.
Combines trajectory-supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning driven mainly by final-answer correctness, without viewpoint or action labels.
Achieves 53.2% average accuracy across six 3D benchmarks, improving its base Qwen model by 22.0% and using 50–70% fewer input frames than existing open-source methods.
Learns question-conditioned exploration: it searches for occluded targets, avoids unnecessary movement, and gathers complementary views for spatial comparisons.
Generalizes to unseen domains, improving 5.9% over supervised initialization; gains are largest for questions requiring extensive exploration.
papers.selection_reason: VLM agent learns to actively explore 3D environments via actions and RL; directly fits embodied vision-language navigation and spatial reasoning.
papers.title: Learning to Think and Explore in 3D World
papers.tldr: ACT3D trains a vision-language model to actively navigate 3D environments and gather only the visual evidence needed to answer questions.

papers.abstract: Aerial vision-language navigation (VLN) agents built on large vision-language models are expensive to query. Executing a complete predicted action chunk before replanning amortizes this cost, reducing model inference from 195 to 42 ms per executed waypoint for our policy. It also moves the states at which the policy is queried away from expert demonstrations, which supervise neither recovery from these states nor termination at the learner's own arrival. On OpenFly test-seen, no-stop failures account for 47.78% of full-chunk behavior cloning (BC) outcomes. We present X-Fly, a staged training framework for full-chunk aerial VLN. Recovery DAgger labels learner-visited decision states with smooth chunks that reconnect to future expert segments and with STOP at the first in-region state. Flow-GRPO then jointly refines the chunked flow controller and a Bernoulli STOP policy from same-task closed-loop outcomes, supplemented by outcome-verified stopping supervision. With eight controls per decision, X-Fly reaches 74.18% SR on test-seen and 51.73% on test-unseen, compared with 16.45% and 18.43% for full-chunk BC and 32.04% and 29.46% for DreamFly.
authors: Ruibin Ju, Ruifeng Cai, Min Xu, Lin Wang
bullets: Full-chunk execution reduces inference cost from 195 to 42 ms per executed waypoint, but creates recovery and termination challenges.
Recovery DAgger labels learner-visited states with reconnecting action chunks and STOP targets at the first in-region state.
Flow-GRPO jointly refines the chunked controller and Bernoulli STOP policy using closed-loop task outcomes.
On OpenFly, X-Fly achieves 74.18% test-seen and 51.73% test-unseen success rates, versus 16.45%/18.43% for full-chunk BC and 32.04%/29.46% for DreamFly.
No-stop errors comprise 47.78% of full-chunk BC failures on test-seen; results are reported with eight controls per decision.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses full-chunk aerial VLN failures (no-stop) using recovery DAgger and Flow-GRPO.
papers.title: X-Fly: Learning to Reach and Stop in Full-Chunk Aerial Vision-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: X-Fly trains aerial VLN agents to recover from off-demonstration states and stop correctly while executing full action chunks, substantially improving navigation success over prior methods.

papers.abstract: Safe and robust robot navigation across diverse environments requires a high-level understanding of complex scenes and the ability to carry it into stable motion. Recent works tackle this with learning-based models trained at scale and with approaches built on vision-language models (VLMs). However, learning-based models break down outside their training distribution, while VLM-based approaches bring that understanding but rarely ground it in the scene or align the action with it. To address these limitations, we present RECAST, a robot navigation framework that combines the reasoning of a VLM with the spatial grounding of vision foundation models to build an Actionable Cost map. Given the robot's front view and the user's instruction, we first decompose the scene with the VLM, judging which surfaces are traversable, which objects pose a risk, which heading to prefer, and which gaps are passable. Vision foundation models then ground these surfaces and objects in the image, and all four judgments are spatially recast into one compact cost map. This map both conditions the trajectory decoders and scores their proposals to select the one to execute. As the VLM's answers trail the live scene, both steps draw on cost maps from two points in time: the pivot frame the VLM judged, which carries all four judgments, and the current frame, whose terrain and collision costs are rebuilt from the current image. RECAST improves success over the strongest prior method by 13.3 points in simulation and 31.4 points on a real quadruped, and reduces the collision rate relative to it by 9.6 and 14.3 points, reaching the lowest collision rate among all methods. The project page is available at https://recast-nav.github.io/
bullets: Addresses the gap between VLM reasoning and spatially grounded, executable actions in diverse environments.
A VLM evaluates traversability, risks, preferred heading, and passable gaps from the robot view and instruction.
Vision foundation models ground these judgments in the image and recast them into a compact cost map.
The map conditions trajectory decoders and ranks their proposals for execution, using both past VLM judgments and current terrain/collision estimates.
Improves success over the strongest prior method by 13.3 points in simulation and 31.4 points on a real quadruped, while reducing collision rates by 9.6 and 14.3 points.
papers.selection_reason: Combines VLM reasoning with spatial grounding for instruction-conditioned robot navigation.
papers.title: RECAST: Recasting Vision-Language Semantics into an Actionable Cost Map for Robot Navigation
papers.tldr: RECAST combines VLM reasoning with spatial grounding to convert scene understanding and user instructions into an actionable cost map for safer robot navigation.

papers.abstract: Urban uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) vision-language navigation (VLN) requires agents to follow instructions across extended urban spaces, inherently demanding long-term memory and geospatial grounding. However, scaling existing benchmarks remains difficult because of their reliance on costly reconstructed 3D assets, limiting geographic diversity and episode scale. To address this, we introduce SatNav, a scalable, long-horizon UAV VLN benchmark built from high-resolution satellite imagery. SatNav targets city-level navigation missions and uses satellite crops as approximations of UAV nadir views for visual observations. Through an automated cue-to-episode pipeline, SatNav constructs 118K episodes from 59 scenes across 18 cities, with an average trajectory length of 379 m. To stress-test long-horizon memory and geospatial reasoning, SatNav defines three task families: Boundary, Landmark, and Route, targeting loop progress tracking, landmark-based spatial grounding, and route following with counting cues. Benchmarking classical VLN agents and recent agents based on large vision-language models (LVLMs) on SatNav shows that city-scale navigation remains challenging. We further introduce SwiftVLN, a modular framework with switchable memory components, and conduct systematic memory-design ablations. Finally, satellite-to-UAV transfer experiments show that satellite-trained navigation models can operate on real-flight UAV observations, showing the practical relevance of SatNav. Our project page: https://eku127.github.io/SatNav/
bullets: Addresses the cost and limited geographic diversity of existing UAV VLN benchmarks built from reconstructed 3D assets.
Provides 118K episodes across 59 scenes in 18 cities, with average trajectories of 379 m.
Defines Boundary, Landmark, and Route tasks to evaluate memory, spatial grounding, and route following.
Finds that both classical VLN and large vision-language-model agents struggle with city-scale navigation.
Introduces SwiftVLN for modular memory studies and demonstrates transfer from satellite-trained models to real UAV observations.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a scalable UAV vision-language navigation benchmark with long-horizon memory challenges.
papers.title: SatNav: A Scalable Benchmark for Long-Horizon UAV Vision-Language Navigation from Satellite Imagery
papers.tldr: SatNav is a large-scale benchmark for testing long-horizon UAV vision-language navigation using satellite imagery as a scalable alternative to 3D environments.

papers.abstract: Rapid progress in AI agents and robotics makes it a matter of the near future that humans are served by a team of robots. Such a team will receive several goals at once, each specified in whatever form is convenient for the human, such as a category name, a photo, or a spoken description. Existing benchmarks study multi-agent, multi-modal, and multi-object goal navigation in isolation, and a benchmark that places all three in one episode is missing. To fill this gap, we introduce HM3D-M3. A team of K agents starts at distributed locations in a photorealistic indoor scene and searches for an unordered set of M object goals, each given as an open-vocabulary category, an instance image, or an instance description. HM3D-M3 provides 1,000 validation episodes over 3,926 goals from 379 open-vocabulary categories, 100K observation-assignment training samples, and two team-level metrics, goal-level SR and makespan-normalized SPL. We further contribute two baselines. HiGA is a trained hierarchical goal assigner on top of a frozen open-vocabulary navigation policy, and LaViRA-M3 is a training-free team of VLM agents with shared mapping and progress analysis. Adapted multi-robot and zero-shot methods reach 16--27% SR, while our baselines reach 38--41% with complementary strengths and distinct failure modes. Furthermore, we deploy LaViRA-M3 on a heterogeneous three-robot team. Project page: https://robo-lavira.github.io/hm3d-m3/
authors: Hongyu Ding, Kanyu Xu, Mingjia Chen, Zixuan Chen, Jieqi Shi, Jing Huo, Yifan Zhang, Yang Gao
bullets: Targets the previously uncombined setting of multi-agent, multi-modal, multi-object goal navigation in photorealistic indoor scenes.
Episodes involve K agents searching for an unordered set of M goals expressed as open-vocabulary categories, instance images, or descriptions.
Provides 1,000 validation episodes, 3,926 goals across 379 categories, 100K training samples, and team-level SR and makespan-normalized SPL metrics.
Introduces HiGA, a trained hierarchical goal assigner, and LaViRA-M3, a training-free VLM-agent team with shared mapping and progress analysis.
Adapted and zero-shot methods achieve 16–27% SR, while the proposed baselines reach 38–41%; LaViRA-M3 is also deployed on three heterogeneous robots.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and baselines for multi-agent, multi-modal, multi-object goal navigation.
papers.title: HM3D-M3: A Benchmark for Multi-Agent, Multi-Modal, Multi-Object Goal Navigation
papers.tldr: HM3D-M3 introduces a benchmark for teams of robots jointly navigating to multiple objects specified through mixed language, image, and category goals.

papers.abstract: This paper presents $S^3$-Nav, a structured spatial-semantic decision-making framework for language-guided robot navigation under partial observability. Rather than assuming a complete environment representation in advance, $S^3$-Nav incrementally constructs persistent spatial-semantic state while exposing only a capacity-controlled, task-conditioned view to the high-level policy. This separation decouples what the robot must retain from what the policy needs to inspect, allowing decision complexity to be controlled without discarding grounded evidence required for subsequent reasoning and validation. High-level navigation outputs remain provisional and are independently grounded and validated against persistent semantic evidence and current geometric observations before physical execution or task termination. Evaluations across multiple environments and object- and relation-goal tasks demonstrate that separating persistent state, decision-facing evidence, and execution authority improves closed-loop navigation reliability while reducing policy reasoning cost.
bullets: Incrementally builds a persistent spatial-semantic representation instead of requiring a complete environment model.
Provides the high-level policy with a compact, task-conditioned view to control decision complexity.
Independently grounds and validates provisional navigation decisions using stored semantic evidence and current geometry.
Evaluations across multiple environments and object- and relation-goal tasks show improved closed-loop reliability with lower policy reasoning cost.
papers.selection_reason: Language-guided robot navigation with structured spatial-semantic state directly fits vision-language navigation.
papers.title: $S^3$-Nav: Structured Spatial-Semantic Decision Making for Language-Guided Robot Navigation
papers.tldr: S³-Nav improves language-guided robot navigation under partial observability by separating persistent spatial-semantic memory from capacity-controlled policy inputs and validating actions before execution.

papers.abstract: Simulated environments enable scalable training data generation for embodied agents, but more data does not necessarily provide what a particular agent needs to learn. Existing environment-generation pipelines largely optimize generic properties such as realism, diversity, or task coverage, while different pretrained policies can fail for different environmental reasons. We therefore introduce WEDGE, a framework for weakness-guided navigation learning in which the failure modes of a pretrained agent guide the generation of training environments at each adaptation round. Given a pretrained policy, WEDGE uses an LLM to propose executable weakness features from contrasting successful and failed rollouts, automatically validates them on the diagnostic set, and selects the strongest validated weakness based on its success-rate gap. The validated weaknesses are then mapped to the environmental factors that control them. WEDGE varies these factors to construct environments in the difficulty regimes where the policy struggles, producing targeted training experience for adaptation. Across three navigation agents with different adaptation mechanisms, we find that policies exhibit distinct weakness profiles and benefit from different training environments. Weakness-conditioned adaptation consistently outperforms matched random and hard-example alternatives on ProcTHOR, while the resulting gains for Uni-NaVid and Gemini also extend to HM3D after ProcTHOR adaptation. Iterative re-diagnosis further shows that dominant weaknesses can persist or shift as the policy improves, providing updated guidance for subsequent environment construction. Together, these results show that policy failures are not only diagnostic signals, but actionable guidance for constructing training environments that target a policy's current weaknesses.
authors: Yue Zhang, Han Lin, Zun Wang, Yidong Huang, Zaid Khan, Mohit Bansal
bullets: Generic realism, diversity, and task coverage may not target the distinct failure modes of different pretrained navigation policies.
An LLM extracts and validates weakness features from contrasting successful and failed rollouts, then selects the strongest weakness by success-rate gap.
The framework maps validated weaknesses to controllable environmental factors and generates environments in the difficulty regimes where the policy struggles.
Across three navigation agents, weakness-conditioned adaptation outperforms matched random and hard-example alternatives on ProcTHOR; gains for Uni-NaVid and Gemini transfer to HM3D.
Iterative re-diagnosis tracks weaknesses that persist or shift as policies improve, enabling updated environment generation.
papers.selection_reason: Weakness-guided environment generation for embodied navigation agents.
papers.title: From Failures to Learnable Worlds: Policy-Conditioned Environment Generation for Navigation Agents
papers.tldr: WEDGE uses a policy’s observed failures to generate targeted training environments that address its current navigation weaknesses.

papers.abstract: Embodied visual tracking requires a robot to identify a designated target from visual observations and control its own motion to follow that target through an environment. Following an isolated person is a comparatively simple demonstration of embodied visual tracking, but following the intended person among distractors remains challenging. Existing methods exhibit a substantial drop in success from single-target to distractor tracking, motivating a focus on the shared spaces that person-following robots must navigate. We present \method{}, a vision--language waypoint policy built around the hypothesis that visual and language representations should be aligned before tracking-specific motion is learned. The policy combines complementary frozen visual encoders, multiscale temporal context, a transformer backbone, and a lightweight head for robot-centric waypoint prediction. Its training progresses through vision--language alignment, multimodal reasoning mid-training, and tracking specialization on 19,532 oracle episodes. Compared with 41.54\% distractor-tracking success for our earlier OmTrackVLA model, the complete multi-stage recipe achieves 55.80\%. We then explore on-policy refinement using filtered oracle labels for states visited by the policy. This preliminary study adds 2.42 percentage points of distractor-tracking success, reaching 58.22\%, while reducing collision rate by 1.99 pts. The final policy records the highest distractor- and ambiguous-tracking success rates among the compared methods. These results support staged multimodal learning as a promising direction for tracking among distractors and motivate further study of on-policy refinement for person following in shared spaces.
authors: Kyusong Lee, Heting Ying, Tiancheng Zhao
bullets: Targets the challenge of following the intended person in shared spaces with visual distractors.
Uses frozen visual encoders, multiscale temporal context, a transformer, and waypoint prediction.
Trains in stages: vision-language alignment, multimodal reasoning, and tracking specialization.
On-policy refinement raises distractor-tracking success from 55.80% to 58.22% and reduces collision rate by 1.99 percentage points.
The study is preliminary and motivates further work on on-policy refinement for person following.
papers.selection_reason: Vision-language waypoint policy for embodied tracking, relevant to embodied navigation and VLA.
papers.title: VLX-Go: Robust Embodied Tracking through Multi-Stage Learning and On-Policy Refinement
papers.tldr: VLX-Go improves robot person-following among distractors through staged vision-language learning and on-policy refinement.

papers.abstract: Robots following persistent language instructions must decide which cached room judgments remain valid as their environment changes. We present MIND (Maintenance via INstruction-conditioned Dependencies), a framework for maintaining target-room decisions without re-evaluating every room after each event. A language model compiles each instruction into dependencies for semantic qualification and target selection. The controller intersects semantic dependencies with event footprints, refreshes affected judgments, and updates reachability and selection separately. For fixed deterministic evaluation, planning, and selection, conservative dependency and footprint coverage preserves the decisions of full recomputation. On 240 five-event ProcTHOR sequences with an exact benchmark predicate, MIND reduces mean semantic evaluations from 30.6 to 11.2 while preserving all 1,200 post-event decisions. Frozen-evaluator experiments with Phi-4 and Qwen3-14B also preserve all 1,200 decisions, without improving the evaluators' underlying task accuracy. In 32 closed-loop AI2-THOR episodes using exact-predicate qualification and metadata-derived footprints, MIND matches the final target decision of full recomputation in every episode. Unitree G1 experiments demonstrate target reuse and reselection across room transitions without additional semantic evaluations under MIND, and abstention after a barrier and an object removal at 4 evaluations against 15 to 18. Additional materials are available at https://mind-icra27.github.io/.
authors: Mohamed Abouagour, Junhyun Nam, Wonse Jo, Byung-Cheol Min

papers.title: MIND: Instruction-Conditioned Incremental Grounding for Robots
papers.tldr: MIND efficiently maintains robot room-selection decisions after environmental changes by recomputing only instruction-relevant, affected judgments while preserving full-recomputation decisions.

papers.abstract: Surface navigation on the Moon is subject to extreme illumination contrast and deployment-time perceptual disturbances. While modular navigation pipelines have long supported planetary rover navigation, robustness is compromised by measurement errors that propagate through hand-engineered components. End-to-end learned policies are an alternative approach to navigation, which maps observations directly to control actions without intermediate components. Vision-language-action models, in particular, have driven significant breakthroughs in robotics and autonomous vehicle research. By leveraging internet-scale vision-language pretraining, these models can be exploited for their commonsense reasoning and visual understanding to provide robust generalization with limited task-specific data. However, their applicability and performance have yet to be characterized for lunar surface operations. In this study, we design a vision-language-action policy for autonomous lunar rover docking and characterize its performance relative to a modular navigation pipeline. We develop a scalable training framework that generates safety-aware expert demonstrations in a high-fidelity lunar simulation environment. In closed-loop evaluations, our policy performs competitively relative to the modular baseline under perceptual disturbances unseen during training. To address the tradeoff between compute consumption and closed-loop safety, the policy adapts its execution horizon by determining how far the rover may safely travel in open loop. Adaptive-horizon execution reduces inference frequency while limiting hazard-contact rates relative to fixed horizons in the evaluated scenarios.
bullets: Addresses robustness challenges from extreme lunar illumination and deployment-time perceptual disturbances.
Uses an end-to-end vision-language-action policy mapping observations directly to rover control actions.
Trains with safety-aware expert demonstrations generated in a high-fidelity lunar simulation.
Performs competitively with a modular navigation baseline in closed-loop evaluation under unseen disturbances.
Adaptive execution horizons reduce inference frequency while limiting hazard-contact rates versus fixed horizons in evaluated scenarios.
papers.selection_reason: End-to-end VLA policy for lunar rover docking; directly relevant to embodied navigation and VLA.
papers.title: End-to-End Vision-Language-Action Policies for Autonomous Lunar Rover Docking
papers.tldr: A vision-language-action policy enables robust autonomous lunar rover docking under unseen perceptual disturbances while reducing inference through safety-aware adaptive-horizon control.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) have shown strong potential for embodied vision-language navigation (VLN), yet their performance degrades on long-horizon trajectories due to context-length limits, redundant historical observations, and unstable spatial alignment across time. These issues make it difficult to both compress long navigation histories and reliably reuse past spatial experience. To address these limitations, we propose \textbf{MemoryVLN}, a unified memory-driven navigation system built around memory construction and management. During memory construction, \emph{Long Sequence Compression} employs forgetting-curve-inspired temporal sampling to preserve dense recent evidence and sparse yet representative distant observations under a limited token budget. \emph{Ego-Aware Memory Representation} further integrates 2D semantic tokens, 3D geometric tokens, and 6D agent poses, allowing each memory to encode both what was observed and where it was observed. During memory management, \emph{Hierarchical Memory Bank} maintains in-episode and context-level memories through cross-context warm-start and confidence-controlled write-back. \emph{Memory Enhancement} then retrieves the Top-$K$ relevant memories according to the current navigation state and fuses them with the current visual tokens. Together, these mechanisms transform raw navigation history into compact, spatially grounded, selectively retrievable, and reusable navigation experience. Extensive experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE demonstrate consistent improvements over the state-of-the-art baselines by a substantial margin (i.e., 2\% and 6.5\% in successful rate).
authors: Xueyao Wei, Yifei Wang, Delun Li, Shaoan Wang, Junzhi Yu, Wenjie Song, Xingyu Chen
bullets: Addresses context-length limits, redundant observations, and unstable spatial alignment in long trajectories.
Compresses history with temporal sampling that preserves recent evidence and representative distant observations.
Represents memories using 2D semantics, 3D geometry, and 6D agent poses for spatial grounding.

Reports successful-rate gains of 2% on R2R-CE and 6.5% on RxR-CE over state-of-the-art baselines.

papers.title: MemoryVLN: From Ego-Aware Memory Representation to Cross-Context Memory Reuse in Vision-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: MemoryVLN improves long-horizon vision-language navigation by compressing, spatially grounding, and selectively reusing navigation history.

papers.abstract: Quadruped robots performing outdoor deliveries must interpret complex scenes, anticipate changes, and navigate in socially compliant ways. Robot demonstrations are costly to collect at the scale needed for generalization. Egocentric web videos offer abundant human navigation experience, but differences in viewpoint and motion make this experience difficult to transfer to robots. We introduce DR-VLA, a Mixture-of-Transformers framework that transfers human navigation experience through a domain-invariant scene representation (DISR). The framework combines vision-language understanding and latent world modeling with a flow-matching action expert. We introduce EgoLynx, comprising 10,000 hours of curated egocentric web video (EgoLynx-Web) and 2,000 clips of teleoperated robot navigation collected during real-world deliveries (EgoLynx-Robot). We pretrain the understanding and world experts on EgoLynx-Web without action labels, then adapt the model to robot observations and train the action expert on EgoLynx-Robot to predict executable trajectories. We also propose the Quadruped Navigation Score (QNS), a pseudo-closed-loop metric combining safety, instruction compliance, comfort, and progress. On the held-out EgoLynx-Robot test split, DR-VLA improves QNS by approximately 5% and reduces open-loop final heading error (FHE) by 14.6%, each relative to the best competing result for that metric. Ablations show that web-video pretraining improves generalization and that the model's key components contribute to performance. As a future-prediction target, DISR outperforms five generic visual representations and yields performance close to task-specific 3D perception without dedicated geometric labels or point clouds for target construction. Trained separately on NAVSIM v1 without web pretraining, DR-VLA achieves 92.1 PDMS, suggesting that the framework also applies to autonomous driving.
authors: Jun Tian, Yingjie Niu, Ruo Chen, Hongyi Lin, Chao Li

papers.title: DR-VLA: Learning Human-Like Quadruped Navigation from Egocentric Web Videos via Domain-Invariant Scene Representations
papers.tldr: DR-VLA transfers human navigation knowledge from egocentric web videos to quadruped robots using domain-invariant scene representations, improving navigation quality and heading accuracy.

papers.abstract: Wheel-legged robots operating in outdoor spaces shared with humans require accurate perception, socially compliant navigation, future-scene reasoning, and scene reconstruction. However, existing datasets typically support these capabilities in isolation and rarely provide dense spatial and behavior-level supervision on real wheel-legged platforms. We introduce LynxScenes, a large-scale real-world dataset and benchmark collected with a LYNX M20 wheel-legged robot. It contains approximately 100K 30-s navigation clips spanning 833.6 h and 3,294.7 km, with 3.0M annotated frames. The synchronized recordings include four fisheye cameras, dual LiDARs, IMU, odometry, and robot states. Annotations comprise 20.82M oriented 3D boxes across 27 categories, 13.89M road-structure annotations, and 20 navigation instructions organized into three layers and aligned with continuous future trajectories. LynxScenes supports four complementary tasks: instruction-conditioned trajectory prediction, BEV-based perception of 3D objects and road structures, future scene prediction, and multi-view scene reconstruction. For trajectory prediction, we further introduce a log-replay-based pseudo-closed-loop evaluator that measures safety, progress, and instruction compliance beyond trajectory imitation. Extensive evaluations across representative navigation, perception, world-model, and reconstruction methods reveal substantial remaining challenges in close-range outdoor robot navigation. The dataset and evaluation toolkit are planned for public release.
authors: Jun Tian, Hao Wu, Ruo Chen, Yili Liao, Hongyi Lin, Jincheng Yu, Chao Li, Yingjie Niu

papers.selection_reason: Large-scale real-world wheel-legged robot benchmark spanning instruction-conditioned navigation, future-scene prediction, and perception.
papers.title: LynxScenes: A Large-Scale Real-World Benchmark for Outdoor Wheel-Legged Robot Perception, Navigation, Imagination and Reconstruction
papers.tldr: LynxScenes is a large-scale real-world benchmark for evaluating outdoor wheel-legged robot perception, navigation, future-scene reasoning, and reconstruction.

papers.abstract: Language provides a natural interface for humans to specify and reason about goals, but training language-conditioned robotic policies and reasoning typically requires expensive manual annotations. We propose Action Self-Distillation (ASD), a method for learning language-conditioned reasoning for robotic navigation without human-annotated language or reasoning labels. ASD uses an open-source VLM, which contains broad world knowledge and reasoning capabilities, as both a teacher network and a student policy. During training, the self-teacher receives privileged trajectory feedback and infers the underlying navigation goal together with goal-oriented reasoning. The student is then trained to condition on the inferred navigation goal, predict future ego-frame trajectory, and provide a description of the scene semantics, plan, and reasoning, from onboard observations alone. Across 13 challenging indoor and outdoor real-world navigation tasks, our method improves success rate over the strongest baseline by $30\%$ in indoor settings, $30\%$ on multi-stage tasks, and achieves $95\%$ success rate on outdoor tasks, validating that privileged trajectory feedback can enable self-distillation for scalable generalist navigation policies without human annotations.
authors: Bowen Feng, Keqin Wang, Yulong Yang, Amogh Joshi, Christine Allen-Blanchette, Dhruv Shah, Felix Heide

papers.title: Training Generalist Navigation Policies via Action Self-Distillation
papers.tldr: Action Self-Distillation trains language-conditioned generalist navigation policies without human language or reasoning annotations by distilling privileged trajectory feedback from a vision-language model.

papers.abstract: Vision-language navigation requires agents to follow natural-language instructions to reach target locations, making high-quality language supervision essential. Since human annotation is costly, prior work has explored scalable data synthesis methods. However, existing methods typically either use separate models for navigation and instruction generation or couple the two tasks through task-specific components; most also annotate the full trajectory corpus with a fixed model before updating, which can cause generated supervision to lag behind the evolving policy. Therefore, we introduce RSI-Nav, a data-centric recursive self-improvement framework for navigation via policy-synchronized language-action dual bootstrapping, which unifies vision-language-to-action instruction following and vision-action-to-language instruction generation within a shared model. Specifically, after supervised fine-tuning establishes fundamental capabilities, RSI-Nav progressively processes unlabeled trajectories in small shards. The current model generates instructions for these trajectories, executes them to evaluate goal completion and path efficiency, retains qualified samples, and immediately updates itself before processing the next shard. This shard-wise update keeps newly generated supervision aligned with the evolving policy. We also incorporate spatial understanding data, since stronger spatial reasoning benefits navigation. Extensive experiments show that RSI-Nav reaches 68.6% SR on R2R-CE and 72.4% SR on RxR-CE, while providing stronger instruction-generation utility and modestly improved spatial understanding after recursive evolution.
authors: Songze Li, Haoming Gu, Ziyang Gong, Zhitong Wang, Gengze Zhou, Zun Wang, Yuhan Zhu, Tianxiang Jiang, Juanzi Li, Qi Wu, Weinan Zhang, Yu Qiao, Wenwei Zhang, Yi Wang
bullets: Targets costly human language supervision and stale synthetic annotations in vision-language navigation.
Uses one shared model for instruction following (vision-language-to-action) and instruction generation (vision-action-to-language).
Processes unlabeled trajectories in small shards, evaluates generated instructions by goal completion and path efficiency, then updates immediately.
Adds spatial-understanding data to strengthen navigation reasoning.
Reports 68.6% SR on R2R-CE and 72.4% SR on RxR-CE, with stronger instruction-generation utility and modest spatial-understanding gains.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses vision-language navigation with recursive self-improvement and language-action dual bootstrapping.
papers.title: Data-Centric Recursive Self-Improvement for Navigation via Policy-Synchronized Language-Action Dual Bootstrapping
papers.tldr: RSI-Nav recursively improves vision-language navigation by generating, filtering, and learning from instructions synchronized with the evolving policy.

papers.abstract: In real-world indoor fire environments, visual degradation severely impairs instruction grounding, waypoint prediction, and long-horizon exploration in vision-language navigation (VLN). Although image restoration offers a natural means to mitigate such visual degradation, existing methods primarily optimize reconstruction fidelity, which does not necessarily translate into better navigation decisions and may even corrupt task-critical cues when applied indiscriminately. In this paper, we present FireNav, a decision-oriented reconstruction evidence routing framework that aligns visual restoration with navigation utility in VLN. To advance this task, we first contribute FireVLN-Bench, a paired indoor fire navigation benchmark with clean references preserving task semantics, safety supervision, and matched settings for continuous navigation and robot execution with simulated dynamics. Our FireNav retains native visual tokens and treats latent reconstruction features as auxiliary evidence, where a lightweight router leverages visual features, task context, and prior execution states to determine whether such evidence should be admitted and how strongly it should contribute to the visual tokens. To learn when reconstruction is beneficial, we further introduce decision utility calibration, which compares action prediction losses with and without candidate evidence under the same state, thereby supervising evidence selection according to its contribution to waypoint, heading, and arrival prediction. Experiments demonstrate that FireNav consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both navigation success and path efficiency across evaluation settings.
authors: Hongbo Ding, Xiang Chen, Jiangxin Dong, Jinshan Pan
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between reconstruction fidelity and navigation utility, where indiscriminate restoration can damage task-critical cues.
Introduces FireVLN-Bench, a paired indoor-fire VLN benchmark with clean semantic references, safety supervision, and continuous robot-execution settings.
Uses a lightweight router to combine native visual tokens with optional latent reconstruction features based on visual context, task context, and prior execution states.
Trains evidence selection with decision utility calibration using action losses for waypoint, heading, and arrival prediction.
Reports consistent gains over state-of-the-art baselines in navigation success and path efficiency across evaluation settings.
papers.selection_reason: Vision-language navigation in degraded indoor fire environments with decision-oriented reconstruction routing.
papers.title: FireNav: Decision-Oriented Reconstruction Evidence Routing for Vision-Language Navigation in Indoor Fire Environments
papers.tldr: FireNav routes visual reconstruction evidence according to its usefulness for navigation decisions, improving VLN in visually degraded indoor fire environments.

papers.abstract: Real-world Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) requires agents to act under partial observability, where map structure, semantic cues, and target locations may be incomplete or incorrectly inferred by foundation models. This paper presents a lightweight, training-free, and uncertainty-aware framework for cooperative multi-agent multi-target search in mapless environments. Instead of learning an end-to-end navigation policy, the framework separates high-level semantic reasoning from low-level execution through a scalable graph-optimization backbone. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) serve only as hypothesis generators, proposing semantic zones, target-location cues, and possible navigable connections. These outputs are treated as uncertain priors and further refined using online observations and graph-context evidence. Cooperative navigation is then formulated as a rolling-horizon multi-agent mixed-integer linear program with a lexicographic objective that first maximizes target-directed reward and then reduces travel distance, uncertain-edge use, and repeated visits. Experiments derived from 100 Matterport3D test cases show that the proposed framework improves target coverage and search efficiency over representative baseline methods, while shared information and joint planning enable more balanced workloads across agents. By operating on an abstract graph without relying on embodiment-specific policy parameters, the framework scales across varying numbers of agents and targets, generalizes to unseen environments, and accommodates different perception modules and low-level controllers without task-specific retraining.
authors: Fan Pu, Keshu Wu, Jiwan Jiang, Shiyu Shen, Zhiwen Fan, Zhengzhong Tu, Jiachen Li, Yang Zhou
bullets: Addresses partial observability and unreliable foundation-model inferences in multi-target embodied search.
Uses MLLMs as hypothesis generators, then refines semantic zones, target cues, and connectivity with online observations and graph context.
Plans via rolling-horizon multi-agent mixed-integer linear programming with lexicographic priorities for target reward, shorter travel, fewer uncertain edges, and fewer revisits.
Experiments on 100 Matterport3D test cases report improved target coverage and search efficiency over representative baselines, with more balanced workloads.
Its abstract-graph design supports varying agent and target counts, perception modules, and low-level controllers without task-specific retraining.
papers.selection_reason: Cooperative multi-agent embodied search from uncertain vision-language priors; directly relevant to VLN.
papers.title: Training-Free Multi-Agent Cooperative Embodied Search from Uncertain Vision-Language Priors
papers.tldr: A training-free framework turns uncertain vision-language hypotheses into cooperative multi-agent search plans for unseen, mapless environments.

papers.abstract: Despite recent advances in Aerial Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN), single Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) search-and-rescue in outdoor scenarios remains challenging due to partial observability, making cross-altitude collaboration a promising direction. However, existing collaborative navigation methods rely on precise target localization and rigid goal-dispatching paradigms, ignoring high-altitude observation uncertainty and suppressing low-altitude exploration autonomy. To address these issues, we introduce BGC-Nav, a training-free cross-altitude collaboration framework that enables robust navigation via Belief-Guided Coupling (BGC). Specifically, the high-altitude UAV maintains a Global Belief Memory encoding task-conditioned priors, which the low-altitude agent incorporates into decision-making via Local Exhaustion Memory (LEM), Local Attraction Augmentation (LAA), and Directional Belief Prior (DBP) as an advisory bias rather than a rigid command. Extensive experiments on ESARBench show that BGC-Nav consistently outperforms state-of-the-art single-agent and collaborative methods. Code is available at https://github.com/uestchjw/BGC-Nav.
authors: Jiuwu Hao, Yueyang Wu, Liguo Sun, Haolin Song, Zao Zhang, Pin Lv
bullets: Addresses outdoor UAV search-and-rescue challenges caused by partial observability and uncertain high-altitude observations.
Uses a Global Belief Memory on the high-altitude UAV to provide task-conditioned priors.
The low-altitude UAV integrates this guidance through Local Exhaustion Memory, Local Attraction Augmentation, and Directional Belief Prior.
Treats high-altitude information as an advisory bias rather than a rigid goal assignment, preserving low-altitude autonomy.
Experiments on ESARBench report consistent improvements over existing single-agent and collaborative methods.ﬁ
papers.selection_reason: Cross-altitude multi-UAV collaborative navigation with belief-guided coupling, fitting aerial VLN and robot navigation.
papers.title: BGC-Nav: Cross-Altitude Multi-UAV Collaborative Navigation via Belief-Guided Coupling
papers.tldr: BGC-Nav enables training-free cross-altitude multi-UAV navigation by using high-altitude beliefs as flexible guidance for low-altitude exploration under partial observability.

papers.abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) agents are typically evaluated by whether they reach a target and how efficiently they follow an instructed route, yet these metrics provide little information about collision behavior. Moreover, continuous VLN evaluation commonly uses a sliding regime, where an agent can slide along obstacles after a collision, potentially masking the effect of unsafe actions on navigation performance. We introduce VLN-Safe, a benchmark for analyzing collision safety under two complementary evaluation regimes: sliding, reflecting common VLN evaluation practice, and blocking, where collision-inducing actions prevent forward motion and more directly expose their consequences. Across six published agents on R2R-CE, 38.5-56.8% of successful episodes contain contact under sliding, while switching to blocking decreases success rate by 11.7-36.1 percentage points. We further analyze signals for anticipating imminent collisions and find that depth geometry and recent movement history are more informative than policy-derived signals, while safe alternatives near the policy's preferred action are rarely available. Motivated by these findings, we introduce a training-free collision guard that vetoes risky forward actions, executes an escape maneuver, and returns control to the original policy. Under blocking, the guard reduces collision steps by 62-98% and improves success rate by 6.9-29.3 percentage points across five recurrent, topological, and vision-language-action agents. Under sliding, it leaves success rate unchanged while raising the share of collision-free successes by 4.1-12.4 points. These results reveal a substantial gap between task success and collision-safe navigation and show that lightweight collision-aware intervention can improve both safety and navigation performance.
authors: Hieu D. Pham, Quoc-An Luong, Dung D. Le
bullets: Introduces VLN-Safe, a benchmark comparing sliding evaluation with blocking evaluation that prevents motion after collisions.
Across six agents on R2R-CE, 38.5–56.8% of successful sliding episodes involve contact; blocking lowers success by 11.7–36.1 percentage points.
Depth geometry and recent movement history better predict imminent collisions than policy-derived signals, while nearby safe alternatives are uncommon.
The training-free guard vetoes risky forward actions, performs an escape maneuver, and returns control to the original policy.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes collision safety in VLN and proposes a training-free collision guard, directly fitting vision-language navigation.
papers.title: Successful but Unsafe: An Analytical Benchmark for Revealing Collisions in Vision-and-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: VLN agents can succeed while frequently colliding, but a lightweight collision guard substantially improves safety and often navigation success.

papers.abstract: Continuous indoor-outdoor navigation connects destination-level reasoning with motion decisions that must respond to current observations. We present VbotNav-0, a cloud-edge dual-policy framework that links these processes through asynchronous policy-to-policy conditioning. The cloud policy produces subgoal guidance from visual history, navigation instructions, and route tokens; the edge policy combines available guidance with current RGB and LiDAR observations to generate local trajectories. This formulation allows the local perception-action loop to continue between cloud updates. A common route representation connects indoor paths and outdoor map routes, and the training recipe combines navigation demonstrations, corrective data, and grounded visual question answering (VQA). In the reported closed-loop evaluation of 258 episodes across 145 scenes, VbotNav-0 achieves 55.04% success rate and 55.03% success weighted by path length.
authors: Shiqi Tan, Yujun Zhang, Keyu Li, Shuaixi Pan, Siyu Zhou, Hailong Qin, Yinan Yu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of linking destination-level reasoning with observation-driven motion across indoor and outdoor environments.
Uses a cloud policy for subgoal guidance from visual history, instructions, and route tokens, while an edge policy generates trajectories from guidance, RGB, and LiDAR.
Asynchronous policy conditioning lets local perception and action continue between cloud updates.
A shared route representation connects indoor paths with outdoor map routes; training combines demonstrations, corrective data, and grounded VQA.
In closed-loop evaluation across 258 episodes and 145 scenes, it reports 55.04% success and 55.03% success weighted by path length.
papers.selection_reason: Cloud-edge dual-policy navigation using visual history and instructions, fitting vision-language navigation and robot navigation.
papers.title: VbotNav-0: Asynchronous Cloud-Edge Dual-Policy Navigation across Indoor and Outdoor Environments
papers.tldr: VbotNav-0 enables continuous indoor–outdoor navigation by asynchronously combining cloud-based subgoal planning with edge-based local control.

papers.abstract: Emerging strong Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have advanced navigation foundation models. However, these models still have unsatisfactory performance on goal-oriented navigation settings. In this paper, we first conduct a motivating study revealing that the key issue lies in the insufficient utilization of streaming observations and imprecise target localization. To tackle these challenges, we propose GG-Nav, a simple yet effective navigation framework that learns a structured chain-of-thought (CoT) mechanism via supervised fine-tuning to explicitly localize goal-relevant instances, accumulate grounding evidence, and support more reliable decision-making. Specifically, the structured CoT is designed with two key stages: (i) Observation-to-Evidence, which reasons over all intermediate frames between adjacent decision steps to retain useful goal-related evidence; and (ii) Evidence-to-Decision, which integrates the current observation with accumulated evidence to ground the target and support the generation of navigation actions or clarification questions. Extensive experiments show that GG-Nav outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in terms of success rates on the HM3D ObjectNav, VL-LN, and CoIN benchmarks by 3.1%, 16.6%, and 5.3%, respectively. Ablation studies further show that accumulating evidence from intermediate observations reduces evidence-missing failures by 11.6%, while explicit grounding reduces stopping errors by 49.4%. We also deploy GG-Nav on a Unitree Go2 robot, demonstrating its zero-shot generalization capability in unseen real-world environments.
authors: Shaohao Zhu, Wensi Huang, Siqi Zhang, Yuqiang Yang, Meng Wei, Chenyang Wan, Tianle Liu, Tai Wang, Jinming Xu
bullets: Identifies insufficient use of intermediate observations and imprecise target localization as key navigation challenges.
Uses supervised fine-tuning to learn a two-stage reasoning process: Observation-to-Evidence and Evidence-to-Decision.
Accumulates goal-relevant evidence across frames, then combines it with current observations to select actions or ask clarification questions.
Reports higher success rates on HM3D ObjectNav, VL-LN, and CoIN, with gains of 3.1%, 16.6%, and 5.3%, respectively.
Ablations link evidence accumulation to fewer evidence-missing failures and explicit grounding to fewer stopping errors; robot deployment demonstrates zero-shot real-world generalization.
papers.selection_reason: Goal-oriented navigation foundation model with VLM grounding chain-of-thought, evaluated on navigation benchmarks and a real robot.
papers.title: GG-Nav: Goal-oriented Grounding Chain-of-Thought Elicits Reasoning in Navigation Foundation Models
papers.tldr: GG-Nav improves goal-oriented navigation by using structured grounding chains of thought to accumulate evidence from streaming observations and localize targets more reliably.

papers.abstract: We present CoPlanVLM, which uses a Vision Language Model (VLM) to translate a single natural-language instruction and image into coordinated paths for a team of two robots. While VLMs offer a flexible, natural-language interface for commanding robot teams, their weak spatial reasoning has greatly limited VLM-based path planning. CoPlanVLM improves the VLM's spatial reasoning and path planning abilities through three components: (1) an image overlay marking both free space and obstacles, (2) task classification that selects the most appropriate low-level planner and reasoning prompt for each instruction, and (3) task-specific chain-of-thought reasoning that prompts the VLM to identify key objects, allocate roles, and verify routes are collision-free before committing to a plan. Together, these components enable the team to complete complex coordinated maneuvers requiring both robots and divide large tasks between robots to increase efficiency. CoPlanVLM also supports detailed maneuvers involving specific routes, loops, and coverage of large areas, as well as tasks requiring directional reasoning such as north/south or left/right. We validate CoPlanVLM in both Gazebo simulation and on physical Turtlebot 4 hardware. CoPlanVLM attains an average success rate of 84.4% compared to 50.0% for the closest baseline. On trials where both methods succeed, CoPlanVLM's paths are 27% shorter on average. Project code is available at https://github.com/AICPS/CoPlanVLM.
authors: David R. Martin, Jared Paquet, Mohammad Abdullah Al Faruque, Pramod Khargonekar, Kyle Volle, J. Humberto Ramos, Scott Nivison
bullets: Addresses weak VLM spatial reasoning for multi-robot path planning.
Uses free-space/obstacle overlays, task classification, and task-specific chain-of-thought reasoning.
Supports role allocation, collision-free route verification, coordinated maneuvers, task division, and directional or coverage-based instructions.
Validated in Gazebo and on Turtlebot 4 hardware, achieving 84.4% average success versus 50.0% for the closest baseline.
When both methods succeed, its paths are 27% shorter on average.
papers.selection_reason: VLM-based coordinated path planning for robot teams with spatial reasoning enhancements from language and image input.
papers.title: CoPlanVLM: Coordinated Path Planning for a Robot Team using Vision Language Models
papers.tldr: CoPlanVLM combines visual overlays, task-specific planning, and structured VLM reasoning to generate coordinated paths for two robots from a single instruction and image.

papers.abstract: Zero-Shot Object Navigation (ZSON) in unknown multi-floor environments presents a significant challenge. Recent methods, mostly based on semantic value greedy waypoint selection, spatial topology-enhanced memory, and Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) as a decision-making framework, have led to improvements. However, these architectures struggle to balance exploration and exploitation for ZSON when encountering unseen environments, especially in multi-floor settings, such as robots getting stuck at narrow intersections, endlessly wandering, or failing to find stair entrances. To overcome these challenges, we propose AERR-Nav, a Zero-Shot Object Navigation framework that dynamically adjusts its state based on the robot's environment. Specifically, AERR-Nav has the following two key advantages: (1) An Adaptive Exploration-Recovery-Reminiscing Strategy, enables robots to dynamically transition between three states, facilitating specialized responses to diverse navigation scenarios. (2) An Adaptive Exploration State featuring Fast and Slow-Thinking modes helps robots better balance exploration, exploitation, and higher-level reasoning based on evolving environmental information. Extensive experiments on the HM3D and MP3D benchmarks demonstrate that our AERR-Nav achieves state-of-the-art performance among zero-shot methods. Comprehensive ablation studies further validate the efficacy of our proposed strategy and modules.
authors: Jingzhi Huang, Junkai Huang, Haoyang Yang, Haoang Li, Yi Wang
bullets: Targets common failures such as getting stuck at narrow intersections, wandering indefinitely, and missing stair entrances.
Uses an Adaptive Exploration-Recovery-Reminiscing Strategy to select navigation states based on environmental conditions.
Its exploration state combines Fast- and Slow-Thinking modes to balance exploration, exploitation, and higher-level reasoning.
Experiments on HM3D and MP3D report state-of-the-art performance among zero-shot methods, with ablations supporting the proposed components.
papers.selection_reason: Zero-shot object navigation with adaptive exploration-recovery-reminiscing and MLLM-based decision-making; directly fits embodied navigation and embodied memory.
papers.title: AERR-Nav: Adaptive Exploration-Recovery-Reminiscing Strategy for Zero-Shot Object Navigation
papers.tldr: AERR-Nav improves zero-shot object navigation in unseen multi-floor environments by adaptively switching among exploration, recovery, and reminiscing behaviors.

papers.abstract: Autonomous Surface Vehicles (ASVs) are increasingly expected to operate in ports and harbour environments, where operators may specify navigation targets through language-based descriptions rather than predefined coordinates or fixed target identifiers. However, existing ASV navigation methods mainly execute predefined geometric goals or task-specific objectives and give limited attention to language-grounded target specification. This study proposes Semantically Grounded Navigation (SGNav), a framework that enables an ASV to identify and approach a maritime target from an operator-provided description. SGNav integrates text-guided semantic grounding, harbour-aware candidate filtering, CLIP-based semantic verification, grounded target control-state construction, and Proximal Policy Optimisation-based closed-loop control. It grounds the target description in onboard RGB observations, suppresses visually or semantically irrelevant distractors, and converts the selected target into a compact control-oriented representation for policy execution. Experiments in simulated port environments show that SGNav achieves success rates of $97.0\pm1.2\%$, $92.0\pm1.5\%$, and $90.0\pm1.8\%$ across three representative target-reaching tasks, with semantic target accuracy above $97\%$ and wrong-target rates below $3\%$. SGNav also maintains $97.7$--$98.7\%$ success rates across held-out port layouts. In the Task~3 ablation study, removing harbour-aware filtering or semantic consistency reduces the success rate to $40.4\pm2.6\%$ and $50.4\pm3.1\%$, respectively. These findings demonstrate the importance of semantic grounding, harbour-aware filtering, and semantic verification for reliable language-grounded ASV navigation. These results indicate that the proposed perception-to-control framework can support language-grounded target approach manoeuvres of ASV under the complex port environments.
bullets: Addresses the gap between language-specified navigation targets and conventional coordinate- or task-based ASV navigation.
Uses text-guided grounding, harbour-aware candidate filtering, CLIP-based verification, and PPO control from RGB observations.
Achieves 90.0–97.0% success across three simulated port tasks, with over 97% semantic target accuracy and under 3% wrong-target rates.
Maintains 97.7–98.7% success on held-out port layouts.
Ablations show substantial degradation without harbour-aware filtering or semantic consistency, indicating their importance.
papers.selection_reason: Language-grounded semantic target navigation for autonomous surface vehicles.
papers.title: Language-Grounded Semantic Target Navigation for Autonomous Surface Vehicles
papers.tldr: SGNav enables autonomous surface vehicles to navigate to maritime targets described in natural language by combining semantic perception, target verification, and closed-loop control.

papers.abstract: Multimodal AI, powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs), is transforming assistive technologies by enabling simultaneous processing of visual and textual data. This advancement holds significant promise for over 43 million visually impaired and neuro-divergent individuals worldwide who face persistent challenges in navigating indoor and outdoor environments due to limited spatial awareness and insufficient environmental cues. Existing navigation aids often lack comprehensive 3D scene understanding, relying on constrained route-based strategies that hinder user autonomy. In this paper, we introduce a novel end-to-end framework that integrates LLMs, VLMs and digital twin technologies to deliver a spatially cognitive navigation support for visually impaired and neuro-divergent users. Our system captures video input via standard mobile phone cameras, and employs SLAM3R to generate dense 3D point clouds from monocular RGB sequences in real-time. Our custom post-processing algorithm ensures accurate point cloud alignment across multiple viewpoints without requiring predefined reference points. This enhances the capabilities of SpatialLM to produce structured 3D representations, including architectural elements and oriented object bounding boxes. The enriched spatial data is then processed by a locally deployed LLM, which interprets 3D contexts to generate detailed scene descriptions and precise distance measurements between users and surrounding objects. We evaluated our approach across diverse video scenarios featuring various perspectives, looped walking views and captured in multiple environments. The evaluation results demonstrate consistent accuracy in 3D scene interpretation and object localisation, underscoring the potential of our system as a transformative assistive navigation solution that combines advanced visual perception with spatial reasoning
bullets: Addresses the limited spatial awareness and environmental cues provided by conventional route-based navigation aids.
Uses monocular video, SLAM3R, and custom point-cloud alignment to construct dense, consistent 3D environments without predefined reference points.
Extends SpatialLM with structured representations of architectural elements and oriented object bounding boxes.
A locally deployed LLM converts 3D context into scene descriptions and user-to-object distance estimates.
Evaluation across varied viewpoints, walking sequences, and environments reports consistent 3D scene interpretation and object-localisation accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Integrates VLMs and LLMs for spatial cognition and navigation of visually impaired users, utilizing 3D scene understanding.
papers.title: Assisted Spatial Cognition Through Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: A mobile-camera system combines VLMs, LLMs, SLAM, and digital twins to build 3D scene understanding for more autonomous navigation by visually impaired and neuro-divergent users.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) in unseen indoor environments is useful in real-world robotics, where an agent must follow natural-language instructions, locate objects, and answer spatial questions without a pre-built map or fixed object vocabulary. Multimodal vision-language models (VLMs) provide strong open-vocabulary grounding and zero-shot reasoning, but struggle to emit reliable metric quantities such as range, bearing, and comparative spatial relations directly from images. Existing approaches address this by folding geometry into hand-engineered pipelines or asking models to output waypoints, requiring changes to the control stack for different robots, tasks, or vocabularies. We introduce AnchorVLN, an open-vocabulary VLN system built on a simple rule: the VLM proposes semantics; geometry decides metrics. It is realised as EMBODIED-NAV-MCP, a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server driven by a VLM agent through a compact set of callable tools. Since no tool accepts distance in metres or bearing in radians, the schema enforces the semantic-geometry boundary without modifying the downstream autonomy stack. We benchmark both tasks of the CMU Vision-Language Navigation Challenge 2026: 30 instruction-following questions over 15 scenes and a frozen 45-question object-reference set. The full system achieves 64.4 percent on instruction following, dropping by 13.3 percentage points without controller modeling (t = 2.77). On object reference, geometric anchoring clears the challenge overlap threshold on 10 of 45 questions, versus 0 of 45 for direct coordinate estimation, reducing median center error from 3.37 m to 2.48 m.
bullets: Targets VLN in unseen indoor environments without pre-built maps or fixed object vocabularies.
